translation: And if a woman fears from her husband contempt or aversion, there is no blame upon them if they reconcile between themselves with an amicable settlement, and reconciliation is best.  And souls are predisposed to avarice. But if you do good and fear Allah, then indeed Allah is ever, with what you do, Acquainted.
interpretation: This verse addresses marital discord, specifically when a wife perceives her husband's behavior as displaying contempt (nushooz, often translated as rebellion or ill-treatment) or aversion/turning away (i'raad).  It promotes reconciliation and amicable settlement between the spouses when such situations arise.  It emphasizes that there's no blame on either party for seeking such a resolution, indicating that taking initiative for reconciliation is encouraged, even if the issue originates from the husband's side. The verse highlights that reconciliation and amicable settlement (sulh) are the preferred course of action, literally stating that "sulh is best."  It acknowledges the human tendency towards selfishness and greed (shuhh), which can hinder compromise and forgiveness. However, it reminds us that if the spouses act righteously (ihsan) and maintain God-consciousness (taqwa) during this process, Allah is fully aware of their efforts and will reward them accordingly.  This verse provides guidance on conflict resolution within marriage, emphasizing mutual understanding, compromise, and the importance of seeking peaceful solutions rooted in righteousness and awareness of God.
orig: وإن امرأة خافت من بعلها نشوزا أو إعراضا فلا جناح عليهما أن يصلحا بينهما صلحا والصلح خير وأحضرت الأنفس الشح وإن تحسنوا وتتقوا فإن الله كان بما تعملون خبيرا

translation: And you will never be able to be perfectly just between wives, even if you strive to do so. So do not incline completely [to one] and leave another hanging. And if you reconcile and fear Allah, then indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse addresses the complexities of polygyny, permitted in Islam under specific conditions. It acknowledges the inherent difficulty, even impossibility, of treating multiple wives with absolute equality in terms of emotions and affection.  The Arabic word "تعدلوا" (ta'diloo) refers to perfect justice, particularly in matters of the heart. The verse doesn't negate fairness in providing materially for all wives, which is obligatory, but recognizes the human inability to perfectly balance love and emotional intimacy.  Therefore, it cautions against extreme favoritism, symbolized by "inclining completely" to one wife and leaving the other "hanging"—in a state of emotional neglect and uncertainty.  The verse encourages striving for fairness and emphasizes the importance of reconciliation and God-consciousness (taqwa) within the marriage. It ultimately offers hope and reassurance that God is forgiving and merciful, acknowledging the human struggle in navigating these complex relationships. It's important to note that this verse is often discussed in conjunction with other verses relating to marriage and justice, and is interpreted within the broader context of Islamic teachings promoting kindness, respect, and responsibility in all relationships.
orig: ولن تستطيعوا أن تعدلوا بين النساء ولو حرصتم فلا تميلوا كل الميل فتذروها كالمعلقة وإن تصلحوا وتتقوا فإن الله كان غفورا رحيما

translation: And if they separate, Allah will enrich each [of them] from His abundance. And Allah is Ever-Expanding and Wise.
interpretation: This verse (most commonly understood in the context of divorce) speaks to God's provision and care even in situations of separation or hardship.  The Arabic word "يتفرقا" (yatafarraqaa) primarily means to separate or disperse, and while often applied to divorce, it can also refer to other forms of parting ways.  The verse assures that if two people separate, God's bounty is sufficient for both.  "يغن الله كلا من سعته" (yughni Allahu kullan min sa'atihi) means that God will enrich each of them from His bounty, according to their needs and circumstances. The word "سعته" (sa'atihi) refers to God's ample provision, but it also implies that the enrichment will be tailored to each individual's specific situation.  God doesn't simply provide equally, but rather in a way that is most beneficial for each person. The verse concludes with the attributes of God as "واسعا" (Wasi'an - Ever-Expanding, All-Encompassing) and "حكيما" (Hakiman - Wise). This emphasizes that God's resources are limitless, and His distribution of those resources is governed by perfect wisdom.  He knows what is best for each individual and will provide accordingly, even in seemingly difficult circumstances like separation. This offers comfort and reassurance, reminding individuals that they are not alone and will be provided for, even when facing life's challenges.
orig: وإن يتفرقا يغن الله كلا من سعته وكان الله واسعا حكيما

translation: To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth. And We certainly instructed those who were given the Scripture before you, and you [as well], to be conscious of Allah. But if you disbelieve - then to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth. And Allah is Free of need and Praiseworthy.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute sovereignty of God over all creation, both in the heavens and on earth.  It highlights that this dominion isn't affected by human belief or disbelief. The verse reminds both Muslims and those of previous Abrahamic faiths (Jews and Christians, who received scriptures) of the fundamental command to have Taqwa (God-consciousness, piety, reverence).  This Taqwa implies living in awareness of God's presence and adhering to His guidance.  The repetition of God's ownership of everything reinforces the point that even if humanity chooses to disbelieve, it doesn't diminish His power or possession.  Disbelief only harms the disbelievers themselves.  The verse concludes by describing God as 'Ghaniyy' (Free of need, self-sufficient) and 'Hameed' (Praiseworthy), indicating that He isn't dependent on human belief for His existence or perfection, and is always deserving of praise regardless of human actions.
orig: ولله ما في السماوات وما في الأرض ولقد وصينا الذين أوتوا الكتاب من قبلكم وإياكم أن اتقوا الله وإن تكفروا فإن لله ما في السماوات وما في الأرض وكان الله غنيا حميدا

translation: And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.
interpretation: This verse asserts God's absolute sovereignty and ownership over all of creation, both in the heavens and on earth.  Everything that exists, visible and invisible, animate and inanimate, belongs to Him.  The phrase "وكفى بالله وكيلا" (wa kafā biLlāhi wakīlā) emphasizes God's role as the ultimate trustee, guardian, and manager of all affairs.  It conveys the idea that God is not only the owner but also the perfect administrator of the universe.  He is completely capable of managing and controlling everything, and believers should trust in His wisdom and power.  This verse encourages reliance on God and surrender to His will, knowing that He is in control and everything ultimately belongs to Him. It instills a sense of peace and security in the believer, understanding that even amidst life's uncertainties, God is the ultimate caretaker and disposer of all things.
orig: ولله ما في السماوات وما في الأرض وكفى بالله وكيلا

translation: If He wills, He can do away with you, O people, and bring others; and Allah is over that [all] able.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's absolute power and authority over creation.  It highlights the contingent nature of human existence and reminds humanity of its dependence on God's will.  God can, if He chooses, replace the current generation with another.  This isn't necessarily a threat of punishment, but rather a statement of fact about God's omnipotence and the transient nature of earthly life. It encourages humility and discourages arrogance, reminding us that our existence is a gift and not a right. The verse can also be understood as a call to responsibility, suggesting that if people fail to fulfill their purpose or become corrupt, God has the power to replace them with others who will.  The mention of God's ability (قديرا) reinforces the idea that this replacement wouldn't be a difficult task for Him, further emphasizing His unlimited power.
orig: إن يشأ يذهبكم أيها الناس ويأت بآخرين وكان الله على ذلك قديرا

translation: Whoever desires the reward of this world, then with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the nature of reward and God's encompassing knowledge and power.  It addresses those who primarily seek worldly gains, reminding them that true and lasting reward ultimately resides with God. While acknowledging that worldly rewards can be attained, the verse emphasizes that God provides both worldly and otherworldly rewards (those of the Hereafter). This implies that seeking worldly rewards exclusively is a shortsighted approach, as God holds the keys to both realms.  Furthermore, the verse's conclusion, "And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing," reinforces God's complete awareness of our intentions and actions. He understands our desires, whether they are focused on the immediate or the eternal, and will ultimately dispense rewards accordingly.  Therefore, it encourages believers to align their intentions with the ultimate reward of the Hereafter, even while pursuing legitimate worldly goals, recognizing that God is the source of all blessings, both temporal and eternal.
orig: من كان يريد ثواب الدنيا فعند الله ثواب الدنيا والآخرة وكان الله سميعا بصيرا

translation: O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives. Whether one is rich or poor, Allah is more worthy of both. So follow not [personal] inclination, lest you not be just. And if you distort [your testimony] or refuse [to give it], then indeed Allah is ever, with what you do, Acquainted.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the paramount importance of upholding justice and truthfulness, even when it's difficult.  It calls upon believers to be steadfast in their commitment to justice (qawameen bil qist), acting as witnesses for God's truth regardless of personal relationships or worldly considerations.  Even if testifying against oneself, one's parents, or close relatives, justice must prevail. This demonstrates the absolute nature of truth and its precedence over personal loyalties. The verse also highlights God's ultimate authority and care for all, rich or poor, emphasizing that He is more concerned with their well-being than any human.  Therefore, personal desires (hawa) should not influence our pursuit of justice. Any deviation from truth, whether through twisting testimony or refusing to bear witness, is known to God, who is all-knowing (Khabeer) and will hold us accountable.  This verse serves as a powerful reminder of the responsibility that comes with faith – a responsibility to prioritize justice above all else, recognizing that true justice aligns with God's will and leads to a more righteous society.
orig: يا أيها الذين آمنوا كونوا قوامين بالقسط شهداء لله ولو على أنفسكم أو الوالدين والأقربين إن يكن غنيا أو فقيرا فالله أولى بهما فلا تتبعوا الهوى أن تعدلوا وإن تلووا أو تعرضوا فإن الله كان بما تعملون خبيرا

translation: O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger and the Book that He sent down upon His Messenger, and the Scripture which He sent down before. And whoever disbelieves in Allah , His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day has certainly gone far astray.
interpretation: This verse is a powerful call to reaffirm faith and a stern warning against disbelief. It emphasizes the interconnectedness of belief in God, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and the divine scriptures, including both the Quran and previous revelations like the Torah, Psalms, and Gospel.  The verse begins by addressing believers, implying that even those who profess faith need constant reminders and reinforcement.  It highlights the comprehensive nature of Islamic belief, encompassing not just God but also His messengers, His angels who carry out His commands, the divine books which contain His guidance, and the belief in the Day of Judgment. The final part of the verse underscores the severity of disbelief in these core tenets, describing it as a profound and far-reaching deviation from the truth.  Essentially, this verse serves as a foundational statement on the fundamental articles of faith in Islam and the consequences of rejecting them.
orig: يا أيها الذين آمنوا آمنوا بالله ورسوله والكتاب الذي نزل على رسوله والكتاب الذي أنزل من قبل ومن يكفر بالله وملائكته وكتبه ورسله واليوم الآخر فقد ضل ضلالا بعيدا

translation: Indeed, those who believe and then disbelieve, then believe and then disbelieve, then increase in disbelief - never will Allah forgive them, nor will He guide them to a way.
interpretation: This verse addresses the issue of repeated apostasy, a grave matter in Islam.  It speaks specifically of those who cycle through belief and disbelief, not merely wavering in faith due to doubts or temptations, but consciously and willfully rejecting faith after accepting it, and then reinforcing their disbelief over time.  The key phrase here is "then increase in disbelief" (ثم ازدادوا كفرا). This suggests a hardening of the heart and a deliberate turning away from God, compounding the initial act of disbelief with further acts that solidify their rejection.  The verse states that God will neither forgive such individuals nor guide them. This is not to say God is incapable of forgiveness, but rather that their persistent and escalating rejection of faith makes them unreceptive to divine guidance and mercy.  It's important to distinguish this from someone who struggles with doubts and seeks guidance.  This verse pertains to those who embrace faith, then reject it, then perhaps return momentarily only to reject it again more forcefully, demonstrating a clear pattern of increasing rejection and a hardening of the heart against God.  Their actions demonstrate a rejection of the very principle of faith, making forgiveness and guidance impossible in their chosen state.
orig: إن الذين آمنوا ثم كفروا ثم آمنوا ثم كفروا ثم ازدادوا كفرا لم يكن الله ليغفر لهم ولا ليهديهم سبيلا

translation: Give the hypocrites the good news that there is for them a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse addresses the hypocrites, those who outwardly professed Islam during the Prophet Muhammad's time but inwardly harbored disbelief and ill intentions.  The Arabic word "بشر" (bashshir), often translated as "give good news," is used ironically here.  It's not good news in the conventional sense, but rather a forewarning of the severe consequences of their hypocrisy.  The "painful punishment" (عذابا أليما - 'athaban alima) refers to the punishment in the Hereafter, highlighting the gravity of their deceptive actions. This verse serves as both a warning to the hypocrites and a reassurance to the true believers that hypocrisy will not go unpunished. It emphasizes the importance of sincerity and genuine faith in Islam.
orig: بشر المنافقين بأن لهم عذابا أليما

translation: Those who take disbelievers as allies instead of the believers - do they seek power with them? Verily, all power belongs to Allah.
interpretation: This verse condemns the act of Muslims seeking alliances and protection from non-believers, prioritizing them over fellow believers.  It emphasizes that true power and authority reside solely with God (Allah).  Seeking worldly strength or influence through alliances with those who reject faith is a misguided pursuit, as it implies a lack of trust in God's ultimate power and plan.  It signifies a misplaced reliance on worldly sources of support rather than faith and the strength of the believing community. The verse serves as a reminder that true strength and honor come from God alone, and believers should seek support and alliance primarily within their own community, placing their trust in God above all else.
orig: الذين يتخذون الكافرين أولياء من دون المؤمنين أيبتغون عندهم العزة فإن العزة لله جميعا

translation: It has already been revealed to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of Allah being disbelieved in and mocked at, do not sit with them until they engage in a discussion other than that. Indeed, you would then be like them. Indeed Allah will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers in Hell, all together.
interpretation:
This verse addresses the proper conduct of believers when encountering those who mock or deny the verses of God (Allah).  It instructs Muslims to avoid remaining in the company of people who actively engage in such behavior until the conversation shifts to a different topic. The reasoning behind this instruction is twofold:

1. **Preservation of Faith:**  Remaining present while God's message is being ridiculed risks weakening one's own faith and potentially normalizing such disrespectful behavior. It creates an environment conducive to doubt and can lead to the believer being negatively influenced.

2. **Dissociation from Disbelief:**  By leaving the company of those who mock God's verses, believers demonstrate their disapproval of such behavior and distance themselves from it.  This act serves as a form of protest and reinforces the sanctity of the divine message. The verse emphasizes that staying in such company makes one "like them" in the eyes of God, implying complicity or tacit approval of their actions.

Finally, the verse concludes with a strong warning. It states that God will ultimately gather both the hypocrites (those who outwardly profess faith but harbor disbelief in their hearts) and the outright disbelievers together in Hell. This serves as a reminder of the serious consequences of disbelief and the importance of upholding and respecting God's message.
orig: وقد نزل عليكم في الكتاب أن إذا سمعتم آيات الله يكفر بها ويستهزأ بها فلا تقعدوا معهم حتى يخوضوا في حديث غيره إنكم إذا مثلهم إن الله جامع المنافقين والكافرين في جهنم جميعا

translation: Those who wait and watch concerning you: if you gain a victory from Allah, they say, "Were we not with you?" But if the disbelievers gain a share (of victory), they say (to them), "Did we not gain the upper hand over you and defend you from the believers?" So Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection. And Allah will never grant the disbelievers any way (of dominance) over the believers.
interpretation: This verse describes the hypocritical behavior of certain individuals during the early Muslim community in Medina. These people were not truly committed to the Islamic cause but rather sought personal gain and safety. Their loyalty shifted depending on the prevailing circumstances. If the Muslims were victorious, they would feign support and claim to have been part of the struggle. However, if the disbelievers gained an advantage, they would quickly switch sides, even boasting about protecting the disbelievers from the Muslims. This verse highlights the importance of sincere faith and condemns opportunistic behavior.  It emphasizes that true allegiance lies with God and the believers, and that those who prioritize self-interest and betray their community will ultimately face divine judgment. The verse also carries a message of hope and assurance for the believers, affirming that God will not allow the disbelievers to ultimately triumph over them.
orig: الذين يتربصون بكم فإن كان لكم فتح من الله قالوا ألم نكن معكم وإن كان للكافرين نصيب قالوا ألم نستحوذ عليكم ونمنعكم من المؤمنين فالله يحكم بينكم يوم القيامة ولن يجعل الله للكافرين على المؤمنين سبيلا

translation: Indeed, the hypocrites [think to] deceive Allah, but He is deceiving them. And when they stand for prayer, they stand lazily, showing off to the people and not remembering Allah except a little.
interpretation: This verse delves into the nature of hypocrisy, specifically concerning prayer.  It highlights the self-deception of hypocrites who believe they can fool God by feigning piety.  Their outward actions contradict their inner state. They perform prayer lackadaisically, motivated by a desire to be seen as righteous by others (riyaa') rather than genuine devotion to God.  Their hearts are distant, and their remembrance of God during prayer is minimal.  The verse underscores the futility of their attempts at deception, emphasizing that God is fully aware of their true intentions and will ultimately hold them accountable.  It serves as a warning against outward displays of faith that lack sincerity and inner connection with the Divine.
orig: إن المنافقين يخادعون الله وهو خادعهم وإذا قاموا إلى الصلاة قاموا كسالى يراءون الناس ولا يذكرون الله إلا قليلا

translation: Wavering between that [faith and disbelief], belonging neither to these nor to those. And whoever Allah leaves astray - never will you find for him a way.
interpretation: This verse describes the precarious state of those who are indecisive in their faith, caught between belief and disbelief. They are neither fully committed to the believers nor the disbelievers, constantly wavering and lacking conviction.  They attempt to please both sides, ultimately belonging to neither.  This lack of commitment and clarity leaves them susceptible to misguidance. The verse concludes by emphasizing the profound consequence of this indecision: if God allows someone to stray due to their own unwillingness to choose the right path, no one can guide them back. This highlights the importance of sincere faith and resolute commitment to truth.  It's not enough to simply straddle the fence; true guidance requires a conscious and firm decision to follow the path of righteousness.  The "way" mentioned here refers not only to physical guidance but also to spiritual and intellectual clarity, which becomes unattainable for those who deliberately choose to remain lost in ambiguity.
orig: مذبذبين بين ذلك لا إلى هؤلاء ولا إلى هؤلاء ومن يضلل الله فلن تجد له سبيلا

translation: O you who have believed, do not take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Do you wish to give Allah a clear authority against yourselves?
interpretation: This verse addresses believers and warns them against taking disbelievers as close confidants and allies in preference to fellow believers.  The Arabic term "Awliya" (أولياء) implies close allies, protectors, or those to whom one turns for support and counsel. The verse emphasizes that such alliances with disbelievers, particularly when they come at the expense of relationships with believers, constitute a betrayal of faith and provide "clear authority" or evidence (Sultanan Mubeena - سلطانا مبينا) against the believers in the eyes of God. This evidence could refer to a demonstration of hypocrisy or a weakening of the Muslim community by aligning with those who may oppose its values and interests.  The rhetorical question at the end of the verse underscores the seriousness of this transgression, suggesting that such actions are detrimental to the believers themselves and their standing before God.  It doesn't necessarily prohibit general interaction with disbelievers in everyday life or business dealings, but rather cautions against forming deep alliances and prioritizing them over the bonds of faith.
orig: يا أيها الذين آمنوا لا تتخذوا الكافرين أولياء من دون المؤمنين أتريدون أن تجعلوا لله عليكم سلطانا مبينا

translation: Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire, and you will never find for them a helper.
interpretation: This verse speaks about the severe punishment awaiting hypocrites in the afterlife.  "Hypocrites" (munafiqun) in the Quranic context refers to those who outwardly professed Islam but inwardly harbored disbelief and malice. Their hypocrisy is considered a grave sin because it represents a betrayal of trust and a corruption of faith from within.  "The lowest depths of the Fire" (al-dark al-asfal min an-nar) signifies the most intense and humiliating level of punishment in Hell, reserved for the worst offenders.  The phrase "and you will never find for them a helper" (wa lan tajida lahum nasiran) emphasizes the utter desolation and hopelessness of their situation.  No one will be able to intercede or alleviate their suffering. This verse serves as a stern warning against hypocrisy and emphasizes the importance of sincerity and genuine faith in God.
orig: إن المنافقين في الدرك الأسفل من النار ولن تجد لهم نصيرا

translation: Except for those who repent, reform, hold fast to Allah, and dedicate their religion sincerely to Allah.  Those will be with the believers, and Allah will give the believers a great reward.
interpretation:
This verse outlines the path to forgiveness and attaining a place among the believers deserving of God's great reward. It emphasizes four crucial actions:

1. **Repentance (تابوا):**  This signifies a genuine turning away from past sins and wrongdoing. It involves acknowledging one's mistakes, feeling remorse, and making a firm commitment to change one's behavior.

2. **Reform (وأصلحوا):**  This goes beyond mere repentance. It involves actively correcting past wrongs and making amends where possible.  It also implies striving to live a righteous life, performing good deeds, and avoiding future sins. This shows a commitment to positive change, not just regret.

3. **Holding fast to Allah (واعتصموا بالله):** This means clinging firmly to Allah's guidance and seeking refuge in Him. It implies trusting in His promises, adhering to His commands, and seeking His help in staying on the right path. This demonstrates a dependence on God for strength and guidance.

4. **Sincerity in religion (وأخلصوا دينهم لله):** This means dedicating one's faith and actions solely to Allah, without any ulterior motives or seeking the approval of others. It emphasizes pure intention and sincerity in worship and all aspects of religious life. This highlights the importance of internalizing faith and making it a guiding principle in all aspects of life.

The verse then assures those who fulfill these conditions that they will be considered among the true believers and will receive a great reward from Allah. This reward is not explicitly defined, leaving it open to encompass the blessings of both this world and the hereafter. The greatness of the reward underscores the significance of these four actions in achieving spiritual fulfillment and divine favor.
orig: إلا الذين تابوا وأصلحوا واعتصموا بالله وأخلصوا دينهم لله فأولئك مع المؤمنين وسوف يؤت الله المؤمنين أجرا عظيما

translation: What would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful and believe? And Allah is Appreciative, All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse highlights the relationship between human gratitude, faith, and divine mercy. It poses a rhetorical question, implying that Allah has no need to punish those who are genuinely thankful for His blessings and maintain their belief in Him.  "Shukr" (gratitude) here isn't merely expressing thanks, but also actively demonstrating it through obedience and righteous actions.  "Iman" (belief) signifies a deep-seated conviction that shapes one's life. Allah's attributes of "Shakir" (Appreciative) and "Alim" (All-Knowing) are emphasized.  He appreciates and acknowledges even the smallest acts of gratitude and faith, as He is fully aware of the sincerity of our hearts and actions. Therefore, this verse encourages believers to cultivate gratitude and strengthen their faith, assuring them that Allah responds to such positive attributes with mercy and forgiveness, not punishment. It suggests that punishment is a consequence of ungratefulness and disbelief, not something Allah inflicts arbitrarily.
orig: ما يفعل الله بعذابكم إن شكرتم وآمنتم وكان الله شاكرا عليما

translation: Allah does not like that evil should be uttered in public except by one who has been wronged. And ever is Allah, Hearing and Knowing.
interpretation: This verse highlights the Islamic emphasis on speaking kindly and avoiding public complaints or backbiting.  Generally, airing grievances openly is discouraged as it can lead to further discord and damage reputations.  However, the verse makes an important exception for those who have been wronged or oppressed. They are permitted to speak out and seek justice for the wrong they have suffered.  This exception recognizes that silence in the face of injustice can perpetuate harm and allows for victims to seek redress. The concluding phrase, "And ever is Allah, Hearing and Knowing," emphasizes God's awareness of all things, both the spoken and the unspoken. This serves as a reminder that even if someone is unjustly silenced, God is aware of their suffering and will ultimately judge with fairness.  It also implies a warning against false accusations, as God knows the truth of every situation.
orig: لا يحب الله الجهر بالسوء من القول إلا من ظلم وكان الله سميعا عليما

translation: If you disclose [acts of] good or conceal them or pardon [people for] evil, then indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning and Competent.
interpretation:
This verse highlights the divine attributes of Allah's forgiveness and power, while also encouraging virtuous behavior in humans. It presents three scenarios related to good deeds and dealing with wrongdoing:

1. **Disclosing good deeds (إن تبدوا خيرا):** While humility is encouraged in Islam, publicly showcasing good deeds can inspire others and serve as a positive example. This doesn't imply showing off or seeking praise, but rather demonstrating good actions openly when appropriate. 

2. **Concealing good deeds (أو تخفوه):** This emphasizes the importance of sincerity in good deeds.  Concealing charitable acts, for instance, protects the dignity of the recipient and avoids any ostentation on the part of the giver. It fosters a purer intention, solely for God's pleasure.

3. **Pardoning evil (أو تعفوا عن سوء):**  This encourages forgiveness and overlooking the faults of others. It highlights the value of mercy and compassion, promoting reconciliation and peaceful coexistence. Forgiveness is a powerful tool for personal and societal well-being. 

The verse concludes by affirming that Allah is "عفوا قديرا" (Ever-Pardoning and Competent). This implies that regardless of our actions - whether we disclose good, conceal it, or forgive others - Allah's forgiveness is all-encompassing.  "قديرا" (Competent) emphasizes His absolute power and authority. He is capable of both punishing wrong and forgiving it, showcasing his mercy and justice.  Ultimately, the verse encourages us to emulate God's attribute of forgiveness in our own lives and reminds us of His infinite mercy.
orig: إن تبدوا خيرا أو تخفوه أو تعفوا عن سوء فإن الله كان عفوا قديرا

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers and wish to make distinction between Allah and His messengers and say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in some," and wish to adopt a way in between -
interpretation: This verse condemns a hypocritical attitude towards faith. It describes those who claim to believe in God (Allah) but selectively reject some of His messengers.  This partial acceptance is seen as a form of disbelief because it undermines the fundamental principle of divine unity and the interconnectedness of God's message through His various prophets.  The verse highlights the flawed logic of trying to create a middle ground between belief and disbelief, attempting to pick and choose convenient aspects of faith while rejecting others.  It underscores that true faith requires complete acceptance of God's will and recognition of all His messengers as legitimate conduits of divine revelation. This 'path in between' they seek is a path of delusion, ultimately a rejection of God's complete and unified message.
orig: إن الذين يكفرون بالله ورسله ويريدون أن يفرقوا بين الله ورسله ويقولون نؤمن ببعض ونكفر ببعض ويريدون أن يتخذوا بين ذلك سبيلا

translation: Those are the true disbelievers, and for the disbelievers We have prepared a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: This verse definitively declares certain individuals as "true disbelievers" (الكافرون حقا). The term "true disbelievers" emphasizes the firmness and certainty of their disbelief, suggesting a persistent rejection of truth despite clarity and evidence.  It distinguishes them from those who may harbor doubts or be temporarily misguided.  The verse then states that a "humiliating punishment" (عذابا مهينا) has been prepared for such disbelievers. This punishment isn't merely physical pain, but includes the disgrace and degradation that comes with the realization of their error after death, when it's too late for repentance. The use of the divine "We" (أعتدنا) emphasizes God's absolute authority and justice in dispensing this punishment.  The verse serves as a stern warning about the consequences of persistent disbelief and the importance of seeking truth and guidance.
orig: أولئك هم الكافرون حقا وأعتدنا للكافرين عذابا مهينا

translation: And those who believe in Allah and His messengers and do not differentiate between any of them - to those He will give their rewards. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the importance of believing in all of God's messengers without making distinctions or showing favoritism towards some over others.  It highlights the concept of inclusivity in faith, recognizing the interconnectedness of the divine message brought forth by various prophets throughout history.  Believing in some messengers while rejecting or diminishing others is presented as a sign of incomplete faith. The verse promises divine rewards to those who maintain this comprehensive belief.  It concludes by reiterating God's attributes of forgiveness and mercy, suggesting that even those who have previously made distinctions may still find divine grace if they embrace the principle of accepting all messengers.
orig: والذين آمنوا بالله ورسله ولم يفرقوا بين أحد منهم أولئك سوف يؤتيهم أجورهم وكان الله غفورا رحيما

translation: The People of the Scripture ask you to bring down to them a book from the heaven. But they had asked of Moses even greater than that, saying, "Show us Allah openly." So the thunderbolt struck them for their wrongdoing. Then they took [for worship] the calf after clear proofs had come to them. And We pardoned that. And We gave Moses clear authority.
interpretation: This verse addresses a demand from the People of the Scripture (Jews and Christians) for a miraculous sign from the Prophet Muhammad, specifically a book descending from heaven. The verse highlights the hypocrisy and persistent doubt of these people by reminding them of a similar demand made by their own ancestors to Moses.  They not only asked for a book but went even further, demanding to see God directly.  This audacious request, born from their disbelief and arrogance, resulted in divine punishment – they were struck by lightning.  Despite this punishment, and even after receiving clear evidence of God's power and oneness through other miracles, they continued to stray, worshipping a golden calf.  The verse emphasizes God's mercy by stating that He forgave even this transgression.  Furthermore, it underscores Moses's authentic prophethood and God-given authority, highlighting the consistency of divine guidance and the recurring pattern of rejection by some despite receiving clear signs.
orig: يسألك أهل الكتاب أن تنزل عليهم كتابا من السماء فقد سألوا موسى أكبر من ذلك فقالوا أرنا الله جهرة فأخذتهم الصاعقة بظلمهم ثم اتخذوا العجل من بعد ما جاءتهم البينات فعفونا عن ذلك وآتينا موسى سلطانا مبينا

translation: And We raised over them the Mount as a sign of their covenant, and We said to them, "Enter the gate prostrating yourselves," and We said to them, "Do not transgress on the Sabbath," and We took from them a firm covenant.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Israelites and God's covenant with them at Mount Sinai.  "Raising the Mount over them" is generally interpreted metaphorically as a demonstration of God's power and the seriousness of the covenant being made.  The commands to "enter the gate prostrating" and "not transgress on the Sabbath" are specific stipulations within this covenant, emphasizing humility before God and observance of His laws. The "firm covenant" highlights the solemnity and binding nature of the agreement between God and the Israelites.  It signifies the weight of responsibility placed upon them to adhere to its terms and the potential consequences of breaking it.
orig: ورفعنا فوقهم الطور بميثاقهم وقلنا لهم ادخلوا الباب سجدا وقلنا لهم لا تعدوا في السبت وأخذنا منهم ميثاقا غليظا

translation: So because they broke their covenant and disbelieved in the signs of Allah and killed the prophets without right and said, "Our hearts are wrapped [i.e., sealed]", rather, Allah has sealed them because of their disbelief, so they believe not, except for a few.
interpretation:
This verse describes the reasons for the spiritual blindness and disbelief of a specific group of people.  It highlights their transgressions, which led to their hearts becoming sealed. These transgressions include:

1. **Breaking their covenant:** This refers to breaking their agreement with God, likely through disobedience and abandoning their religious obligations.  This demonstrates a lack of commitment and trustworthiness.

2. **Disbelieving in the signs of Allah:**  This indicates a rejection of the evidence and guidance provided by God, choosing instead to ignore or deny the truth. This reveals a closed-mindedness and resistance to divine wisdom.

3. **Killing the prophets without right:** This represents the ultimate form of rejection, as the prophets were messengers of God, sent to guide humanity. Killing them signifies a defiance against God's authority and a disregard for human life.

4. **Saying, "Our hearts are wrapped [i.e., sealed]":** This is a defensive statement, suggesting that their hearts are impervious to truth and understanding. However, the verse clarifies that it is not a natural state but a consequence of their actions. 

The phrase "rather, Allah has sealed them because of their disbelief" emphasizes that their hearts are sealed as a divine consequence of their continuous rejection of truth. This seal is not a physical barrier but a spiritual one, preventing them from accepting faith. The result is that only a few among them will believe.

Overall, the verse highlights the connection between actions and spiritual state.  Continuous disobedience and rejection of truth lead to a hardening of the heart, making it difficult to accept faith. It serves as a warning against the dangers of such behavior and the importance of upholding covenants, believing in God's signs, and respecting His messengers.
orig: فبما نقضهم ميثاقهم وكفرهم بآيات الله وقتلهم الأنبياء بغير حق وقولهم قلوبنا غلف بل طبع الله عليها بكفرهم فلا يؤمنون إلا قليلا

translation: And [We cursed them] for their disbelief and their saying against Mary a great slander
interpretation: This verse refers to the false accusations made against Mary, the mother of Jesus.  The specific slander, though not explicitly mentioned in this verse, is understood by Muslim commentators to be the accusation of fornication and illegitimacy directed at Jesus' birth. The verse condemns those who disbelieved in God's message and slandered Mary, highlighting the gravity of their transgression.  The "great slander" (بهتانا عظيما) emphasizes the enormity of the false accusation, both in its nature and its consequences.  It points to the injustice of accusing a righteous woman of such a grave sin and the damage such accusations can inflict on an individual's reputation and honor. The verse also connects this slander with disbelief (كفرهم), suggesting that rejecting God's truth and spreading falsehoods are intertwined.  It underscores the importance of upholding truth and justice, especially concerning the innocent and virtuous.
orig: وبكفرهم وقولهم على مريم بهتانا عظيما

translation: And [for] their saying, "Indeed, we have killed the Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary, the messenger of Allah." And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him; but [another] was made to resemble him to them. And indeed, those who differ over it are in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption. And they did not kill him, for certain.
interpretation: This verse addresses the claim that Jesus was crucified and killed. The Quran refutes this claim unequivocally, stating that it did not happen.  The phrase "but [another] was made to resemble him to them" suggests that someone else was mistaken for Jesus, and this person was crucified instead. This interpretation leaves open the possibility of a substitution, a miraculous rescue, or an illusion. The verse emphasizes the lack of certainty and knowledge among those who believe Jesus was crucified, highlighting that their belief is based on assumption and conjecture (following of 'zann' or الظن) rather than factual evidence. The final emphatic statement, "And they did not kill him, for certain," reinforces the Quran's denial of the crucifixion of Jesus.  This verse is crucial for Islamic Christology, as it maintains Jesus's status as a respected prophet of God and denies his death on the cross, a central tenet of Christian theology.  Different Islamic schools of thought have varying interpretations on the precise nature of how the crucifixion was avoided, but they all agree on the core message: Jesus was not killed on the cross.
orig: وقولهم إنا قتلنا المسيح عيسى ابن مريم رسول الله وما قتلوه وما صلبوه ولكن شبه لهم وإن الذين اختلفوا فيه لفي شك منه ما لهم به من علم إلا اتباع الظن وما قتلوه يقينا

translation: Nay, Allah raised him up to Himself; and Allah is Exalted in Power, Wise.
interpretation: This verse, often referring to the Prophet Jesus (Isa), denies the claim that he was killed or crucified.  Instead, it asserts that God raised him directly to Himself.  The Arabic word 'rafa'a' implies elevation, both physically and spiritually.  This ascension doesn't necessarily mean a physical bodily ascent, but could also signify an elevation in status and honor before God.  The subsequent description of God as 'Aziz' (Exalted in Power) and 'Hakim' (Wise) emphasizes that this act was within God's absolute power and aligned with His perfect wisdom.  Different interpretations exist within Islamic theology regarding the precise nature of this ascension, but the core message remains consistent: God saved Jesus from his enemies and honored him.  The verse also serves to reinforce God's ultimate authority and control over all events.
orig: بل رفعه الله إليه وكان الله عزيزا حكيما

translation: And there is none from the People of the Book but that he will surely believe in him (i.e., Jesus, or the truth about him) before his death. And on the Day of Resurrection he will be against them a witness.
interpretation:
This verse has been a subject of much discussion and varying interpretations among scholars.  The "People of the Book" refers to Jews and Christians.  The pronoun "him" can refer either to Jesus or the truth about him, specifically his prophethood as revealed in Islam. 

One interpretation suggests that every Jew and Christian will ultimately recognize the truth about Jesus before they die, even if only in their final moments. This doesn't necessarily mean a formal conversion to Islam, but an acknowledgement of Jesus' true status as a prophet of God, not divine as some Christians believe, and not rejected as some Jews believed.  Another interpretation posits that the verse refers to their acknowledgment of the truth upon meeting Jesus on the Day of Judgment. 

The phrase "before his death" can be understood literally or metaphorically.  Literally, it means just before physical death. Metaphorically, it could refer to a point of spiritual awakening or realization before the Day of Judgement. The final part of the verse, "And on the Day of Resurrection he will be against them a witness," reinforces the idea of ultimate accountability.  Jesus will testify to their beliefs and actions concerning him and his message during their earthly lives. This highlights the importance of recognizing the truth about prophets and the consequences of rejecting them.
orig: وإن من أهل الكتاب إلا ليؤمنن به قبل موته ويوم القيامة يكون عليهم شهيدا

translation: So for the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things which had been lawful to them, and for their diverting many from the way of Allah,
interpretation: This verse discusses the consequences faced by some of the Jewish community due to their transgressions.  The phrase "those who were Jews" specifies that the verse refers to a specific group within the Jewish community at that time, not all Jews throughout history.  It highlights that the prohibitions were a direct result of their actions, not an inherent characteristic of their faith.  The "good things" that were forbidden are understood by many commentators to refer to specific dietary allowances that were temporarily revoked.  "Diverting many from the way of Allah" refers to their hindering others from following the path of righteousness, perhaps through misinterpretation of scripture, discouraging belief, or setting a negative example.  The verse emphasizes the principle of accountability for one's actions and the potential consequences of straying from divine guidance.
orig: فبظلم من الذين هادوا حرمنا عليهم طيبات أحلت لهم وبصدهم عن سبيل الله كثيرا

translation: And they took interest, although they had been forbidden from it, and they devoured people's wealth unjustly. And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse condemns two intertwined sins: taking interest (riba) and unjustly consuming the wealth of others.  It highlights the prohibition of riba, which in Islamic finance refers to any excess earned beyond the principal amount in a loan or transaction, considered exploitative. The verse connects this with the broader act of consuming wealth unjustly (batil), suggesting that riba is a specific form of this injustice.  It emphasizes that this prohibition had already been communicated and disregarded. The verse concludes with a warning of a painful punishment for those who persist in these practices, specifically those who disbelieve, indicating the severity of these transgressions in the eyes of God.  The connection between riba and consuming wealth unjustly underscores the importance of ethical and just financial dealings in Islam.
orig: وأخذهم الربا وقد نهوا عنه وأكلهم أموال الناس بالباطل وأعتدنا للكافرين منهم عذابا أليما

translation: But those firmly rooted in knowledge among them and the believers believe in what has been revealed to you, [O Muhammad], and what was revealed before you, and those who establish prayer and those who give zakah and the believers in Allah and the Last Day - those We will give a great reward.
interpretation:
This verse highlights the qualities of those who will receive a great reward from God. It emphasizes a layered belief system.  It begins by distinguishing those with deep, established knowledge ('rasikhoon fi al-'ilm') among the believers. These are not simply those who possess information but those who have internalized and live by it. They believe not only in the revelation given to Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) but also in the divine messages revealed to previous prophets, demonstrating an understanding of the continuity and universality of God's guidance.

Furthermore, this verse underscores the importance of action alongside belief.  It mentions the establishment of prayer ('iqamat as-salah'), which refers to performing prayers regularly and with sincerity, and the giving of zakah (obligatory charity), which signifies social responsibility and care for the less fortunate. This emphasizes that true faith manifests itself in righteous deeds.

Finally, the verse concludes by mentioning belief in Allah and the Last Day.  This reinforces the fundamental tenets of Islamic faith, highlighting that belief in God and accountability in the hereafter are crucial for attaining the promised reward. This 'great reward' ('ajran 'atheeman') is not explicitly defined, leaving it open to the vastness of God's mercy and blessings in the afterlife, further motivating believers to strive for these qualities.
orig: لكن الراسخون في العلم منهم والمؤمنون يؤمنون بما أنزل إليك وما أنزل من قبلك والمقيمين الصلاة والمؤتون الزكاة والمؤمنون بالله واليوم الآخر أولئك سنؤتيهم أجرا عظيما

translation: Indeed, We have revealed to you, [O Muhammad], as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him. And we revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the Descendants, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon, and to David We gave the Psalms.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the continuity and consistency of divine revelation across time and through various prophets.  It positions Muhammad within a long line of messengers, receiving the same core message from God as his predecessors.  The verse lists prominent figures from Jewish and Christian traditions, acknowledging their roles as recipients of divine guidance.  It asserts that Islam is not a new religion, but a continuation and culmination of the same primordial faith revealed to earlier prophets.  By mentioning the Psalms given to David, it also highlights the importance of revealed scripture. The verse serves to legitimize Muhammad's prophethood and the Quran's authority by connecting them to a respected lineage of divine communication. It suggests a shared heritage and underlying unity among these Abrahamic faiths, originating from a single divine source.
orig: إنا أوحينا إليك كما أوحينا إلى نوح والنبيين من بعده وأوحينا إلى إبراهيم وإسماعيل وإسحاق ويعقوب والأسباط وعيسى وأيوب ويونس وهارون وسليمان وآتينا داوود زبورا

translation: And [We sent] messengers whom We have related to you before and messengers We have not related to you. And Allah spoke to Moses with [direct] speech.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the vastness of God's communication with humanity through prophets. It acknowledges that the Quran, while a comprehensive revelation, doesn't contain the stories of all the prophets God sent.  The stories mentioned in the Quran are carefully selected to serve specific purposes, such as providing moral guidance, historical context, or strengthening faith.  Those prophets whose stories are not explicitly mentioned are still recognized as legitimate messengers of God. The final part of the verse highlights the special nature of Moses's prophethood, specifying that God spoke to him directly (takliman), a distinction that emphasizes the importance of the Mosaic law and its influence on later prophetic traditions.  This direct communication, without intermediary, signifies the elevated status of Moses among the prophets and the weight of the message entrusted to him.  The verse therefore serves as a reminder of God’s continuous communication throughout history and the unique role each prophet played in delivering His message.
orig: ورسلا قد قصصناهم عليك من قبل ورسلا لم نقصصهم عليك وكلم الله موسى تكليما

translation: (We sent) messengers as bearers of good news and as warners so that mankind would have no argument against Allah after the messengers. And Allah is Exalted in Might, Wise.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the justice and mercy of God in sending messengers.  The 'good news' refers to the rewards of faith and righteous actions, essentially the promise of Paradise.  The 'warnings' pertain to the consequences of disbelief and wrongdoing, namely the threat of Hellfire. By sending messengers with both glad tidings and admonitions, God ensures that humanity has no excuse for their actions on the Day of Judgment.  They cannot claim ignorance of His will. The phrase 'no argument against Allah' highlights the removal of any justifiable grounds for rejecting faith after clear guidance has been provided.  The verse concludes by affirming God's attributes of 'Exalted in Might' (Aziz) and 'Wise' (Hakim).  'Aziz' signifies God's absolute power and authority, while 'Hakim' underscores His perfect wisdom in all His actions, including the sending of messengers.
orig: رسلا مبشرين ومنذرين لئلا يكون للناس على الله حجة بعد الرسل وكان الله عزيزا حكيما

translation: But Allah bears witness to what He has revealed to you, [O Muhammad], He has revealed it with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness [as well]. And sufficient is Allah as Witness.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the divine origin and authority of the Qur'an.  It asserts that the revelation given to Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is not from any human source, but directly from God, based on His perfect knowledge.  The angels, as beings of pure obedience and closeness to God, also bear witness to its truth.  Ultimately, however, God's testimony alone is sufficient to establish the Qur'an's authenticity and veracity. This highlights the supreme authority of God and the unquestionable nature of His word.  The verse serves as a powerful reassurance of the Qur'an's divine source and a reminder of God's all-encompassing knowledge and ultimate authority.
orig: لكن الله يشهد بما أنزل إليك أنزله بعلمه والملائكة يشهدون وكفى بالله شهيدا

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve and avert [others] from the path of Allah have certainly gone far astray.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the severity of both disbelieving in God (kufr) and actively preventing others from following God's path.  The phrase "ضلوا ضلالا بعيدا" literally translates to "have strayed a distant straying," powerfully conveying the idea that their deviation is not minor but significant and irreversible, leading them far from the truth and salvation.  It highlights the gravity of not only rejecting faith but also actively hindering others from embracing it.  The verse serves as a warning and a lament for those who choose this path, emphasizing the profound spiritual consequences of their actions.
orig: إن الذين كفروا وصدوا عن سبيل الله قد ضلوا ضلالا بعيدا

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve and commit wrong - never will Allah forgive them, nor will He guide them to a way.
interpretation: This verse speaks about the consequences of disbelief (kufr) combined with wrongdoing (zulm).  It emphasizes that forgiveness and divine guidance are withheld from those who persistently reject faith and engage in oppressive actions.  'Kufr' here signifies not merely a lack of belief but an active rejection of truth, while 'zulm' encompasses various forms of injustice and transgression against God, oneself, and others.  The verse suggests that such a combination of disbelief and wrongdoing creates a barrier that prevents divine mercy and guidance from reaching the individual. It's important to note that some interpretations differentiate between persistent, unrepentant disbelief and wrongdoing, and situations where individuals may seek forgiveness and guidance before death. This verse serves as a warning and emphasizes the importance of both faith and righteous action.
orig: إن الذين كفروا وظلموا لم يكن الله ليغفر لهم ولا ليهديهم طريقا

translation: Except the path of Hell, wherein they will abide forever. And that, for Allah, is [always] easy.
interpretation: This verse typically appears in the context of describing the ultimate fate of those who reject faith and righteous actions.  "Except the path of Hell" indicates an exclusion; it highlights that while Allah offers guidance and mercy, those who deliberately choose to disobey will be excluded from this and confined to Hell.  "Khalidin fiha abadan" emphasizes the permanence of their punishment, signifying an eternal stay with no possibility of reprieve.  The final clause, "And that, for Allah, is [always] easy," should not be misinterpreted as minimizing the severity of the punishment or suggesting ease in condemning people.  Rather, it affirms Allah's absolute power and authority.  Carrying out this judgment, while a grave matter, poses no difficulty for the All-Powerful.  It underscores the certainty and inevitability of the consequences for those who reject truth. This serves as a stark warning and a reminder of the seriousness of choosing one's path in life.
orig: إلا طريق جهنم خالدين فيها أبدا وكان ذلك على الله يسيرا

translation: O mankind, the Messenger has certainly come to you with the truth from your Lord, so believe; it is better for you. But if you disbelieve - then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth. And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: This verse addresses all of humanity, emphasizing the universality of the Prophet's message. It highlights that the Prophet brings the truth, not his own opinions or fabrications, but a divine truth from God (Allah).  Believing this truth is presented as beneficial and in humanity's best interest. The consequence of disbelief is then stated, not as a direct punishment, but as an affirmation of God's absolute sovereignty and ownership of everything in the heavens and the earth. Whether people believe or not, God remains the ultimate power. The verse concludes by emphasizing God's attributes of knowledge and wisdom, implying that this divine decree is not arbitrary but based on perfect knowledge and wisdom. This serves both as a warning and a reassurance; a warning to those who disbelieve and a reassurance to those who believe that God's plan is just and wise.
orig: يا أيها الناس قد جاءكم الرسول بالحق من ربكم فآمنوا خيرا لكم وإن تكفروا فإن لله ما في السماوات والأرض وكان الله عليما حكيما

translation: O People of the Scripture! Do not exaggerate in your religion nor utter aught concerning Allah save the truth. The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, was only a messenger of Allah and His word which He conveyed unto Mary, and a spirit from Him. So believe in Allah and His messengers, and say not, "Three." Cease! It is better for you. Allah is only One God. Far be it from His glory that He should have a son. To Him belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth. And Allah is sufficient as a Disposer of affairs.
interpretation: This verse addresses the People of the Scripture, which traditionally refers to Jews and Christians. It cautions against extremism and distortion of religious beliefs, specifically targeting exaggerated claims about Jesus. It emphasizes Jesus' true nature as a messenger of God, born miraculously through God's word and spirit, but not divine himself.  The verse rejects the Christian doctrine of the Trinity, asserting the absolute oneness of God and denying the possibility of God having offspring.  It affirms God's sole ownership and control over all creation and highlights His sufficiency as a guardian and protector. The verse encourages adherence to the true message brought by God's messengers and promotes a balanced understanding of faith, urging believers to avoid theological excesses and embrace the simple and pure concept of God's unity.
orig: يا أهل الكتاب لا تغلوا في دينكم ولا تقولوا على الله إلا الحق إنما المسيح عيسى ابن مريم رسول الله وكلمته ألقاها إلى مريم وروح منه فآمنوا بالله ورسله ولا تقولوا ثلاثة انتهوا خيرا لكم إنما الله إله واحد سبحانه أن يكون له ولد له ما في السماوات وما في الأرض وكفى بالله وكيلا

translation: The Messiah does not disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor do the angels who are near [to Him]. And whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant - He will gather them all to Himself.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute sovereignty of God and the humility even the highest of creations – Jesus (the Messiah) and the angels closest to God – display before Him.  It asserts that Jesus, despite his elevated status as a prophet, acknowledges God's ultimate authority and willingly submits to His will as a servant. Similarly, the angels closest to God, who are often associated with power and might, also demonstrate complete subservience and lack any arrogance before Him.  The verse then warns against the grave sin of arrogance and refusal to worship God. It highlights that anyone, regardless of their perceived status or power, who disdains God's worship and harbors arrogance will ultimately be held accountable and gathered before Him for judgment.
orig: لن يستنكف المسيح أن يكون عبدا لله ولا الملائكة المقربون ومن يستنكف عن عبادته ويستكبر فسيحشرهم إليه جميعا

translation: As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full and will increase them out of His bounty. But as for those who turn away and are arrogant, He will punish them with a painful punishment, and they will not find for themselves besides Allah any protector or helper.
interpretation: This verse highlights the contrasting destinies awaiting those who choose different paths in life.  It emphasizes the justice and mercy of God. Those who embrace faith (\"alladhina amanu\": those who believed) and demonstrate that faith through righteous actions (\"wa 'amiloo as-salihati\": and do righteous deeds) are promised not only the just recompense for their deeds (\"yu'fihim ujurahum\": He will give them their rewards in full) but also an additional blessing from God's overflowing generosity (\"wa yaziduhum min fadlihi\": and will increase them out of His bounty).  This additional bounty signifies God's boundless grace and love for those who strive to please Him.  Conversely, those who reject faith and truth (\"alladhina istankafu\": those who disdained/turned away) out of arrogance and pride (\"wa istakbaru\": and were arrogant/prideful) are warned of a severe and painful punishment (\"yu'adhdhibuhum 'adhaban alima\": He will punish them with a painful punishment).  Their arrogance prevents them from recognizing God's authority and guidance, leading them to a state of vulnerability where they will find no one to protect or help them (\"wa la yajiduna lahum min duni Allahi waliyan wa la nasira\": and they will not find for themselves besides Allah any protector or helper) against God's judgment.  This verse underscores the importance of humility, obedience, and righteous action in earning God's favor, while warning against the destructive consequences of pride and rejection of truth.
orig: فأما الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات فيوفيهم أجورهم ويزيدهم من فضله وأما الذين استنكفوا واستكبروا فيعذبهم عذابا أليما ولا يجدون لهم من دون الله وليا ولا نصيرا

translation: O mankind! Indeed, there has come to you a conclusive proof from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a clear light.
interpretation: This verse addresses all of humanity, emphasizing the universality of the message.  "Burhan" (conclusive proof) refers to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the Quran itself. This proof confirms God's existence and guidance.  The "clear light" (Nur Mubin) that is sent down can be understood as the Quran's teachings, which illuminate the path of truth and righteousness, dispelling ignorance and misguidance.  It offers clarity on matters of faith, morality, and purpose in life, providing guidance for individuals and society as a whole.  The verse underscores the importance of recognizing and accepting this divine guidance for achieving true success and fulfillment.
orig: يا أيها الناس قد جاءكم برهان من ربكم وأنزلنا إليكم نورا مبينا

translation: As for those who believe in Allah and hold fast to Him, He will admit them to His mercy and grace, and guide them to Himself on a straight path.
interpretation:
This verse highlights the blessings bestowed upon those who possess true faith in God (Allah) and firmly adhere to His guidance.  "Holding fast to Him" (wa'tasimū bihi) implies not only believing but also acting upon that belief, seeking refuge in Him, and following His commandments. The promise for such individuals is threefold:

1. **Admission to His mercy and grace (rahmatan minhu wa fadlan):**  This signifies God's boundless compassion and favor encompassing both forgiveness for past transgressions and bestowal of blessings in this life and the hereafter.  "Fadlan" (grace) emphasizes the unearned and abundant nature of these divine gifts.

2. **Guidance to Himself (yahdihim ilayhi):**  This points to a continuous process of divine guidance leading towards a deeper understanding and closer relationship with God.  It signifies not just guidance to the right path, but also guidance towards ultimate spiritual realization and proximity to the Divine.

3. **A straight path (ṣirāṭan mustaqīman):** This represents the clear and direct path of Islam, free from deviation and confusion.  It embodies a life lived in accordance with God's will, leading to righteousness and ultimate salvation. 

In essence, the verse emphasizes that true faith, coupled with steadfast adherence to God's guidance, leads to divine mercy, continuous spiritual growth, and the attainment of ultimate felicity.
orig: فأما الذين آمنوا بالله واعتصموا به فسيدخلهم في رحمة منه وفضل ويهديهم إليه صراطا مستقيما

translation: They ask you for a legal ruling. Say, "God gives you a ruling concerning the 'Kalalah' (one who dies leaving no descendants but may have ascendants and/or siblings). If a man dies, leaving no child but a sister, she will inherit half of what he leaves. And he inherits from her if she leaves no child. But if there are two sisters, they will inherit two-thirds of what he leaves. If the heirs are both brothers and sisters, the male will receive a share equivalent to that of two females. God makes this clear to you, so that you will not go astray. And God is all-knowing about everything.
interpretation:
This verse addresses inheritance laws in the specific case of 'Kalalah,' which refers to a person who dies without leaving any direct descendants (children or grandchildren).  It outlines the shares allocated to different siblings in such a scenario.  Here's a breakdown:

* **Single Sister:** If the deceased leaves only one sister, she inherits half of his estate.  Reciprocally, if a sister dies without children, her brother (the deceased in the first scenario) would inherit from her.
* **Two or More Sisters:** If the deceased leaves two or more sisters, they collectively inherit two-thirds of the estate, shared equally among them.
* **Brothers and Sisters:** If the deceased leaves both brothers and sisters, the male siblings each receive a share equivalent to the combined share of two female siblings.  This reflects the general principle of male inheritance being double that of a female in Islamic inheritance law.

The verse emphasizes the importance of divine guidance in these matters to prevent disputes and ensure fairness.  It highlights God's wisdom and comprehensive knowledge in providing clear regulations for inheritance distribution. The concept of 'Kalalah' and its specific rules were designed to address potential ambiguity and ensure equitable distribution of wealth within the family when direct descendants are absent. It's a demonstration of the detailed and comprehensive nature of Islamic inheritance law, striving to provide clear guidelines for various familial situations.
orig: يستفتونك قل الله يفتيكم في الكلالة إن امرؤ هلك ليس له ولد وله أخت فلها نصف ما ترك وهو يرثها إن لم يكن لها ولد فإن كانتا اثنتين فلهما الثلثان مما ترك وإن كانوا إخوة رجالا ونساء فللذكر مثل حظ الأنثيين يبين الله لكم أن تضلوا والله بكل شيء عليم

translation: O you who have believed, fulfill [all] contracts. Lawful for you are the animals of grazing livestock except for that which is recited to you [in prohibition], not permitting hunting while you are in the state of ihram. Indeed, Allah decrees what He wills.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the paramount importance of upholding agreements and contracts in Islam.  It highlights the sanctity of promises and commitments, reminding believers of their obligation to fulfill them. The verse then addresses dietary laws, specifying that livestock animals are generally permissible for consumption, with certain exceptions that are explicitly prohibited elsewhere in the Qur'an (such as swine).  The verse then clarifies a specific prohibition against hunting while in the sacred state of ihram during pilgrimage. This reinforces the sanctity of the pilgrimage and the required focus on spiritual devotion during this time. The concluding phrase, "Indeed, Allah decrees what He wills," affirms God's ultimate authority and wisdom in establishing these laws.
orig: يا أيها الذين آمنوا أوفوا بالعقود أحلت لكم بهيمة الأنعام إلا ما يتلى عليكم غير محلي الصيد وأنتم حرم إن الله يحكم ما يريد

translation: O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah or [the sanctity of] the sacred month or [the offerings of] the sacrificial animals or [the garlands of] the marked [for sacrifice] or [those coming to] the Sacred House seeking bounty from their Lord and [His] approval. But when you are free from the sacred months, then [you may] hunt. And do not let the hatred of a people for having obstructed you from al-Masjid al-Haram lead you to transgress. And cooperate in righteousness and piety, but do not cooperate in sin and aggression. And fear Allah ; indeed, Allah is severe in penalty.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Ma'idah 5:2) addresses the believers and outlines important principles regarding conduct during pilgrimage and in general life. It begins by prohibiting the violation of several sacred things: the rites of Allah, which encompass all acts of worship and religious observance; the sacred months (Rajab, Dhul-Qa’dah, Dhul-Hijjah, and Muharram), during which warfare was traditionally forbidden; the sacrificial animals designated for pilgrimage rituals; the garlands marking these animals; and the pilgrims themselves who are seeking God's favor by visiting the Kaaba.  The verse then permits hunting after the sacred months have ended, signifying a return to normal life. Critically, it warns against letting past grievances or animosity towards those who may have prevented access to the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram in Mecca) incite acts of transgression or revenge. This highlights the importance of maintaining peace and not letting personal feelings override religious and ethical principles. Finally, the verse emphasizes the vital principle of cooperating in righteousness and piety while refraining from assisting in sin and aggression. It concludes with a reminder of the powerful consequences of disobeying God's commands, urging mindfulness and fear of divine retribution. In essence, this verse promotes respect for the sacred, restraint in conflict, and active collaboration in virtuous deeds while avoiding wrongdoing, all grounded in a conscious awareness of God's authority and justice.
orig: يا أيها الذين آمنوا لا تحلوا شعائر الله ولا الشهر الحرام ولا الهدي ولا القلائد ولا آمين البيت الحرام يبتغون فضلا من ربهم ورضوانا وإذا حللتم فاصطادوا ولا يجرمنكم شنآن قوم أن صدوكم عن المسجد الحرام أن تعتدوا وتعاونوا على البر والتقوى ولا تعاونوا على الإثم والعدوان واتقوا الله إن الله شديد العقاب

translation: Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been dedicated to other than God, and [those animals] strangled, or beaten to death, or killed by a fall, or gored by horns, and that which has been eaten by a wild animal - except what you slaughter [before its death] - and that which is sacrificed on stone altars, and [forbidden is] that you seek your decisions through divining arrows. That is [all] transgression. Today those who disbelieve have despaired of [defeating] your religion; so fear them not, but fear Me. Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favor upon you and have approved for you Islam as religion. But whoever is forced by severe hunger with no inclination to sin - then indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation:
This verse (5:3) details dietary prohibitions and practices forbidden to Muslims. It expands on the concept of halal (permissible) and haram (forbidden) in Islamic law, specifically regarding food consumption.  The prohibited items are primarily carrion (dead animals), blood, pork, and animals dedicated to idols.  It also forbids meat from animals that died from strangulation, beating, falling, or being gored unless properly slaughtered before death. Divination, particularly using arrows, is also explicitly condemned. 

The verse then transitions to a declaration of religious completion and God's favor upon the believers.  It proclaims that Islam is the finalized and chosen religion.  This signifies a sense of security and confidence for the believers against those who oppose them. The emphasis shifts from fearing adversaries to fearing God alone.  Finally, it addresses exceptional circumstances, allowing for forbidden food consumption if one is facing starvation, provided there is no intention of sinning. This demonstrates the mercy and compassion of God, recognizing the dire needs that may override strict adherence under extreme duress.
orig: حرمت عليكم الميتة والدم ولحم الخنزير وما أهل لغير الله به والمنخنقة والموقوذة والمتردية والنطيحة وما أكل السبع إلا ما ذكيتم وما ذبح على النصب وأن تستقسموا بالأزلام ذلكم فسق اليوم يئس الذين كفروا من دينكم فلا تخشوهم واخشون اليوم أكملت لكم دينكم وأتممت عليكم نعمتي ورضيت لكم الإسلام دينا فمن اضطر في مخمصة غير متجانف لإثم فإن الله غفور رحيم

translation: They ask you, [O Muhammad], what has been made lawful for them. Say, "Lawful for you are good things and [the game caught by] what you have trained of hunting animals which you train as Allah has taught you. So eat of what they catch for you, and mention the name of Allah upon it, and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is swift in account.
interpretation:
This verse addresses the permissibility of eating meat obtained through trained hunting animals.  It responds to a question posed to the Prophet Muhammad about what is lawful to consume.  The verse highlights several key points:

1. **Permissibility of "Good Things (At-Tayyibat):"** This refers to things that are wholesome, pure, and beneficial, both physically and spiritually.  It encompasses a general principle of consuming what is good and avoiding what is harmful.

2. **Hunting with Trained Animals:**  The verse specifically permits consuming the meat of animals caught by trained hunting animals, such as dogs and falcons.  This highlights the permissibility of utilizing animals for sustenance, provided they are trained according to Islamic principles.

3. **Training According to Divine Guidance:** The phrase "as Allah has taught you" emphasizes that the training methods must be ethical and humane, aligning with the overall teachings of Islam regarding animal welfare.  It implies that the animals should be trained to hunt effectively while minimizing suffering.

4. **Mentioning the Name of Allah:**  The instruction to "mention the name of Allah upon it" refers to invoking God's name before consuming the hunted animal.  This act acknowledges God as the provider and expresses gratitude for the sustenance.

5. **Fear of Allah (Taqwa):**  The concluding phrase "and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is swift in account" serves as a reminder of accountability.  It emphasizes that even in matters of sustenance, Muslims are expected to act with consciousness of God and adhere to ethical principles.  It also implies the importance of avoiding excesses and being mindful of the resources provided.

In essence, this verse provides practical guidance on lawful consumption, highlighting the permissibility of hunting with trained animals while emphasizing ethical treatment, gratitude, and accountability before God.
orig: يسألونك ماذا أحل لهم قل أحل لكم الطيبات وما علمتم من الجوارح مكلبين تعلمونهن مما علمكم الله فكلوا مما أمسكن عليكم واذكروا اسم الله عليه واتقوا الله إن الله سريع الحساب

translation: This day [all] good things are permitted to you. And the food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you and your food is lawful for them. And [lawful in marriage are] chaste women from among the believers and chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you, when you have given them their due compensation, desiring chastity, not unlawful sexual intercourse or taking [secret] lovers. And whoever denies the faith - his work has become worthless, and he, in the Hereafter, will be among the losers.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Ma'idah 5:5) deals with dietary laws and marriage regulations for Muslims. It declares that all good and wholesome foods are lawful for Muslims, including the food of the People of the Book (Jews and Christians) as their food is also lawful for Muslims.  This promotes peaceful coexistence and mutual respect.  Reciprocally, the food prepared by Muslims is permissible for Jews and Christians.  The verse then addresses marriage, permitting marriage with chaste women from among both Muslims and the People of the Book, provided the marriage is conducted properly, with a dowry given and a commitment to marital fidelity. It emphasizes the importance of a formal marriage contract and condemns illicit relationships and extramarital affairs. The term 'Muhsineen' refers to those entering marriage with sincerity and a commitment to upholding its sanctity. The verse concludes with a strong warning against rejecting faith, stating that such an act nullifies good deeds and leads to loss in the Hereafter. This highlights the importance of faith as the foundation of righteous actions.
orig: اليوم أحل لكم الطيبات وطعام الذين أوتوا الكتاب حل لكم وطعامكم حل لهم والمحصنات من المؤمنات والمحصنات من الذين أوتوا الكتاب من قبلكم إذا آتيتموهن أجورهن محصنين غير مسافحين ولا متخذي أخدان ومن يكفر بالإيمان فقد حبط عمله وهو في الآخرة من الخاسرين

translation: O you who have believed, when you rise to [perform] prayer, wash your faces and your forearms to the elbows and wipe over your heads and wash your feet to the ankles. And if you are in a state of janabah, then purify yourselves. But if you are ill or on a journey or one of you comes from the place of relieving himself or you have contacted women and find no water, then perform tayammum with clean earth and wipe over your faces and hands with it. Allah does not intend to make difficulty for you, but He intends to purify you and complete His favor upon you that you may be grateful.
interpretation:
This verse, 5:6, details the ritual ablutions (wudu) required before prayer and the alternative dry ablution (tayammum) when water is unavailable or one is ill.  It emphasizes the importance of purity and cleanliness before engaging in prayer, a central act of worship in Islam. 

Wudu involves washing the face, forearms to the elbows, wiping the head, and washing the feet to the ankles.  If in a state of major impurity (janabah, usually following sexual intercourse), a full bath (ghusl) is required. 

The verse then outlines the situations where tayammum is permissible: illness, travel, after using the toilet, or after sexual intimacy, when water is scarce or inaccessible.  Tayammum involves using clean earth to wipe the face and hands, symbolically achieving purification in the absence of water.

Crucially, the verse highlights God's mercy and ease. The provision of tayammum demonstrates that God doesn't want to burden believers with hardship but desires their purification and to complete His favor upon them so they may express gratitude.  This signifies that the intention behind purification is what truly matters, and God understands human limitations and circumstances.
