interpretation: This verse addresses a situation where the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was likely being pressured by his adversaries, particularly the disbelievers of Mecca, to bring about immediate divine punishment or some miraculous sign to prove his prophethood. They were impatient and demanded instant gratification.  The verse conveys that God's timetable is not dictated by human demands. True judgment and ultimate justice rest with God, who is all-knowing, particularly regarding those who transgress and act unjustly.  It emphasizes God's wisdom and patience in dealing with wrongdoers, and implicitly warns those who challenge the Prophet that they will ultimately be held accountable by God.  The verse also highlights the Prophet's human limitations. He could not arbitrarily bring about divine intervention; it is solely God's prerogative. This reinforces the concept of God's absolute power and authority. The Prophet's role was to deliver the message and trust in God's plan. Therefore, the verse serves both as a response to the impatient demands of the disbelievers and as a reassurance to the believers to have patience and trust in God's justice.
orig: قل لو أن عندي ما تستعجلون به لقضي الأمر بيني وبينكم والله أعلم بالظالمين

translation: And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him. And He knows what is on the land and in the sea. Not a leaf falls but that He knows it. And no grain is there within the darknesses of the earth and no moist or dry [thing] but that it is [written] in a clear record.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's absolute and comprehensive knowledge.  "Keys of the unseen" refers to God's exclusive knowledge of all things hidden and unknown to humanity, encompassing the past, future, and the mysteries of creation. This knowledge isn't merely general but extends to minute details: the falling of a leaf, a single seed hidden deep within the earth, whether something is fresh or dry.  Everything is within His awareness. The "clear record" (often interpreted as the 'Preserved Tablet') signifies a divine ledger where everything is meticulously documented, highlighting God's perfect knowledge and meticulous accounting of all things.  This verse reinforces the concept of divine omniscience and serves as a reminder of God's all-encompassing awareness and control over the universe.
orig: وعنده مفاتح الغيب لا يعلمها إلا هو ويعلم ما في البر والبحر وما تسقط من ورقة إلا يعلمها ولا حبة في ظلمات الأرض ولا رطب ولا يابس إلا في كتاب مبين

translation: And it is He who takes your souls by night and knows what you have earned by day. Then He revives you therein that a term named may be fulfilled. Then to Him will be your return, and He will then inform you of what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse speaks to God's complete knowledge and control over life, death, and resurrection.  "He who takes your souls by night" refers to sleep, a state resembling death where our conscious awareness is diminished.  God is aware of all our actions ("what you have earned by day") whether good or bad.  "Then He revives you therein" refers to waking up, a symbolic resurrection, highlighting God's power to give and take life. This cycle of sleep and wakefulness continues until "a term named may be fulfilled" - meaning our appointed lifespan.  Ultimately, we return to God ("Then to Him will be your return") for final judgment where He will hold us accountable for our deeds ("He will then inform you of what you used to do"). The verse emphasizes the importance of living a righteous life, as God is aware of everything we do, and we will eventually be held responsible for it. It also highlights the cyclical nature of life and death with sleep as a daily reminder of our ultimate return to God.
orig: وهو الذي يتوفاكم بالليل ويعلم ما جرحتم بالنهار ثم يبعثكم فيه ليقضى أجل مسمى ثم إليه مرجعكم ثم ينبئكم بما كنتم تعملون

translation: And He is the All-Overpowering [al-Qaahir] above His servants, and He sends over you guardians [hufazah] until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers [rusulunaa] take him, and they do not neglect [their duty].
interpretation:
This verse emphasizes God's absolute power and control over all creation, including life and death.  The term *al-Qaahir* highlights God's dominance and irresistible authority.  He is the ultimate power, above all His servants. The verse then speaks of 'guardians,' which can be interpreted in several ways. Some scholars understand them as angels appointed to protect and record a person's deeds throughout their life. Others suggest they refer to the various forces and factors that sustain life, from our internal bodily functions to the external environment.  

The crucial point is that even with these guardians, death is inevitable, and when it arrives, God's 'messengers,' often understood as angels of death, come to claim the soul. The phrase 'they do not neglect [their duty]' underscores the precision and inevitability of death, highlighting that there is no escaping God's decree. It also signifies the care and order with which this transition is carried out, emphasizing that even in death, we are under God's watchful eye.  This verse offers comfort in the face of mortality, reminding us that even in death, we are within God's divine plan.
orig: وهو القاهر فوق عباده ويرسل عليكم حفظة حتى إذا جاء أحدكم الموت توفته رسلنا وهم لا يفرطون

translation: Then they will be returned to Allah, their true protector. Surely, His is the judgment, and He is the swiftest of accountants.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the ultimate accountability of all beings to God.  After death, all will return to God, their true and ultimate authority ('Mawla', often translated as protector, implies a much deeper relationship encompassing ownership, guardianship, and source of help).  The phrase 'His is the judgment' emphasizes God's sole authority and right to judge all actions and intentions.  The concluding part, 'He is the swiftest of accountants,' signifies God's complete and immediate knowledge of everything, leaving nothing unaccounted for.  It highlights the precision and comprehensiveness of divine justice, implying that the reckoning will be swift and just.
orig: ثم ردوا إلى الله مولاهم الحق ألا له الحكم وهو أسرع الحاسبين

translation: Say, "Who rescues you from the darknesses of the land and the sea [when] you supplicate Him humbly and secretly, [saying], 'If He should save us from this [situation], we will surely be among the thankful.'"
interpretation: This verse highlights the reliance of humanity on God, especially in times of distress and vulnerability. The "darknesses of the land and the sea" symbolize perilous situations, both physical and metaphorical.  When faced with such difficulties, people instinctively turn to God, often in private and with humility, promising gratitude if delivered.  The verse emphasizes the power of sincere supplication and the inherent human inclination to seek divine help in moments of need. It also implicitly suggests that true thankfulness should not be conditional but rather a constant state of being, regardless of circumstance.  However, the verse subtly questions the sincerity of those who only remember God in times of trouble, implying that true faith involves consistent gratitude and remembrance.
orig: قل من ينجيكم من ظلمات البر والبحر تدعونه تضرعا وخفية لئن أنجانا من هذه لنكونن من الشاكرين

translation: Say, "Allah saves you from it and from every distress; then you [still] associate others with Him."
interpretation: This verse highlights the inherent contradiction in human behavior, particularly concerning faith and gratitude.  God, according to the verse, delivers people from difficulties and anxieties, big and small (represented by "it" and "every distress"). Yet, despite experiencing this divine rescue, some people turn to associating partners with God (shirk), effectively denying His sole power and authority. This can manifest in various forms, from worshipping idols to attributing success and good fortune to other forces besides God.  The verse emphasizes the irony and ingratitude of such actions, questioning how one can acknowledge God's aid in times of trouble and then immediately diminish His role by ascribing power elsewhere. It serves as a reminder of the importance of recognizing God's grace and maintaining consistent faith, even after the immediate crisis has passed.
orig: قل الله ينجيكم منها ومن كل كرب ثم أنتم تشركون

translation: Say, "He is able to send upon you a punishment from above you or from beneath your feet or to confuse you [so you become] sects and make you taste the violence of one another." See how We diversify the signs that they might understand.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's absolute power and warns against disobedience.  The "punishment from above" could refer to natural disasters like storms or meteorites, while "punishment from beneath your feet" could signify earthquakes or volcanic eruptions.  The phrase "confuse you [so you become] sects" speaks to the potential for societal division and internal conflict as a form of divine punishment.  Making people "taste the violence of one another" illustrates the devastating consequences of such discord. The verse concludes by highlighting God's varied signs (both blessings and warnings) as opportunities for reflection and understanding, ultimately urging people to heed His message and return to the right path. The use of "We" (royal We) reinforces the majesty and authority of God. The verse serves as a potent reminder of accountability and the importance of unity and righteous conduct.
orig: قل هو القادر على أن يبعث عليكم عذابا من فوقكم أو من تحت أرجلكم أو يلبسكم شيعا ويذيق بعضكم بأس بعض انظر كيف نصرف الآيات لعلهم يفقهون

translation: And your people have denied it, while it is the truth. Say, "I am not over you a disposer of affairs."
interpretation: This verse speaks to the Prophet Muhammad's (peace be upon him) frustration and reaffirmation of his role. His people, the Quraysh, rejected his message and the divine truth of the Qur'an.  The phrase "while it is the truth" emphasizes the undeniable reality of the message despite their rejection. The statement "I am not over you a disposer of affairs" clarifies the Prophet's limited authority. He is a messenger, delivering God's message, not a controller of people's decisions or destinies.  He cannot force them to believe; their acceptance or rejection is ultimately their own responsibility. It highlights the concept of free will in Islam, where individuals are accountable for their choices. The verse also offers comfort and reassurance to the Prophet, absolving him of responsibility for their disbelief and emphasizing his role solely as a conveyor of truth.
orig: وكذب به قومك وهو الحق قل لست عليكم بوكيل

translation: For every matter there is a fixed time, and you will come to know.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the concept of divine timing and predestination in Islam.  Everything, every event, every piece of news (nab'a) has a predetermined time (mustaqarr) appointed by God.  It suggests patience and trust in God's plan, even when things seem uncertain or delayed. The phrase 'and you will come to know' implies that eventually the wisdom behind these timings will be revealed, either in this life or the hereafter. It encourages believers to persevere through difficulties, knowing that there is a purpose and a designated time for everything.
orig: لكل نبإ مستقر وسوف تعلمون

translation: And when you see those who engage in vain discourse concerning Our verses, then turn away from them until they engage in a discourse other than that. And if Satan should cause you to forget, then do not remain after the remembrance with the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: This verse instructs believers on how to respond to those who mock or trivialize the verses of the Qur'an.  It emphasizes the importance of disengaging from such conversations.  "Turning away" doesn't necessarily mean physical departure, but rather a withdrawal from the disrespectful discussion.  This demonstrates a respect for the divine message and avoids further fueling the inappropriate behavior. The verse also acknowledges the possibility of forgetting this instruction due to Satan's influence. If one inadvertently finds themselves engaged in such a conversation, they should immediately remove themselves once they remember the divine guidance.  It highlights the importance of not giving tacit approval or encouragement to those who disrespect God's word. The term "wrongdoing people" (al-qawm al-zalimin) refers to those who persist in this mockery and disrespect, emphasizing the gravity of their actions.  Therefore, this verse provides practical guidance for maintaining one's faith and upholding the sanctity of the Qur'an in the face of ridicule and trivialization.
orig: وإذا رأيت الذين يخوضون في آياتنا فأعرض عنهم حتى يخوضوا في حديث غيره وإما ينسينك الشيطان فلا تقعد بعد الذكرى مع القوم الظالمين

translation: And there is no blame upon those who are righteous concerning their past deeds, but it is a reminder so that perhaps they may be righteous.
interpretation: This verse offers a nuanced perspective on accountability and the purpose of divine guidance.  It starts by seemingly absolving the righteous ("alladhina yattaqoon") from blame regarding their accounts. This doesn't imply a complete disregard for past actions, but rather suggests a focus on the present and future. Those who strive for righteousness are not burdened by their past mistakes; their sincere repentance and commitment to a righteous path are what matter. The phrase "min hisabihim min shay'" (concerning their account from anything) might imply a lifting of the burden of those past actions, not necessarily their complete erasure. The verse then highlights the purpose of divine reminders, like the Qur'an itself. These reminders ("dhikra") are not meant to condemn or constantly remind individuals of their past shortcomings, but rather to encourage continued and increasing righteousness ("la'allahum yattaqoon").  It emphasizes the ongoing nature of piety and the importance of continuous striving towards a better self. It encourages a forward-looking approach where the focus is not on past failures, but on present commitment to righteousness.  Therefore, this verse promotes hope and encourages continued growth and development on the path of righteousness.  It suggests that the emphasis is on present and future actions, fueled by sincere intention and commitment to God-consciousness (taqwa).
orig: وما على الذين يتقون من حسابهم من شيء ولكن ذكرى لعلهم يتقون

translation: And leave those who have taken their religion as amusement and diversion and whom the worldly life has deceived. But remind [them] with it lest a soul be given up to destruction for what it has earned; it will have other than Allah neither protector nor intercessor. And if it offers every equivalent, it will not be accepted from it. Those are the ones delivered to destruction for what they have earned. For them is a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment for what they used to disbelieve.
interpretation: This verse speaks about the consequences for those who treat their faith lightly, taking it as a game or a mere pastime, and allowing themselves to be fully absorbed by the fleeting pleasures of this worldly life.  They are being warned of the grave danger they face, a danger so severe that it could lead to their spiritual ruin. The "reminder" (dhikr) mentioned is likely the Qur'an itself, serving as a wake-up call.  The verse emphasizes the utter helplessness of such individuals in the Hereafter.  No matter how much they might try to compensate or offer excuses for their actions, nothing will be accepted from them. They will have no protector or intercessor before God to plead their case. Their fate is sealed because of their choices, and they will face the painful consequences, symbolized by the "drink of scalding water" and the "painful punishment." This punishment is directly linked to their disbelief (kufr), highlighting the seriousness of their disregard for faith and their pursuit of worldly distractions over the divine.
orig: وذر الذين اتخذوا دينهم لعبا ولهوا وغرتهم الحياة الدنيا وذكر به أن تبسل نفس بما كسبت ليس لها من دون الله ولي ولا شفيع وإن تعدل كل عدل لا يؤخذ منها أولئك الذين أبسلوا بما كسبوا لهم شراب من حميم وعذاب أليم بما كانوا يكفرون

translation: Say, "Should we invoke besides Allah that which neither benefits us nor harms us, and turn back on our heels after Allah has guided us, like one whom the devils have enticed [to wander] upon the earth confused, [while] he has companions who invite him to guidance, [saying], 'Come to us?'" Say, "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is [true] guidance. And we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absurdity and danger of abandoning God's guidance after receiving it. It draws a parallel between those who turn away from God and a person lost and confused, misled by demonic influences. Even when offered help and guidance by their companions, this person remains disoriented. The verse reinforces that true guidance comes only from God and highlights the believers' commitment to submitting to Him, the Lord of all creation.  It underscores the importance of remaining steadfast on the path of faith and resisting temptations that may lead to straying from God's guidance. The verse also emphasizes the believer's duty to follow divine commands and surrender to God's will. The mention of "companions who invite him to guidance" could refer to righteous individuals or prophets, highlighting the availability of guidance for those who seek it. Ultimately, the verse asserts that God's guidance is the only path to truth and salvation, and following any other path leads to confusion and loss.
orig: قل أندعو من دون الله ما لا ينفعنا ولا يضرنا ونرد على أعقابنا بعد إذ هدانا الله كالذي استهوته الشياطين في الأرض حيران له أصحاب يدعونه إلى الهدى ائتنا قل إن هدى الله هو الهدى وأمرنا لنسلم لرب العالمين

translation: And establish prayer and fear Him. And it is He to whom you will be gathered.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the fundamental importance of prayer (Salah) and God-consciousness (Taqwa) in Islam.  'Establish prayer' implies not just performing the ritualistic movements, but also understanding its significance and maintaining its consistency with sincerity and humility.  'Fear Him' (Taqwa) encompasses a wide range of meanings, including reverence, awe, and a conscious effort to avoid actions that displease God. It promotes a life lived in awareness of God's presence and encourages righteous conduct.  The final part, 'He to whom you will be gathered,' serves as a powerful reminder of accountability and the Day of Judgment.  It underscores that all actions have consequences and that ultimately, everyone will return to God for final reckoning.  Thus, the verse connects prayer and God-consciousness to the ultimate purpose of human existence and the inevitability of facing divine judgment.
orig: وأن أقيموا الصلاة واتقوه وهو الذي إليه تحشرون

translation: And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in truth, and the Day He says, "Be," and it is, His word is the truth. And His is the dominion on the Day the Horn is blown. [He is] Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He is the Wise, the Acquainted.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's absolute power and authority over creation.  It affirms the truth of His creation of the heavens and earth, highlighting its purposefulness and not being random or accidental.  The phrase "ويوم يقول كن فيكون" (and the Day He says, "Be," and it is) illustrates His instantaneous creative power. His mere command brings things into existence. This power is further connected to the Day of Judgment, symbolized by the blowing of the Horn.  The verse asserts God's complete knowledge encompassing both the unseen (الغيب - *al-ghayb*) and the witnessed (الشهادة - *ash-shahada*), demonstrating his omniscience.  Finally, it concludes with His attributes of wisdom (الحكيم - *al-Hakim*) and profound knowledge (الخبير - *al-Khabir*), signifying His perfect understanding and governance of all things.
orig: وهو الذي خلق السماوات والأرض بالحق ويوم يقول كن فيكون قوله الحق وله الملك يوم ينفخ في الصور عالم الغيب والشهادة وهو الحكيم الخبير

translation: And [mention, O Muhammad], when Abraham said to his father Azar, "Do you take idols as deities? Indeed, I see you and your people in manifest error."
interpretation: This verse recounts a key moment in Abraham's prophetic narrative, highlighting his rejection of idolatry and his courageous confrontation of his own father, Azar (though some scholars dispute whether Azar was his biological father or an uncle or guardian).  Abraham's statement is a direct challenge to the prevalent polytheistic beliefs of his time. He doesn't merely disagree; he accuses them of being in "manifest error," suggesting the absurdity of worshipping created objects instead of the Creator. This verse emphasizes the clarity of monotheism versus the misguided nature of polytheism.  It showcases Abraham's unwavering conviction in the oneness of God even in the face of familial and societal pressure. It also underscores the importance of speaking truth to power, even when that power resides within one's own family.  The verse serves as a reminder to Muslims of the importance of tawhid (the oneness of God) and the courage required to uphold it, even when facing opposition from loved ones.
orig: وإذ قال إبراهيم لأبيه آزر أتتخذ أصناما آلهة إني أراك وقومك في ضلال مبين

translation: And thus We showed Abraham the kingdom of the heavens and the earth that he might be among those who are certain.
interpretation: This verse describes a profound experience granted to Abraham by God.  The phrase "kingdom of the heavens and the earth" (ملكوت السماوات والأرض) refers not just to the physical creation but also to the dominion, power, and intricate workings within the universe. God revealed this "kingdom" or majestic reality to Abraham, not merely as a demonstration of His power, but with a specific purpose: "that he might be among those who are certain" (ليكون من الموقنين).  This suggests that witnessing the vastness and complexity of creation strengthened Abraham's faith and solidified his certainty in God.  It reinforces the idea that true knowledge and understanding of the universe lead to a deeper conviction in the Creator. This 'showing' could have been a visionary experience, a deep understanding granted through reflection on creation, or a combination of both. Ultimately, it led Abraham to a higher level of certainty (yaqeen) – a state beyond mere belief, characterized by unwavering conviction and trust in God.
orig: وكذلك نري إبراهيم ملكوت السماوات والأرض وليكون من الموقنين

translation: When the night covered him [Abraham], he saw a star. He said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "I do not love those that set."
interpretation: This verse describes a stage in Abraham's search for God, highlighting his innate monotheistic inclination and his process of reasoning.  Seeing the bright star in the night sky, Abraham initially thought it might be his Lord.  However, when the star set, disappearing below the horizon, he realized that something which vanishes could not possibly be the eternal, ever-present Lord. This demonstrates Abraham's rejection of celestial bodies as deities, as anything subject to change and disappearance cannot be the ultimate source of creation and sustenance.  The verse illustrates Abraham's use of observation and logic to arrive at the truth about God, showcasing his intellectual and spiritual journey towards true monotheism.  It emphasizes the importance of critical thinking and the pursuit of knowledge in understanding the divine.
orig: فلما جن عليه الليل رأى كوكبا قال هذا ربي فلما أفل قال لا أحب الآفلين

translation: So when he saw the moon rising, he said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "Unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among the misguided people."
interpretation: This verse describes a stage in the story of Abraham's search for God.  It illustrates the process of someone seeking truth. Abraham, upon seeing the moon rising in its splendor, initially mistakes it for his lord. This highlights the human tendency to be captivated by impressive, immediately visible phenomena. However, when the moon sets, its disappearance reveals its impermanence and thus its inability to be the ultimate, eternal Lord. This leads Abraham to realize his error and express his reliance on true divine guidance to avoid misguidance. The verse underscores the importance of seeking a Lord that is constant, unchanging, and the ultimate source of guidance, unlike created things subject to change and disappearance.  It also emphasizes Abraham's humility and his earnest desire to be guided to the truth, recognizing his vulnerability to error without divine assistance.
orig: فلما رأى القمر بازغا قال هذا ربي فلما أفل قال لئن لم يهدني ربي لأكونن من القوم الضالين

translation: So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my lord; this is greater." But when it set, he said, "O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate with Allah."
interpretation: This verse describes a stage in the Prophet Abraham's search for God.  He observed the sun rising in all its majesty and initially thought it must be the ultimate power, the divine being.  The use of "greater" (أكبر - 'akbar') suggests a comparison, perhaps to other celestial bodies he had previously considered. However, when the sun set, disappearing from view, Abraham realized it couldn't be the true, eternal Lord.  Something that comes and goes, that is dependent on other factors, couldn't be the source of all creation. This led him to declare his dissociation from the idolatry of his people, who worshipped celestial bodies and other created things. The verse highlights Abraham's reasoning and his journey towards monotheism, emphasizing the importance of recognizing God's eternal and unchanging nature, unlike the transient nature of created things.
orig: فلما رأى الشمس بازغة قال هذا ربي هذا أكبر فلما أفلت قال يا قوم إني بريء مما تشركون

translation: Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who created the heavens and the earth, inclining toward truth, and I am not of those who associate others with Him.
interpretation: This verse, often attributed to Prophet Abraham (Ibrahim), declares a monotheistic devotion.  "I have turned my face" signifies a resolute turning away from false gods and a wholehearted dedication to the one true God, the Creator of the heavens and the earth.  The word "Hanifan" (translated here as "inclining toward truth") implies a primordial, natural inclination towards monotheism, a pure and upright way. It suggests a turning away from corrupted or fabricated beliefs and a return to the inherent truth within creation.  The final phrase, "I am not of those who associate others with Him (Al-Mushrikeen)", emphatically rejects polytheism and any form of idolatry. This verse powerfully encapsulates the core of Islamic belief: the absolute oneness of God and the rejection of any partners or equals to Him.  It represents a declaration of pure monotheism, a stance taken by Abraham and affirmed by subsequent prophets, including Muhammad. It highlights the importance of sincerity and purity in faith and serves as a reminder to focus one's devotion solely on the Creator.
orig: إني وجهت وجهي للذي فطر السماوات والأرض حنيفا وما أنا من المشركين

translation: And he argued with his people. He said, "Do you argue with me concerning Allah while He has [indeed] guided me? And I fear not what you associate with Him [and will not be harmed by them] unless my Lord should will something. My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge. Then will you not remember?
interpretation: This verse depicts a prophet, likely Abraham (based on the context often surrounding this verse in the Qur'an), engaged in a debate with his people about their polytheistic beliefs.  He asserts that God has guided him to the truth of monotheism, and therefore, their arguments against it are baseless. He expresses no fear of the idols they worship, clarifying that any harm could only come from God's will. This highlights the prophet's unwavering faith and trust in God's power and control. The phrase "My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge" emphasizes God's omniscience, implying that their polytheistic beliefs are misguided due to their limited understanding compared to God's infinite knowledge. The rhetorical question "Then will you not remember?" serves as a call to reflection and an appeal for them to reconsider their beliefs in light of God's guidance and knowledge.
orig: وحاجه قومه قال أتحاجوني في الله وقد هدان ولا أخاف ما تشركون به إلا أن يشاء ربي شيئا وسع ربي كل شيء علما أفلا تتذكرون

translation: And how should I fear what you associate [with Allah ], while you do not fear that you have associated with Allah that for which He has not sent down to you any authority? So which of the two parties has more right to security, if you should know?
interpretation: This verse reflects a rhetorical challenge posed by a believer (or by the Prophet Muhammad himself, peace be upon him, as understood by many commentators) to those who engage in polytheism (shirk). It highlights the illogical nature of fearing idols or other entities associated with God, while simultaneously having no fear of the grave sin of associating partners with God, an act for which no divine sanction or authority has been given.  The verse emphasizes that the true sense of security and peace comes from adhering to the pure monotheistic worship of God alone, as opposed to the insecurity inherent in ascribing divine attributes to created beings or objects. The rhetorical question at the end compels reflection on who truly deserves to feel secure: those who follow God's guidance or those who deviate from it through shirk. The verse underscores the importance of knowledge ('if you should know') in discerning the right path and attaining true security.
orig: وكيف أخاف ما أشركتم ولا تخافون أنكم أشركتم بالله ما لم ينزل به عليكم سلطانا فأي الفريقين أحق بالأمن إن كنتم تعلمون

translation: Those who believe and do not mix their belief with injustice (Zulm) - it is they who have security and they are the guided.
interpretation: This verse highlights the importance of pure faith and the avoidance of injustice (Zulm).  "Zulm"  is a comprehensive Arabic term encompassing wrongdoing, oppression, transgression, and exceeding due limits in any matter. It includes injustice towards oneself, others, or God.  The verse states that true believers are those who not only embrace faith but also actively avoid any form of Zulm. This intertwining of faith with righteous action is crucial for attaining true security (amn), which refers to peace of mind in this world and salvation in the hereafter.  This security arises from the certainty of faith and the absence of internal conflict caused by wrongdoing.  Furthermore, these individuals are described as "guided" (muhtadoon), meaning they are on the straight path ordained by God, and their actions are in accordance with His will.  This verse emphasizes that genuine faith is not merely a matter of belief, but also of practice, specifically the practice of justice and the avoidance of all forms of Zulm. This harmonious blend of faith and righteous action is the key to achieving true security and guidance in life.
orig: الذين آمنوا ولم يلبسوا إيمانهم بظلم أولئك لهم الأمن وهم مهتدون

translation: And that was Our argument which We gave to Abraham against his people. We raise in degrees whom We will. Indeed, your Lord is Wise and Knowing.
interpretation: This verse refers to the arguments and proofs God granted Abraham (Ibrahim) to use against his people, who were idolaters.  It highlights God's support for Abraham in his monotheistic struggle.  The verse also emphasizes God's absolute sovereignty and authority, stating that He raises whom He wills to higher ranks or degrees. This elevation could refer to worldly status, spiritual understanding, or reward in the afterlife. The concluding affirmation of God's wisdom and knowledge underscores the justice and purpose behind His decisions.  God's wisdom ensures that His choices are perfectly suited to the circumstances, and His knowledge encompasses all things, past, present, and future, allowing Him to judge and act with absolute accuracy and fairness. In the context of Abraham's story, it suggests that God's support and the elevation He bestows are not arbitrary but are based on His profound understanding and wise judgment.
orig: وتلك حجتنا آتيناها إبراهيم على قومه نرفع درجات من نشاء إن ربك حكيم عليم

translation: And We granted him Isaac and Jacob, each of them We guided. And Noah We guided before; and among his descendants, David and Solomon and Job and Joseph and Moses and Aaron. Thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse highlights God's consistent guidance and favor bestowed upon righteous individuals across generations.  It emphasizes the lineage of prophets, starting with Noah and continuing through his descendants, including prominent figures like Abraham (mentioned implicitly as the one granted Isaac and Jacob), David, Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses, and Aaron.  The verse asserts that each of these individuals received divine guidance.  It concludes by stating that this bestowal of guidance and blessings is God's way of rewarding those who do good deeds (al-muhsineen).  This implies that righteousness and piety are key factors in earning God's favor and guidance. The verse also underscores the interconnectedness of these prophets through a shared spiritual legacy and their collective role in conveying God's message to humanity.
orig: ووهبنا له إسحاق ويعقوب كلا هدينا ونوحا هدينا من قبل ومن ذريته داوود وسليمان وأيوب ويوسف وموسى وهارون وكذلك نجزي المحسنين

translation: And Zechariah, and John, and Jesus, and Elias, all of the righteous.
interpretation: This verse (Quran 6:85) lists four prominent prophets of the Abrahamic faiths: Zechariah (father of John the Baptist), John (the Baptist, precursor to Jesus), Jesus, and Elias (Elijah).  The verse emphasizes their shared righteousness and inclusion among the righteous servants of God.  It highlights the continuity of God's message and the interconnectedness of these prophetic figures.  By grouping them together, the Quran underscores the importance of their teachings and their shared commitment to monotheism and righteousness.  It also serves as a reminder to Muslims to respect and honor these prophets and their messages.
orig: وزكريا ويحيى وعيسى وإلياس كل من الصالحين

translation: And [mention] Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah, and Lot. And each [of them] We preferred over the worlds.
interpretation: This verse lists four prophets, Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah, and Lot, highlighting God's favor upon them.  The phrase "We preferred over the worlds" (wa kulan fadḍalnā 'ala l-'ālamīn) is crucial to understanding its meaning.  It doesn't necessarily mean these prophets were superior to everyone who ever lived, but rather that God granted them a special status, distinction, and blessings in their respective times and contexts.  This preference could refer to their steadfast faith, their deliverance from trials, the divine messages entrusted to them, or the impact their lives had on subsequent generations.  The verse emphasizes that God chooses and elevates individuals for His purpose, bestowing upon them special graces. It serves as a reminder of God's power and wisdom in selecting and guiding His messengers.  Furthermore, by mentioning prophets from different lineages and historical periods, the verse underscores the universality of God's message and His consistent support for those who remain steadfast in their devotion to Him.
orig: وإسماعيل واليسع ويونس ولوطا وكلا فضلنا على العالمين

translation: And [We delivered] from among their fathers and their descendants and their brethren, and We chose them and We guided them to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse speaks to God's selective guidance and favor bestowed upon certain individuals throughout history.  The phrase "from among their fathers and their descendants and their brethren" highlights the lineage and familial connections of these chosen people, suggesting that divine guidance can sometimes run within families or communities.  However, it also implies that not everyone within these families was necessarily chosen, emphasizing the individual nature of selection.  The term "We chose them" signifies God's active role in selecting these individuals for guidance, indicating that it is not solely based on merit or lineage but also involves divine grace and will.  Finally, "We guided them to a straight path" (sirat mustaqim) refers to the path of righteousness and truth according to God's will, suggesting that those chosen were given clarity and direction in their lives to follow this path.  Overall, this verse emphasizes God's sovereign choice in guiding certain individuals, often connected through familial or communal ties, towards a righteous life.
orig: ومن آبائهم وذرياتهم وإخوانهم واجتبيناهم وهديناهم إلى صراط مستقيم

translation: That is the guidance of Allah, by which He guides whom He wills of His servants. And if they had associated others with Allah, invalid would have become for them that which they were doing.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the exclusive nature of God's guidance and the critical importance of monotheism (Tawhid) in Islam.  It states that true guidance comes only from Allah, and He grants it to whomever He chooses among His servants.  The verse then highlights the severe consequence of shirk (associating partners with God): if those who received guidance were to engage in shirk, all their previous good deeds would be nullified and rendered worthless. This underscores the absolute incompatibility of shirk with true faith and the gravity of this transgression in Islamic theology.  It signifies that while good deeds are essential, they are only accepted by God if accompanied by sincere belief in His oneness and exclusive right to worship.
orig: ذلك هدى الله يهدي به من يشاء من عباده ولو أشركوا لحبط عنهم ما كانوا يعملون

translation: Those to whom We gave the Scripture, and wisdom, and prophethood - if these [people] disbelieve in it, We have already entrusted it to a people who are not disbelievers in it.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the nature of divine guidance and its preservation. God bestowed the scripture (likely referring to previous revelations like the Torah and Gospels), wisdom (understanding and applying the scripture's principles), and prophethood (divine messengers to convey and explain the message) upon certain communities. However, if these communities reject or disbelieve in these gifts, God will not let His message be lost. He will entrust it to another group of people who will believe in and uphold it.  This highlights the idea that God's guidance is continuous and will always find a receptive audience. It also suggests a warning against rejecting divine favor, implying that such rejection can lead to the transfer of that favor to others.  Furthermore, it emphasizes the responsibility that comes with receiving divine knowledge and the importance of preserving and sharing it with others. The verse doesn't specify who these "other people" are, allowing for interpretations across different contexts and times, potentially including the early Muslim community during the Prophet Muhammad's time.
orig: أولئك الذين آتيناهم الكتاب والحكم والنبوة فإن يكفر بها هؤلاء فقد وكلنا بها قوما ليسوا بها بكافرين

translation: Those are the ones whom Allah has guided, so follow their guidance. Say, "I do not ask of you any reward for it. It is only a reminder for the worlds."
interpretation: This verse speaks to the importance of following the guidance of those whom God has rightly guided.  The context typically refers to prophets and messengers, particularly Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).  It emphasizes that the message he delivers is divinely inspired and for the benefit of all humanity ("the worlds"). The verse also highlights the selfless nature of the prophet's mission. He seeks no personal gain or reward for conveying this message; his sole purpose is to remind and guide people towards the truth.  The phrase "follow their guidance" doesn't mean blind imitation, but rather following the principles and values they exemplified, based on divine guidance. This reinforces the importance of reflecting on the message itself and striving to understand its deeper meanings. Ultimately, the verse encourages individuals to seek guidance from those who have been divinely illuminated and to recognize the universal nature of the message.
orig: أولئك الذين هدى الله فبهداهم اقتده قل لا أسألكم عليه أجرا إن هو إلا ذكرى للعالمين

translation: They have not appraised Allah with true appraisal when they said, "Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being." Say, "Who then sent down the Book that Moses brought as a light and guidance for mankind, which you [now] make into sheets, disclosing [some of] it and concealing much? And you were taught that which you did not know, neither you nor your fathers." Say, "Allah [sent it down]", then leave them to play in their falsehood.
interpretation:
This verse addresses the denial by some people, likely during the Prophet Muhammad's time, that God could reveal scripture to a human being. It challenges their skepticism by pointing to the Torah, revealed to Moses, which they themselves possessed and claimed to follow. The verse highlights the hypocrisy of these people: they accept the divine origin of the Torah, yet reject the possibility of a similar revelation to Muhammad. 

The phrase "They have not appraised Allah with true appraisal" emphasizes their flawed understanding of God's power and ability to communicate with humanity. Their claim that God wouldn't reveal anything to a human limits God's actions and displays a lack of reverence for His capabilities.

The verse also accuses them of selectively revealing and concealing parts of the Torah, possibly to suit their own interests or interpretations, instead of adhering to its true message.  The phrase "And you were taught that which you did not know, neither you nor your fathers" suggests that the revelation contained knowledge beyond their previous understanding, further reinforcing the idea of a divine source.

Finally, the instruction to "Say, 'Allah [sent it down]', then leave them to play in their falsehood" conveys a sense of exasperation with their stubborn denial.  The Prophet is advised to simply state the truth and then let them continue in their misguided beliefs. The term "play" implies a frivolous and ultimately meaningless engagement with the truth, signifying the futility of arguing with those who refuse to see reason. This points to the idea that sometimes the best course of action when faced with entrenched denial is to leave the matter to God's judgment.
orig: وما قدروا الله حق قدره إذ قالوا ما أنزل الله على بشر من شيء قل من أنزل الكتاب الذي جاء به موسى نورا وهدى للناس تجعلونه قراطيس تبدونها وتخفون كثيرا وعلمتم ما لم تعلموا أنتم ولا آباؤكم قل الله ثم ذرهم في خوضهم يلعبون

translation: And this is a blessed Book which We have sent down, confirming that which was before it, that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it. And those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it, and they are constant in their prayers.
interpretation: This verse speaks of the Qur'an's divine origin and its purpose.  "Blessed" signifies its beneficial nature, bringing guidance and blessings.  "Confirming that which was before it" refers to the Qur'an's consistency with previous scriptures, like the Torah and the Gospels, while also correcting distortions and completing the message. "The Mother of Cities" is generally understood as Mecca, the spiritual center of Islam, and "those around it" refers to the surrounding regions, expanding the call to all of humanity. The verse emphasizes the connection between belief in the Hereafter and belief in the Qur'an, highlighting that true acceptance of the Qur'an necessitates belief in the afterlife and accountability before God. This sincere belief manifests in steadfast adherence to prayer, indicating a practical commitment to the faith and a striving for spiritual connection with the Divine. Thus, the verse establishes the Qur'an as a divine guide, affirms its connection to previous scriptures, identifies its target audience as all of humanity starting with Mecca, and connects true belief with consistent prayer.
orig: وهذا كتاب أنزلناه مبارك مصدق الذي بين يديه ولتنذر أم القرى ومن حولها والذين يؤمنون بالآخرة يؤمنون به وهم على صلاتهم يحافظون

translation: And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie about Allah or says, "It has been inspired to me," while nothing has been inspired to him, and one who says, "I will reveal [something] like what Allah has revealed?" And if you could but see when the wrongdoers are in the overwhelming pangs of death while the angels extend their hands, [saying], "Discharge your souls! Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation for what you used to say against Allah other than the truth and [that] you were, toward His verses, arrogant."
interpretation: This verse condemns those who falsely claim divine inspiration or try to replicate the divine revelation of the Quran. It highlights the grave sin of fabricating lies about God and the severe consequences that await such individuals.  The verse paints a vivid picture of the moment of death for these wrongdoers, emphasizing their helplessness and the angels' demand for their souls. The punishment they face is described as 'the punishment of humiliation,' highlighting the disgrace and ignominy associated with their false claims and arrogance towards God's signs.  It serves as a powerful warning against the dangers of religious deception and pride, emphasizing the importance of truthfulness and humility before God.  The contrast between the false claims of revelation during life and the harsh reality of death underscores the ultimate futility of such deception.
orig: ومن أظلم ممن افترى على الله كذبا أو قال أوحي إلي ولم يوح إليه شيء ومن قال سأنزل مثل ما أنزل الله ولو ترى إذ الظالمون في غمرات الموت والملائكة باسطو أيديهم أخرجوا أنفسكم اليوم تجزون عذاب الهون بما كنتم تقولون على الله غير الحق وكنتم عن آياته تستكبرون

translation: And you have certainly come to Us alone as We created you the first time, and you have left behind your backs all that We bestowed upon you. And We do not see with you your intercessors whom you claimed were your partners. Certainly, the bond between you has been severed, and what you used to claim has vanished from you.
interpretation: This verse depicts the Day of Judgement, highlighting the stark reality that individuals stand before God alone, stripped of worldly possessions and social connections.  It emphasizes the individual's direct accountability to God, regardless of any earthly affiliations or beliefs in intermediaries.  The phrase "as We created you the first time" points to the initial state of human creation, innocent and without the accumulated burdens and distractions of worldly life.  The verse then describes the abandonment of material wealth and the absence of intercessors who were falsely believed to hold sway with God.  These previously claimed partnerships and supports are now revealed as illusions, the bonds broken, and the imagined power of intercession vanished.  The finality of this separation and the futility of false beliefs are powerfully conveyed, underscoring the absolute sovereignty of God and the direct relationship between the individual and their Creator.
orig: ولقد جئتمونا فرادى كما خلقناكم أول مرة وتركتم ما خولناكم وراء ظهوركم وما نرى معكم شفعاءكم الذين زعمتم أنهم فيكم شركاء لقد تقطع بينكم وضل عنكم ما كنتم تزعمون

translation: Indeed, Allah is the cleaver of the seed and the date stone. He brings forth the living from the dead and brings forth the dead from the living. That is Allah, so how are you deluded?
interpretation: This verse highlights God's power over life and death, using the imagery of germination as a metaphor for resurrection.  The 'cleaving' of the seed and date stone refers to the sprouting of life from seemingly inert matter.  This process, where a living plant emerges from a 'dead' seed, is compared to God's ability to bring forth the living from the dead (resurrection) and the dead from the living (death).  The verse emphasizes the continuous cycle of life and death, controlled entirely by God.  The rhetorical question at the end, 'so how are you deluded?', challenges those who doubt God's power and the reality of resurrection, particularly given the observable miracle of plant life springing forth from seeds.
orig: إن الله فالق الحب والنوى يخرج الحي من الميت ومخرج الميت من الحي ذلكم الله فأنى تؤفكون

translation: He splits the dawn (from the darkness) and has made the night for rest, and the sun and the moon for calculation (of time). That is the decree of the Exalted in Might, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse highlights God's power and wisdom in creating and regulating the natural world for the benefit of humankind.  The splitting of the dawn signifies the transition from darkness to light, symbolizing the beginning of a new day and the continuous renewal of life. The night is designated for rest and rejuvenation, allowing creatures to recuperate after the day's activities.  The sun and moon are not merely celestial bodies but serve a crucial function: they provide a precise system for measuring time, enabling humans to organize their lives, track seasons, and understand the passage of time.  This intricate and perfectly balanced system is ultimately attributed to God, described as 'Al-Aziz,' the Exalted in Might, and 'Al-Aleem,' the All-Knowing, emphasizing His absolute power and profound wisdom in orchestrating the universe.
orig: فالق الإصباح وجعل الليل سكنا والشمس والقمر حسبانا ذلك تقدير العزيز العليم

translation: And it is He who made the stars for you, that you may be guided by them through the darknesses of the land and sea. We have detailed the signs for a people who know.
interpretation: This verse highlights God's role as the creator and provider of guidance. The stars are presented as a navigational tool, assisting humans in traversing the darkness on both land and sea. This can be understood literally, referring to celestial navigation, a practice employed for centuries by sailors and travelers.  Beyond the literal, the verse also carries a metaphorical meaning. The "darknesses" can represent the uncertainties and challenges of life, while the stars symbolize divine guidance and knowledge offered through the Qur'an and the prophets.  The phrase "We have detailed the signs" emphasizes the clarity and comprehensiveness of God's messages for those who are willing to understand and reflect. This suggests that true guidance requires intellectual effort and a sincere desire for knowledge ("a people who know").  The verse encourages contemplation of the natural world as a testament to God's wisdom and power, and it underscores the importance of seeking knowledge and understanding to navigate the complexities of life.
orig: وهو الذي جعل لكم النجوم لتهتدوا بها في ظلمات البر والبحر قد فصلنا الآيات لقوم يعلمون

translation: And it is He who created you from a single soul and [then made from that soul] a place of settlement and a place of deposit. We have detailed the signs for a people who understand.
interpretation: This verse (Quran 6:98) speaks to the unity of humanity's origin.  God created all of humankind from a single soul (nafs), often understood as Adam.  The terms "place of settlement" (mustaqarr) and "place of deposit" (mustawda') refer to the womb.  This signifies the process of human reproduction and development, highlighting how God provides a safe and nurturing environment for the growth of the embryo and fetus. The verse emphasizes that God has made these processes clear and understandable through the signs (ayat) present in creation and revelation. These signs are specifically directed towards those who possess intellectual and spiritual understanding (yafqahun), implying that reflection and contemplation are necessary to grasp the deeper wisdom embedded within the creation and continuation of human life. The verse, therefore, serves as a reminder of our shared origin and the divine wisdom evident in the processes of procreation and development, encouraging us to contemplate and appreciate these divine signs.
orig: وهو الذي أنشأكم من نفس واحدة فمستقر ومستودع قد فصلنا الآيات لقوم يفقهون

translation: And it is He who sends down rain from the sky, and We produce thereby the growth of all things. Then We produce from it green vegetation, from which We produce grains arranged in layers. And from the date palm, from its emerging fruit, are clusters hanging low, and gardens of grapes and olives and pomegranates, similar yet dissimilar. Look at their fruit, when they bear fruit and ripen. Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the power and wisdom of God as the creator and sustainer of life. It highlights the miraculous process by which rain, a seemingly simple substance, gives rise to the incredible diversity of plant life.  God uses the rain to bring forth vegetation, from which grains grow in layered formations. The verse then draws attention to specific examples like date palms with their low-hanging fruit clusters, and vineyards, olive groves, and pomegranate orchards.  The phrase "similar yet dissimilar" emphasizes the variety within these fruits; although they belong to the general category of fruits, each has its unique characteristics in taste, texture, appearance, and nutritional value.  The verse concludes by urging observation and reflection. The process of fruiting and ripening is presented as a sign of God's divine power and artistry. These signs are meant for those who are open to believing, who are willing to see the hand of God in the wonders of the natural world.  By observing the intricate stages of plant growth and the diverse fruits they bear, believers are encouraged to deepen their faith and appreciation for God's creative power and provision.
orig: وهو الذي أنزل من السماء ماء فأخرجنا به نبات كل شيء فأخرجنا منه خضرا نخرج منه حبا متراكبا ومن النخل من طلعها قنوان دانية وجنات من أعناب والزيتون والرمان مشتبها وغير متشابه انظروا إلى ثمره إذا أثمر وينعه إن في ذلكم لآيات لقوم يؤمنون

translation: And they assigned to Allah partners - the jinn, while He created them. And they falsely attributed to Him sons and daughters without knowledge. Exalted is He and high above what they describe.
interpretation: This verse condemns the practice of associating partners with God (shirk), a major sin in Islam.  It highlights two specific forms of shirk prevalent in pre-Islamic Arabia. Firstly, the verse mentions the attribution of jinn as partners to Allah. While the jinn are recognized as created beings in Islamic cosmology, they hold a lower status than humans and certainly cannot be considered divine or equal to God.  Their association with Allah diminishes His absolute oneness and power. Secondly, the verse addresses the false attribution of sons and daughters to Allah. This reflects the pre-Islamic belief in lesser deities, often conceptualized as offspring of a supreme god.  The Quran rejects this anthropomorphic view of God, emphasizing His transcendence and absolute uniqueness.  The phrase "without knowledge" underscores the ignorance and baselessness of these beliefs. Finally, the verse concludes with a declaration of God's exaltedness and transcendence, highlighting the immense gap between His true nature and the limited, flawed understanding of those who ascribe partners to Him.
orig: وجعلوا لله شركاء الجن وخلقهم وخرقوا له بنين وبنات بغير علم سبحانه وتعالى عما يصفون

translation: Originator of the heavens and the earth. How can He have children when He has no wife? He created all things, and He is, of all things, Knowing.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute uniqueness and transcendence of God (Allah). It negates the possibility of God having offspring by highlighting the logical contradiction: procreation requires a partner, a 'wife,' which is incompatible with God's singular and self-sufficient nature. The verse affirms God as the sole creator of everything, possessing complete knowledge of all creation. This reinforces the Islamic concept of Tawhid (Oneness of God), rejecting any notion of partners or equals to God.  The term 'Badi' (Originator) signifies God's unique and unparalleled act of creation, bringing forth the universe from nothing.  The verse thus serves as a powerful affirmation of God's absolute power, knowledge, and independence from any need or association.
orig: بديع السماوات والأرض أنى يكون له ولد ولم تكن له صاحبة وخلق كل شيء وهو بكل شيء عليم

translation: That is Allah, your Lord; there is no deity except Him, the Creator of all things, so worship Him. And He is Disposer of all things.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the fundamental Islamic principle of Tawhid (Oneness of God). It asserts that Allah is the only true God, the sole creator and sustainer of the entire universe.  Everything that exists owes its being to Him. Therefore, worship is due to Him alone. The term 'wakil' (Disposer of all things) highlights Allah's complete control and authority over all affairs in creation. He manages and governs everything, and nothing happens outside of His knowledge and will. This verse calls for exclusive devotion to Allah and recognizes His ultimate power and authority.
orig: ذلكم الله ربكم لا إله إلا هو خالق كل شيء فاعبدوه وهو على كل شيء وكيل

translation: Vision perceives Him not, but He perceives [all] vision; and He is the Subtle, the Aware.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the transcendent nature of God (Allah).  It emphasizes that God is beyond human comprehension and cannot be perceived by our physical senses, particularly sight.  While we cannot see Him, He sees and knows everything.  The description of God as "al-Lateef" (the Subtle) signifies His profound delicacy and intricate involvement in all things, often unseen and unperceived by us.  He works in ways beyond our grasp.  "Al-Khabeer" (the Aware) highlights God's complete and perfect knowledge of all things, both hidden and manifest.  This combination underscores God's omniscience and intimate awareness of all creation, even though He remains beyond our direct perception.
orig: لا تدركه الأبصار وهو يدرك الأبصار وهو اللطيف الخبير

translation: Clear proofs have come to you from your Lord; so whoever sees [i.e., benefits from them], it is for his own soul; and whoever is blind [i.e., chooses to ignore them], it is to his own detriment. And I am not over you a keeper.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the concept of free will and individual responsibility in accepting or rejecting divine guidance. God has sent clear signs and proofs (بصائر - basā'ir) through the Qur'an and the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).  These "proofs" are not limited to physical miracles but encompass intellectual and spiritual insights as well.  Those who choose to "see" these proofs and follow them will benefit their own souls and find guidance.  Conversely, those who choose to remain "blind" to the truth, ignoring or rejecting these signs, will only harm themselves.  The verse clarifies that the Prophet's role is to deliver the message, not to force belief.  He is a warner, not a "keeper" (حفيظ - hafiz) who controls people's choices or compels them to believe.  The ultimate responsibility for one's fate rests upon oneself.
orig: قد جاءكم بصائر من ربكم فمن أبصر فلنفسه ومن عمي فعليها وما أنا عليكم بحفيظ

translation: And thus We diversify the signs/verses (ayat) so that they may say, "You have studied," and [so] We may make it clear for a people who know.
interpretation:
This verse speaks to the multifaceted nature of the Qur'an's verses (ayat) and how they address different audiences.  "We diversify the signs" can refer to the variety of styles, subjects, and levels of meaning present within the Qur'an.  Some verses are straightforward and easily understood, while others are more complex and require deeper reflection. 

The phrase "so that they may say, 'You have studied'" likely refers to those who might accuse the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) of simply learning these teachings from others. The diversity and depth of the Qur'an's message refute this claim, showcasing a divine origin beyond human fabrication.  It's not simply learned knowledge but divine wisdom. 

The concluding phrase, "and [so] We may make it clear for a people who know," emphasizes that the Qur'an's deeper meanings are accessible to those who possess true knowledge and understanding. This 'knowledge' encompasses not only intellectual learning but also spiritual insight and a sincere desire to seek truth. The verse suggests that the Qur'an caters to different levels of understanding, providing guidance for both the general population and those who delve deeper into its wisdom. It also suggests that the diversity of the verses acts as a test, separating those who are genuinely seeking knowledge from those who are merely superficial in their approach. Therefore, the diversity of the verses serves both as a refutation to accusers and as a means of clarification for those who are truly receptive to its message.
orig: وكذلك نصرف الآيات وليقولوا درست ولنبينه لقوم يعلمون

translation: Follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord; there is no god but He, and turn away from the polytheists.
interpretation: This verse directs the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to adhere strictly to the divine revelation he received from God.  It emphasizes the fundamental Islamic principle of Tawhid (Oneness of God) by declaring that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah.  The command to "turn away from the polytheists" doesn't necessarily imply a complete social boycott, but rather a rejection of their polytheistic beliefs and practices.  It instructs the Prophet to focus on his mission of conveying God's message and not to be swayed or influenced by the pressures or beliefs of those who associate partners with God.  This verse reinforces the importance of unwavering faith and commitment to God's guidance above all else.
orig: اتبع ما أوحي إليك من ربك لا إله إلا هو وأعرض عن المشركين

translation: And had Allah willed, they would not have associated [anything with Him]. And We have not appointed you as a guardian over them, and you are not a manager over them.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the concept of free will in Islam. While God has the power to prevent people from associating partners with Him (shirk), He has chosen to grant them the freedom to choose their beliefs and actions.  This verse absolves the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) from responsibility for the choices people make regarding their faith. He is a messenger, delivering the message of God, not a controller of people's hearts or actions.  The verse uses the words "guardian" (hafiz) and "manager" (wakil) to clarify the Prophet's role. He is not responsible for forcing people to believe or for ensuring their adherence to the faith. Their choices and their accountability rest with them.  It highlights God's ultimate authority and the limitations of the Prophet's role, focusing on delivering the divine message and leaving the choice of acceptance to individuals.
orig: ولو شاء الله ما أشركوا وما جعلناك عليهم حفيظا وما أنت عليهم بوكيل

translation: And do not insult those they invoke other than Allah, lest they insult Allah in enmity without knowledge. Thus We have made pleasing to every nation their deeds. Then to their Lord is their return, and He will inform them about what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the importance of respecting other people's beliefs, even if we disagree with them.  Insulting other deities will likely lead to them insulting Allah in retaliation, but out of ignorance, not genuine malice.  This reciprocal disrespect doesn't benefit anyone. The verse highlights that each community has its own set of practices and beliefs that seem appealing or right to them. However, ultimately, everyone will return to God, who is the ultimate judge and will assess their actions based on true knowledge and divine justice. The focus is on avoiding a cycle of negativity and emphasizing the ultimate accountability of every individual to God. It promotes tolerance and discourages engaging in unproductive arguments based on ignorance.
orig: ولا تسبوا الذين يدعون من دون الله فيسبوا الله عدوا بغير علم كذلك زينا لكل أمة عملهم ثم إلى ربهم مرجعهم فينبئهم بما كانوا يعملون

translation: And they swear by Allah with the strongest of their oaths that if a sign comes to them, they will surely believe in it. Say, "Indeed, the signs are with Allah . And what will make you perceive that when it comes they will not believe?"
interpretation: This verse speaks to the hypocrisy of some who claimed they would believe if only they were shown a miraculous sign. They make emphatic oaths, swearing by God, to underscore their supposed sincerity. However, the verse subtly exposes their disingenuousness.  The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is instructed to respond that true signs are already present, both in the natural world and in the revealed message, yet these individuals choose to ignore them.  The implication is that their demand for a sign is not a genuine search for truth, but rather a pretext for continued disbelief. Even if a spectacular sign were given, their hearts are already closed, and they would likely find a way to rationalize it away or attribute it to something other than divine origin.  The verse thus highlights the importance of sincere intention and open-mindedness in seeking truth, and warns against using the demand for signs as a shield against faith.
orig: وأقسموا بالله جهد أيمانهم لئن جاءتهم آية ليؤمنن بها قل إنما الآيات عند الله وما يشعركم أنها إذا جاءت لا يؤمنون

translation: And We shall turn their hearts and their sights away, as they did not believe in it the first time, and We shall leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the consequence of persistent disbelief and rejection of truth.  It describes a process of spiritual hardening where God, after repeated opportunities for guidance, allows individuals to become further entrenched in their misguided ways.  The "turning of hearts and sights" doesn't imply forced misguidance, but rather a withdrawal of divine grace and allowing the natural consequences of their choices to manifest.  Their initial rejection becomes a pattern, amplified by their continued transgression ('tughyan'), leading to a state of spiritual blindness ('ya'mahun') where they wander aimlessly, unable to discern truth from falsehood. This isn't a punishment in the conventional sense, but a consequence of their own choices and a state of being they have effectively chosen for themselves through their continuous rejection of guidance.
orig: ونقلب أفئدتهم وأبصارهم كما لم يؤمنوا به أول مرة ونذرهم في طغيانهم يعمهون

translation: Even if We had sent down to them the angels, and the dead had spoken to them, and We had gathered before them all things, face to face, they would not have believed unless Allah willed; but most of them are ignorant.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the profound nature of belief and disbelief.  It highlights that sometimes, even overwhelming evidence, like witnessing angels or hearing the dead speak, isn't enough to convince someone of the truth if their heart is closed to it.  True faith, the verse suggests, is ultimately guided by divine will (Allah's willing).  It's not simply a matter of intellectual assent to presented evidence. The verse also points to the role of ignorance (جهل - jahl) in hindering belief. This ignorance isn't merely a lack of knowledge, but rather a lack of understanding, a closed-mindedness that prevents individuals from recognizing and accepting truth even when it's presented clearly.  It implies that a predisposition towards disbelief, coupled with a lack of spiritual insight, can prevent even the most miraculous signs from impacting one's belief system.
orig: ولو أننا نزلنا إليهم الملائكة وكلمهم الموتى وحشرنا عليهم كل شيء قبلا ما كانوا ليؤمنوا إلا أن يشاء الله ولكن أكثرهم يجهلون

translation: And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy - devils from among mankind and jinn, inspiring to one another decorative speech in delusion.  And if your Lord had willed, they would not have done it, so leave them and what they invent.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the universal nature of prophetic struggle.  Every prophet sent by God has faced opposition, and this opposition often comes in the form of deceptive and alluring rhetoric.  The verse identifies two sources of this opposition: devils from among mankind (human beings who act in devilish ways) and jinn (spiritual beings capable of influencing humans).  These enemies collaborate, inspiring each other with embellished and misleading arguments to sway people away from the prophet's message.  The phrase "decorative speech in delusion" (زخرف القول غرورا) highlights the seductive nature of falsehood; it's presented in a way that appears attractive and convincing, but ultimately leads to misguidance.  The verse also emphasizes God's ultimate power and control.  He allows these adversaries to exist and test humanity, but He could prevent their actions if He willed. The instruction to "leave them and what they invent" (فذرهم وما يفترون)  can be interpreted in several ways. It could mean to leave their judgment to God, to avoid engaging with their falsehoods directly, or to focus on one's own path of righteousness despite their efforts.  Ultimately, it underscores the importance of staying steadfast in faith amidst the inevitable presence of deception and opposition.
orig: وكذلك جعلنا لكل نبي عدوا شياطين الإنس والجن يوحي بعضهم إلى بعض زخرف القول غرورا ولو شاء ربك ما فعلوه فذرهم وما يفترون

translation: And that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it (i.e., this worldly life) and that they may be pleased with it and that they may commit what they are committing.
interpretation: This verse describes the behavior and mindset of those who disbelieve in the afterlife.  Their focus is entirely fixed on the present world.  "Incline to it" suggests that their hearts are drawn towards worldly pleasures and possessions, becoming completely absorbed by them.  "Be pleased with it" indicates a state of satisfaction and contentment with their worldly gains, with no aspiration for anything beyond. The final phrase, "and that they may commit what they are committing," can be interpreted in two ways.  First, it acknowledges that their disbelief in accountability in the Hereafter emboldens them to engage in sinful acts without fear of divine retribution. Second, it can also be understood as a form of divine decree, meaning that they are left to their own devices to continue down their chosen path of heedlessness. The verse doesn't necessarily imply God's forcing them to sin, but rather allowing their choices to determine their consequences. Essentially, it illustrates the self-perpetuating cycle of disbelief: a lack of faith in the Hereafter leads to worldly preoccupation, which in turn reinforces their disregard for spiritual and moral values.
orig: ولتصغى إليه أفئدة الذين لا يؤمنون بالآخرة وليرضوه وليقترفوا ما هم مقترفون

translation: Shall I then seek a judge other than God, when it is He who has sent down to you the Book fully detailed? Those to whom We have given the Book know that it is sent down from your Lord in truth, so do not be among those who doubt.
interpretation: This verse asserts the ultimate authority of God and His revealed Book (the Qur'an) as the sole source of judgment and guidance. It emphasizes the clarity and detail of the divine revelation, highlighting that those who have received previous scriptures (Jews and Christians) recognize the truth of the Qur'an's divine origin.  The verse serves as a strong rebuke against seeking judgment or validation from any other source besides God and His revealed word. It warns against succumbing to doubt (expressed by the term 'al-mumtarīn') and emphasizes the importance of unwavering faith in the divine message.  The rhetorical question at the beginning reinforces the absurdity of seeking judgment elsewhere, given the clarity and authority of God's revelation.
orig: أفغير الله أبتغي حكما وهو الذي أنزل إليكم الكتاب مفصلا والذين آتيناهم الكتاب يعلمون أنه منزل من ربك بالحق فلا تكونن من الممترين

translation: And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice.  There is no changer for His words, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse powerfully affirms the absolute truth, unwavering justice, and unchanging nature of God's word.  "Fulfilled" suggests that God's promises and pronouncements are inevitable and will come to pass.  The emphasis on "truth" and "justice" highlights the righteous and equitable nature of God's decrees.  The phrase "There is no changer for His words" underscores God's absolute authority and the immutability of His divine plan.  Nothing can alter, delay, or prevent what God has willed.  Finally, the attributes of "All-Hearing" and "All-Knowing" reinforce God's complete awareness of all things, including our supplications and deeds, further emphasizing His power and authority to fulfill His word.
orig: وتمت كلمت ربك صدقا وعدلا لا مبدل لكلماته وهو السميع العليم

translation: And if you obey most of those upon the earth, they will mislead you from the way of Allah . They follow not except assumption, and they are not except [engaged in] conjecture.
interpretation: This verse cautions against blindly following the majority, especially when it comes to matters of faith and guidance.  It highlights that popularity doesn't equate to truth.  The majority of people on Earth, at any given time, may not be on the right path according to Islamic teachings.  Their guidance often relies on mere assumptions, guesses (ظن - thann), and unfounded conjectures (خرص - khars), lacking a firm basis in divine revelation.  Therefore, a true believer should seek guidance from Allah's revealed word and the teachings of His prophets, rather than being swayed by popular opinion or societal norms that may deviate from the straight path.  This emphasizes the importance of independent thought, critical thinking, and seeking knowledge from reliable sources in matters of religion and life.
orig: وإن تطع أكثر من في الأرض يضلوك عن سبيل الله إن يتبعون إلا الظن وإن هم إلا يخرصون

translation: Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of the [rightly] guided.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's omniscience regarding both those who choose to deviate from the righteous path He has laid out and those who adhere to it and find guidance.  It highlights that God is fully aware of the choices individuals make regarding their faith and actions.  'Straying from His way' can refer to both physical actions and internal beliefs that contradict God's guidance.  The verse doesn't imply a predetermined fate, but rather underscores God's complete knowledge of each person's path and their ultimate destination, be it guidance or misguidance.  This knowledge serves as a reminder of accountability, as God is the ultimate judge, fully aware of the motivations and actions of all.
orig: إن ربك هو أعلم من يضل عن سبيله وهو أعلم بالمهتدين

translation: So eat of that [meat] upon which the name of Allah has been mentioned, if you are believers in His verses.
interpretation: This verse pertains to the Islamic dietary laws, specifically regarding the permissibility of consuming meat.  It mandates that before an animal is slaughtered for consumption, the name of God (Allah) must be invoked. This act signifies a recognition that life is sacred and a gift from God, and that taking a life, even for sustenance, should be done with reverence and gratitude.  The phrase "if you are believers in His verses" emphasizes that adherence to this practice is a demonstration of faith and obedience to God's commands.  Therefore, consuming meat upon which God's name has not been mentioned is considered unlawful. This verse also indirectly highlights the importance of halal slaughter, which involves specific methods designed to minimize the animal's suffering.  It connects the act of eating with a broader spiritual context, emphasizing mindfulness and thankfulness for God's provisions.
orig: فكلوا مما ذكر اسم الله عليه إن كنتم بآياته مؤمنين

translation: And why should you not eat of that upon which the name of Allah has been mentioned, while He has explained in detail to you what He has forbidden you, except under compulsion? And indeed, many lead [others] astray through their desires without knowledge. Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of the transgressors.
interpretation: This verse addresses the issue of permissible and forbidden foods in Islam.  It questions why believers would abstain from eating something upon which the name of God (Allah) has been invoked, signifying its halal (permissible) nature.  God has clearly outlined what is haram (forbidden), and the verse emphasizes that these prohibitions are binding except in situations of dire necessity (e.g., starvation).  The exception of necessity highlights the overarching principle of preserving life. The verse then criticizes those who mislead others by promoting their own desires and opinions regarding dietary restrictions, lacking proper knowledge and deviating from divine guidance. Such individuals are considered transgressors, and God is fully aware of their actions.  This verse therefore encourages adherence to the divinely prescribed dietary laws, emphasizes the importance of knowledge over personal whims, and warns against misleading others in matters of faith.
orig: وما لكم ألا تأكلوا مما ذكر اسم الله عليه وقد فصل لكم ما حرم عليكم إلا ما اضطررتم إليه وإن كثيرا ليضلون بأهوائهم بغير علم إن ربك هو أعلم بالمعتدين

translation: And abandon the outward sin and the inward sin. Indeed, those who earn sin will be recompensed for what they used to commit.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the importance of avoiding both visible and hidden sins. "Outward sin" (Zhahir al-ithm) refers to actions that are openly seen as wrong, such as stealing, lying, or physical harm. "Inward sin" (Batin al-ithm) refers to the inner thoughts, intentions, and feelings that are sinful, like harboring envy, malice, or lustful desires.  The verse warns that accountability isn't just for external actions but also internal states.  Ultimately, all sins, whether public or private, will have consequences, and those who commit them will face appropriate recompense for their deeds.  This underscores the Islamic concept of  God's complete knowledge and the importance of purifying both one's actions and heart.
orig: وذروا ظاهر الإثم وباطنه إن الذين يكسبون الإثم سيجزون بما كانوا يقترفون
