If Allah were to immediately fulfill every request for good, people might not learn patience, gratitude, or the value of striving. Conversely, if every curse or ill wish was instantly realized, humanity would be destroyed rapidly.  The verse then focuses on those who deny the Day of Judgement ("who do not expect Our meeting"). Because they don't believe in ultimate accountability, they remain lost in their transgression, "wandering blindly" without guidance or a true understanding of the consequences of their actions. They are left to their own devices, deepening their straying from the right path.  The verse thus underscores Allah's mercy and wisdom in delaying both the good and the bad, giving people the time and opportunity to repent, to turn to good, and to ultimately find their way back to Him.
orig: ولو يعجل الله للناس الشر استعجالهم بالخير لقضي إليهم أجلهم فنذر الذين لا يرجون لقاءنا في طغيانهم يعمهون

translation: And when adversity touches man, he calls upon Us, whether lying on his side or sitting or standing; but when We remove the adversity from him, he passes on as if he had never called upon Us for an adversity that touched him. Thus is made appealing to the transgressors that which they have been doing.
interpretation: This verse highlights the flawed nature of some people's faith and gratitude.  When faced with hardship or adversity (represented by the Arabic word "ضر" - *ḍurr*),  a person earnestly supplicates to God, regardless of their physical position (lying down, sitting, or standing). They are fully focused on seeking relief and divine intervention. However, once God alleviates their suffering, they often revert to their old ways, behaving as if they never experienced hardship or sought divine aid.  They forget their desperate pleas and the divine grace that answered them.  The verse uses the word "مسرفين" (*musrifīn*) which typically means 'transgressors' or 'those who go beyond limits'. In this context, it refers to those who are excessive in their heedlessness and ingratitude.  Their actions are 'made appealing' (زين - *zuyyina*) to them, implying a self-deception where they justify their lack of gratitude and continue down a path of heedlessness. This verse serves as a reminder of the importance of consistent faith, gratitude, and remembrance of God, both in times of ease and difficulty.
orig: وإذا مس الإنسان الضر دعانا لجنبه أو قاعدا أو قائما فلما كشفنا عنه ضره مر كأن لم يدعنا إلى ضر مسه كذلك زين للمسرفين ما كانوا يعملون

translation: And We have certainly destroyed the generations before you when they wronged, and their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they would not believe. Thus do We recompense the criminal people.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the consistent pattern of divine justice throughout history.  Previous generations, like those before the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), were destroyed due to their persistent wrongdoing (zulm).  This wrongdoing isn't simply individual acts but often societal injustice and rejection of truth.  The verse highlights that these past communities were given clear warnings and guidance through their messengers (rusul), who brought irrefutable evidence (bayyinat). Despite these clear signs, they chose disbelief and persisted in their transgression. This verse serves as a warning to later generations, including the Prophet's own community and subsequent ones, that the same fate awaits those who follow the path of oppression and reject the truth brought to them by God's messengers.  The phrase 'Thus do We recompense the criminal people' (ka-dhālika najzi al-qawm al-mujrimīn) affirms the principle of divine retribution for persistent wrongdoing and rejection of divine guidance.  It underscores God's justice and the consequences of choosing disbelief and oppression over truth and righteousness.
orig: ولقد أهلكنا القرون من قبلكم لما ظلموا وجاءتهم رسلهم بالبينات وما كانوا ليؤمنوا كذلك نجزي القوم المجرمين

translation: Then We made you successors upon the earth after them so that We may observe how you work.
interpretation: This verse speaks to humanity's role as stewards or custodians of the Earth after previous generations.  The term 'khala'if' (successors) implies both inheritance and responsibility.  We inherit the Earth from those who came before and are responsible for how we manage and care for it. The phrase 'observe how you work' suggests a divine evaluation of human actions, highlighting the importance of ethical conduct, justice, and responsible stewardship in all aspects of life, including environmental, social, and political spheres. It implies that humanity's actions have consequences and are being observed, suggesting accountability for how we utilize our position and the resources entrusted to us.
orig: ثم جعلناكم خلائف في الأرض من بعدهم لننظر كيف تعملون

translation: And when Our clear verses are recited to them, those who do not expect to meet Us say, "Bring a Qur'an other than this or change it." Say, "It is not for me to change it on my own accord. I only follow what is revealed to me. Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day."
interpretation: This verse addresses the rejection and demands for alteration of the Qur'an by those who disbelieve in the Day of Judgement ("those who do not expect to meet Us").  They find the message of the Qur'an challenging to their worldview and desires, and therefore, instead of accepting its divine origin, they demand the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to either produce a different scripture altogether or alter the existing one to suit their preferences.  Their demand reveals not only their disbelief but also their lack of understanding of the nature of revelation.  The Prophet's response clarifies that he is not the author of the Qur'an and therefore has no authority to change it. He acts solely as a messenger, conveying the divine revelation as it is revealed to him.  The verse emphasizes the Prophet's complete obedience and submission to God's will. He expresses fear of disobeying God and facing the consequences on the Day of Judgement ("a tremendous Day"), which highlights the gravity of the responsibility entrusted to him and the severity of divine punishment for altering the divine message. This verse ultimately affirms the Qur'an's divine origin, immutability, and the Prophet's role as a faithful conveyor of God's word.
orig: وإذا تتلى عليهم آياتنا بينات قال الذين لا يرجون لقاءنا ائت بقرآن غير هذا أو بدله قل ما يكون لي أن أبدله من تلقاء نفسي إن أتبع إلا ما يوحى إلي إني أخاف إن عصيت ربي عذاب يوم عظيم

translation: Say, "If Allah had willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made it known to you. I have already lived among you a lifetime before this. Do you not then understand?"
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the Prophet Muhammad's reliance on divine will in conveying the Qur'an. It asserts that the revelation isn't his own doing, but rather a message entrusted to him by God.  The mention of his prior life among his audience serves to remind them of his established character and credibility, strengthening the argument that his sudden shift to prophethood is genuine and divinely ordained. The verse concludes with a rhetorical question, prompting the listeners to reflect upon the implications of this message and recognize the truth of its divine origin. It highlights the importance of using intellect and reason alongside observation and experience to understand God's will. It's a call to move beyond mere acceptance and engage actively in comprehending the significance of the Qur'an.
orig: قل لو شاء الله ما تلوته عليكم ولا أدراكم به فقد لبثت فيكم عمرا من قبله أفلا تعقلون

translation: So who is more unjust than one who invents a lie about Allah or denies His signs? Indeed, the criminals will not succeed.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the gravity of two major sins: falsely attributing things to God (fabricating lies about Him) and rejecting His clear signs or verses.  The rhetorical question "So who is more unjust...?" highlights the extreme nature of these transgressions.  Inventing lies about God includes ascribing false attributes, actions, or pronouncements to Him, thereby distorting His true nature and misleading others. Denying His signs encompasses rejecting the truth of the Quran, miracles, and other evidence of His existence and power. The verse concludes by stating that such "criminals" – those guilty of these grave offenses – will ultimately face failure and will not achieve true success or felicity in this life or the hereafter. This failure encompasses both spiritual and worldly consequences.  The verse serves as a stern warning against these sins and underscores the importance of upholding truth and recognizing God's authority.
orig: فمن أظلم ممن افترى على الله كذبا أو كذب بآياته إنه لا يفلح المجرمون

translation: And they worship besides Allah things that neither harm them nor benefit them, and they say, "These are our intercessors with Allah." Say, "Do you inform Allah of what He does not know in the heavens or on the earth?" Exalted is He and high above what they associate [with Him].
interpretation: This verse critiques the practice of idolatry and intercession by anyone other than God.  It highlights the illogical nature of worshipping powerless idols that can neither cause harm nor bring benefit.  People who engage in such practices often justify them by claiming these idols act as intercessors, pleading to God on their behalf. The verse challenges this notion by rhetorically asking if these worshippers are informing God of something He doesn't already know, implying the inherent omniscience of God. The concluding phrase "Exalted is He and high above what they associate [with Him]" emphasizes God's transcendence and absolute uniqueness, rejecting any partners or intermediaries.
orig: ويعبدون من دون الله ما لا يضرهم ولا ينفعهم ويقولون هؤلاء شفعاؤنا عند الله قل أتنبئون الله بما لا يعلم في السماوات ولا في الأرض سبحانه وتعالى عما يشركون

translation: And mankind was [of] one nation [united in belief], but then they differed. And were it not for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been judged between them concerning that over which they differ.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the fundamental unity of humanity's origins.  All people initially shared a single belief system, understood in Islamic tradition as the primordial monotheism of Adam and his early descendants.  However, over time, disagreements and divergent interpretations arose, leading to the diversity of beliefs we see today.  The 'word that preceded from your Lord' refers to God's decree that a period of testing and trial would exist in this world, allowing for the manifestation of differing beliefs.  This divine decree postpones the final judgment and reckoning regarding these differences until the Hereafter.  Thus, while the ultimate truth is known to God, human beings are given the freedom to choose their paths, with the understanding that they will be held accountable for their choices in the next life. This emphasizes both God's foreknowledge and humanity's free will in navigating the complexities of belief and action.
orig: وما كان الناس إلا أمة واحدة فاختلفوا ولولا كلمة سبقت من ربك لقضي بينهم فيما فيه يختلفون

translation: And they say, "Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "Indeed, the unseen belongs to Allah, so wait; indeed, I am with you among those who wait."
interpretation:
This verse addresses the demands of skeptics who challenge the Prophet Muhammad's claim to prophethood by asking for a miraculous sign.  It highlights a few key theological concepts:

1. **Divine Authority over the Unseen (Al-Ghaib):**  The verse emphasizes that knowledge and control of the unseen realm belong solely to God.  Miracles, being a manifestation of the unseen, are not given on demand or as proof to satisfy doubters.  God decides when and how to reveal His signs.

2. **Patience and Waiting (Intizar):**  The Prophet is instructed to respond to these demands with patience and to wait for God's will. This underscores the importance of trusting in God's timing and plan. It also suggests that true faith is not dependent on witnessing spectacular signs but on accepting the message and trusting in God.

3. **Shared Expectation:** The phrase "I am with you among those who wait" conveys a sense of solidarity with the believers.  The Prophet himself is also waiting for God's decree, implying that he is not exempt from the trials of faith and the need for patience.  This promotes unity and shared purpose among the believers facing opposition.

In summary, the verse asserts that God is the ultimate authority over the unseen and that faith requires patience and trust in His timing, rather than demanding miraculous proof.  It also encourages believers to stand firm in their faith alongside the Prophet during times of doubt and adversity.
orig: ويقولون لولا أنزل عليه آية من ربه فقل إنما الغيب لله فانتظروا إني معكم من المنتظرين

translation: And when We let the people taste mercy after adversity has touched them, behold, they devise a plan against Our signs. Say, "Allah is swifter in planning." Indeed, Our messengers record what you devise.
interpretation: This verse describes a recurring pattern of human behavior.  After experiencing hardship and then receiving relief or blessings from God (referred to as 'mercy' or 'rahma'), some people, instead of showing gratitude, begin to doubt or scheme against God's signs (ayat). These 'signs' could refer to the verses of the Quran, the laws of nature, or other manifestations of divine power and wisdom.  They might attribute the improvement in their situation to something other than God's intervention, or they might try to find ways to circumvent God's laws.  The verse asserts God's absolute knowledge and power, stating that He is 'swifter in planning' (asra'u makran).  This means that God is fully aware of their plots and schemes and is ultimately in control.  Their actions are not hidden from Him, and His plan will always prevail. The final part of the verse, 'Our messengers record what you devise,' further emphasizes the accountability of human actions. While 'messengers' can refer to angels, it also reinforces the idea that everything we do is witnessed and recorded, with implications for the ultimate judgment.
orig: وإذا أذقنا الناس رحمة من بعد ضراء مستهم إذا لهم مكر في آياتنا قل الله أسرع مكرا إن رسلنا يكتبون ما تمكرون

translation: It is He who enables you to travel on land and sea, so that when you are in ships and they sail with them by a favorable wind and they rejoice therein, there comes a violent wind and the waves come upon them from every side, and they think that they are encircled. Then they invoke Allah, sincere to Him in religion, "If You deliver us from this, we will surely be among the grateful."
interpretation: This verse vividly portrays a common human experience, highlighting the themes of divine power, human vulnerability, and the importance of sincere faith.  It describes a sea voyage where initially, everything is calm and pleasant. People are enjoying the favorable wind, feeling secure and possibly even forgetting their dependence on God.  Then, a sudden storm erupts, throwing them into a state of fear and desperation as they realize their helplessness against the forces of nature.  Surrounded by waves and believing themselves doomed, they turn to God with a pure and earnest plea.  This desperate situation strips away any pretense or hypocrisy, leaving only a sincere desire for salvation. The verse implies that true faith often emerges in times of adversity. It reminds us of God's control over all circumstances, both favorable and challenging, and emphasizes the importance of turning to Him with sincere devotion, especially in moments of difficulty. The promise to be grateful if saved underscores the fleeting nature of human gratitude and the importance of cultivating a consistent thankfulness for God's blessings.
orig: هو الذي يسيركم في البر والبحر حتى إذا كنتم في الفلك وجرين بهم بريح طيبة وفرحوا بها جاءتها ريح عاصف وجاءهم الموج من كل مكان وظنوا أنهم أحيط بهم دعوا الله مخلصين له الدين لئن أنجيتنا من هذه لنكونن من الشاكرين

translation: So when He saved them, behold, they then began to transgress in the land without right. O mankind, your transgression is only against your own souls. [It is but] the enjoyment of worldly life, then to Us is your return, and We will inform you of what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse highlights the ingratitude and shortsightedness of humans. After being rescued or delivered from hardship by God (the specific context isn't provided within this verse alone but may be understood from the surrounding verses or Surah), instead of showing gratitude and adhering to righteousness, they immediately revert to wrongdoing and transgression ('ibghi' implies seeking something unjustly or exceeding limits).  The verse emphasizes that such transgression ultimately harms only the transgressors themselves.  While they may perceive their actions as beneficial in achieving worldly pleasures or gains (described as 'mata' al-hayat al-dunya' or temporary enjoyment of this worldly life), the ultimate consequence will be accountability before God. The phrase 'then to Us is your return' reinforces the idea of a final judgment where all actions will be assessed, and God will inform each individual of their deeds and their consequences. Thus, the verse serves as a reminder of the fleeting nature of worldly gains compared to the eternal consequences of our actions and the importance of expressing gratitude to God through righteous conduct.
orig: فلما أنجاهم إذا هم يبغون في الأرض بغير الحق يا أيها الناس إنما بغيكم على أنفسكم متاع الحياة الدنيا ثم إلينا مرجعكم فننبئكم بما كنتم تعملون

translation: The example of the life of this world is like water which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it, of which men and cattle eat, until, when the earth has taken on its adornment and is embellished, and its people think that they have power over it, Our command comes to it by night or by day, and We make it as a field mown down, as if it had not flourished yesterday. Thus do We explain the signs in detail for a people who reflect.
interpretation: This verse uses the powerful analogy of a flourishing field to illustrate the transient nature of worldly life and its deceptive allure.  Rain, a blessing from God, nourishes the earth, causing vegetation to grow and providing sustenance for humans and animals.  The earth becomes beautiful and vibrant, leading people to believe they are in control and secure in their prosperity. This sense of security and ownership is an illusion.  God's command can come swiftly and unexpectedly, whether at night or day, transforming the vibrant field into barren stubble, as if its previous flourishing never existed.  This sudden change emphasizes the impermanence of worldly possessions and achievements. Just as the field is ultimately subject to a higher power, so too are human lives and all worldly things.  The verse concludes by highlighting that these signs are presented for those who contemplate and reflect on the true nature of existence and the importance of focusing on the eternal rather than the fleeting.
orig: إنما مثل الحياة الدنيا كماء أنزلناه من السماء فاختلط به نبات الأرض مما يأكل الناس والأنعام حتى إذا أخذت الأرض زخرفها وازينت وظن أهلها أنهم قادرون عليها أتاها أمرنا ليلا أو نهارا فجعلناها حصيدا كأن لم تغن بالأمس كذلك نفصل الآيات لقوم يتفكرون

translation: And Allah invites to the Abode of Peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the merciful and guiding nature of God.  "Dar as-Salam," the Abode of Peace, is commonly understood as a reference to Paradise, the ultimate destination for believers in the afterlife.  It signifies a state of tranquility, security, and freedom from all suffering. God's invitation to this abode is a universal call, offered to all of humanity.  However, the verse also emphasizes God's divine will and wisdom by stating that He guides "whom He wills" to the "straight path." This path, often interpreted as the path of righteousness and adherence to Islam, is not found by everyone.  It requires both God's guidance and the individual's willingness to seek and follow it. The verse, therefore, suggests that while the invitation to salvation is open to all, attaining it depends on God's grace and the individual's active pursuit of truth and righteousness as revealed by God.
orig: والله يدعو إلى دار السلام ويهدي من يشاء إلى صراط مستقيم

translation: For those who have done good is the best [reward], and extra. Neither blackness nor humiliation will cover their faces. Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: This verse describes the ultimate reward for those who consistently perform good deeds (أحسنوا الحسنى).  "The best" (الحسنى) refers to Paradise, but the "and extra" (وزيادة) suggests blessings beyond even the standard joys of Paradise, perhaps heightened spiritual closeness to God, unique honors, or unimaginable delights.  The verse then emphasizes the absence of any shame or disgrace (لا يرهق وجوههم قتر ولا ذلة).  "Blackness" (قتر) can symbolize despair, dejection, or the stain of sin, while "humiliation" (ذلة) represents lowliness and abasement.  The righteous will experience neither in the afterlife.  Their faces will be radiant with joy and honor. The final affirmation, "Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally" (أولئك أصحاب الجنة هم فيها خالدون), definitively establishes their blissful and everlasting destiny in Paradise.
orig: للذين أحسنوا الحسنى وزيادة ولا يرهق وجوههم قتر ولا ذلة أولئك أصحاب الجنة هم فيها خالدون

translation: And those who have earned misdeeds - the recompense of a misdeed is one like it, and humiliation will cover them. They will have no protector from Allah, as if their faces were covered with pieces of a dark night. Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: This verse describes the fate of those who commit sins and do not repent.  The key concepts are just recompense, humiliation, divine abandonment, and eternal damnation.  "A misdeed is one like it" emphasizes the principle of proportionate justice in the afterlife.  The humiliation they experience is not merely social, but a profound spiritual state of degradation stemming from their awareness of their wrongdoing and their separation from God's grace.  The imagery of faces covered by darkness symbolizes their spiritual blindness and the despair that envelops them. The phrase "no protector from Allah" highlights the absolute nature of their accountability; no intercession or excuse can shield them from the consequences of their actions. Finally, their eternal abode in the Fire underscores the irreversible nature of their punishment for persisting in their sinful ways without seeking forgiveness and reformation.
orig: والذين كسبوا السيئات جزاء سيئة بمثلها وترهقهم ذلة ما لهم من الله من عاصم كأنما أغشيت وجوههم قطعا من الليل مظلما أولئك أصحاب النار هم فيها خالدون

translation: And on the Day when We gather them all together, then We will say to those who associated others with Allah, "Remain you in your place, you and your partners." Then We will separate them, and their partners will say, "You were not worshipping us."
interpretation: This verse describes a scene from the Day of Judgment.  God gathers all of humanity. Those who committed *shirk* – the sin of associating partners with God, such as idols or other deities – are addressed along with those they falsely worshipped. God commands them to remain in their place.  A critical separation then occurs between the *mushrikun* (those who committed *shirk*) and the objects or beings they worshipped.  The false 'partners' disavow any worship directed towards them, leaving the *mushrikun* utterly alone and accountable for their misguided beliefs. This highlights the futility of *shirk*; the worshipped idols hold no power and offer no intercession on the Day of Judgement. The verse emphasizes God's absolute sovereignty and the individual's direct responsibility for their beliefs and actions.  It serves as a powerful warning against the fallacy of polytheism and reinforces the central Islamic tenet of God's oneness (Tawhid).
orig: ويوم نحشرهم جميعا ثم نقول للذين أشركوا مكانكم أنتم وشركاؤكم فزيلنا بينهم وقال شركاؤهم ما كنتم إيانا تعبدون

translation: So sufficient is Allah as a witness between us and you that we were certainly unaware of your worship.
interpretation: This verse reflects a declaration of innocence and ignorance regarding the worship of others besides God.  The speakers, likely early Muslims, are addressing those who accused them of participating in or acknowledging their idolatrous practices.  They firmly deny any involvement, stating that God is the ultimate witness to their true beliefs and actions.  The phrase "sufficient is Allah as a witness" emphasizes the absolute authority and knowledge of God, implying that divine judgment is the only one that truly matters.  The term "ghafilin" (unaware) suggests not only a lack of participation but also a detachment and disinterest in those practices, reinforcing the monotheistic focus of their faith. They are asserting that their attention and devotion were directed solely towards God and not towards the idols or practices of those they are addressing. This verse can also be seen as a form of self-preservation in the face of potential persecution, emphasizing their innocence and lack of complicity with practices considered heretical in their burgeoning monotheistic faith.
orig: فكفى بالله شهيدا بيننا وبينكم إن كنا عن عبادتكم لغافلين

translation: There, every soul will be recompensed for what it previously earned, and they will be returned to Allah, their true protector. And lost from them is whatever falsehoods they used to invent.
interpretation: This verse speaks of the Day of Judgment.  It emphasizes the principle of individual accountability where each person will be held responsible for their actions in this life. The phrase "every soul will be recompensed for what it previously earned" highlights the justice and fairness of God's judgment. Good deeds will be rewarded, and bad deeds will have consequences. The verse also asserts the ultimate authority and ownership of God by stating that all will be "returned to Allah, their true protector."  This return signifies not just physical resurrection but also a spiritual reckoning. Finally, the verse concludes by highlighting the futility of falsehoods and invented beliefs.  On the Day of Judgment, any fabricated narratives or deviations from the truth will be exposed and rendered useless. The truth, represented by God, will prevail, and those who clung to falsehoods will lose their fabricated support systems.
orig: هنالك تبلو كل نفس ما أسلفت وردوا إلى الله مولاهم الحق وضل عنهم ما كانوا يفترون

translation: Say, "Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth? Or who controls hearing and sight? And who brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living? And who directs the affair?" They will say, "Allah." Then say, "So will you not fear Him?"
interpretation: This verse poses a series of rhetorical questions designed to emphasize God's absolute power and control over all aspects of existence.  It highlights God's role as the ultimate provider, the one who governs the senses, the one who orchestrates life and death, and the one who manages all affairs of the universe.  The expected answer to these questions is undeniably "Allah."  Knowing this, the verse concludes with another crucial question: "So will you not fear Him?"  This concluding question isn't simply about fear as terror, but rather about taqwa, a profound reverence and awareness of God, leading to conscious obedience and avoidance of actions that would displease Him.  It emphasizes that recognizing God's power and authority should naturally lead to a life lived in accordance with His will.  The verse serves as a powerful reminder of God's omnipotence and the importance of living a life guided by piety and mindfulness of Him.
orig: قل من يرزقكم من السماء والأرض أمن يملك السمع والأبصار ومن يخرج الحي من الميت ويخرج الميت من الحي ومن يدبر الأمر فسيقولون الله فقل أفلا تتقون

translation: That then is Allah, your Lord, the Truth. So what is there after truth except error? So how are you averted?
interpretation: This verse powerfully affirms the absolute truth of God (Allah) as the one true Lord.  It emphasizes that anything deviating from the recognition and worship of this truth constitutes error and misguidance.  The rhetorical question "So what is there after truth except error?" highlights the exclusivity of truth residing in God, implying that all other paths are inherently flawed.  The concluding question "So how are you averted?" expresses bewilderment and lament at how people, despite being presented with this clear truth, can still turn away from it.  It's a call to reflect on their choices and return to the straight path.  The verse can be interpreted as both a statement of fact about God's nature and a rebuke to those who choose to ignore or reject it. It underscores the importance of seeking and adhering to the truth, as represented by Allah, and the detrimental consequences of straying from it.
orig: فذلكم الله ربكم الحق فماذا بعد الحق إلا الضلال فأنى تصرفون

translation: Thus is the word of your Lord justified against those who have transgressed, that they will not believe.
interpretation: This verse affirms the inevitability of disbelief for those who persist in transgression (fisq).  The term "fisq" refers to going beyond the bounds set by God, encompassing disobedience, rebellion, and deviation from the righteous path.  The verse suggests that their continuous transgression hardens their hearts, making them incapable of accepting faith. It's not simply that they choose not to believe, but their actions have led them to a state where belief becomes virtually impossible. The 'word of your Lord' likely refers to the divine decree or judgment regarding their fate.  Their disbelief is not a surprise to God, but rather a consequence of their chosen path.  This verse underscores the importance of adhering to God's guidance and avoiding actions that lead to spiritual blindness.  It emphasizes the connection between actions and the state of one's heart, suggesting that consistent disobedience can ultimately lead to an inability to believe.
orig: كذلك حقت كلمت ربك على الذين فسقوا أنهم لا يؤمنون

translation: Say, "Is there among your 'partners' any who originates creation and then repeats it?" Say, " Allah originates creation and then repeats it. So how are you deluded?"
interpretation: This verse challenges the polytheistic beliefs prevalent at the time of the Prophet Muhammad.  The Arabic word 'shuraka' (partners), often translated as 'gods', refers to the deities or idols that people associated with God. The verse questions the power of these supposed partners to perform the fundamental act of creation and then to bring it back to life after death (resurrection).  It emphasizes that only God (Allah) possesses this ultimate power of originating creation and repeating it, highlighting His uniqueness and absolute control over the universe. The rhetorical question "So how are you deluded?" (fa'anna tu'fakun) serves as a strong rebuke, prompting reflection on the illogical nature of associating partners with the sole Creator.  It emphasizes the absurdity of ascribing divine attributes to powerless idols and calls for a return to the pure monotheistic understanding of God.
orig: قل هل من شركائكم من يبدأ الخلق ثم يعيده قل الله يبدأ الخلق ثم يعيده فأنى تؤفكون

translation: Say, "Is there among your 'partners' any who guides to the truth?" Say, "Allah guides to the truth. So is He who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed or he who does not guide unless he is guided? Then what is [the matter] with you - how do you judge?"
interpretation:
This verse challenges the polytheistic beliefs prevalent at the time of the Prophet Muhammad's revelation.  It poses a fundamental question about the nature of divinity and guidance.  The 'partners' (شركاء - shurakā') refers to the idols and deities that people worshipped alongside Allah. The verse asks if these idols possess any inherent power to guide humanity towards truth. The rhetorical question implies a resounding 'no.'  It asserts that true guidance comes only from Allah.  

The verse then contrasts Allah, the source of all guidance, with those false deities who themselves need guidance.  It highlights the absurdity of following something that is itself lost and requires direction. The final question, "Then what is [the matter] with you - how do you judge?" expresses bewilderment at the faulty reasoning of those who choose to follow such powerless entities over the one true guide, Allah. It emphasizes the importance of using intellect and reason to discern truth from falsehood and choose the correct path in life. It calls for critical thinking and self-reflection on one's beliefs and practices.
orig: قل هل من شركائكم من يهدي إلى الحق قل الله يهدي للحق أفمن يهدي إلى الحق أحق أن يتبع أمن لا يهدي إلا أن يهدى فما لكم كيف تحكمون

translation: And most of them follow not except assumption. Indeed, assumption avails not against the truth at all. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do.
interpretation: This verse highlights the danger of relying on assumptions and conjectures, especially in matters of faith and truth.  The majority of people, it suggests, tend to follow their own opinions and guesses rather than seeking true knowledge and evidence.  The verse emphasizes that mere assumptions, no matter how strongly held, cannot replace or substitute the truth. They offer no protection or benefit when confronted with reality.  Ultimately, God is fully aware of all actions, including those based on assumptions, and will judge accordingly. The verse serves as a warning against blind faith and encourages the pursuit of genuine knowledge and understanding, grounded in evidence and reason, rather than unsubstantiated beliefs.
orig: وما يتبع أكثرهم إلا ظنا إن الظن لا يغني من الحق شيئا إن الله عليم بما يفعلون

translation: And it is not [the case] that this Qur'an could have been fabricated/forged without Allah, but [it is] a confirmation of what was before it and a detailed explanation of the Book, about which there is no doubt, from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation:
This verse asserts the divine origin of the Qur'an. It refutes the idea that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) authored it himself or that it was fabricated by any other human or worldly source. The verse makes two key points:

1. **Confirmation of previous scriptures:** The Qur'an confirms the truth found in the divine scriptures revealed before it (e.g., the Torah, Psalms, and Gospel). It affirms the core message of monotheism and the guidance sent through previous prophets, while correcting any corruptions or distortions that had entered those scriptures over time.  It isn't meant to replace them entirely but to purify and complete them.

2. **Detailed explanation of the Book:** The term "the Book" (Al-Kitab) can refer to a preserved tablet in heaven containing God's complete knowledge or to previous scriptures. This phrase highlights the Qur'an's role in clarifying and elaborating on fundamental religious truths and ethical principles, providing further details and guidance for humanity. It explains the core message of God’s unity and the path to salvation more comprehensively.  

Finally, the verse concludes with a powerful affirmation: this revelation is undoubtedly from the "Lord of the worlds" (Rabb al-`alamin). This emphasizes God's absolute authority and the authenticity of the Qur'an as His divine word. The phrase "Lord of the worlds" also reminds us that the Qur'an's message is universal and applies to all of creation, not just a particular group or time period.
orig: وما كان هذا القرآن أن يفترى من دون الله ولكن تصديق الذي بين يديه وتفصيل الكتاب لا ريب فيه من رب العالمين

translation: Or do they say, "He invented it?" Say, "Then bring forth a surah like it and call upon [for assistance] whomever you can besides Allah, if you should be truthful."
interpretation: This verse is a challenge to those who disbelieve in the divine origin of the Qur'an.  It asserts that the Qur'an is inimitable and that no human or other being could produce anything comparable to it.  The challenge is to create just one surah (chapter) similar in eloquence, wisdom, spiritual depth, and legislative power.  The verse invites skeptics to seek assistance from any source they deem powerful, highlighting the confidence in the Qur'an's unique nature.  The phrase "if you should be truthful" emphasizes the implication that their claim of the Qur'an being fabricated is false, and that they will be unable to meet this challenge, thus proving its divine source.
orig: أم يقولون افتراه قل فأتوا بسورة مثله وادعوا من استطعتم من دون الله إن كنتم صادقين

translation: Rather, they have denied that which they do not comprehend, and whose interpretation has not yet come to them. Thus did those before them deny. So observe how was the end of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the rejection of truth by those who lack complete understanding.  It highlights a common human tendency to dismiss what we don't fully grasp or what hasn't yet been fully revealed or explained. The phrase 'whose interpretation has not yet come to them' can refer to a future clarification, a deeper understanding that unfolds over time, or the consequences of actions that become apparent only later.  The verse connects this behavior with past generations who similarly rejected truths that they couldn't or wouldn't comprehend, emphasizing a cyclical pattern of denial.  Finally, it warns of the negative consequences ('observe how was the end of the wrongdoers') faced by those who persistently reject truth due to their limited understanding or impatience for complete knowledge.  This suggests that true understanding requires humility, open-mindedness, and a willingness to accept that some truths may unfold gradually or require deeper reflection.  Rejecting something simply because it is not immediately comprehensible is portrayed as a form of wrongdoing that ultimately leads to a negative outcome.
orig: بل كذبوا بما لم يحيطوا بعلمه ولما يأتهم تأويله كذلك كذب الذين من قبلهم فانظر كيف كان عاقبة الظالمين

translation: And of them are those who believe in it, and of them are those who do not believe in it. And your Lord is most knowing of the corrupters.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the inevitability of differing responses to the message of the Qur'an, acknowledging the existence of both belief and disbelief.  The pronoun "it" likely refers to the Qur'an or the message of God in a broader sense. The verse emphasizes God's omniscience, specifically highlighting His knowledge of those who actively spread corruption or mischief (al-mufsidoon). This can be interpreted in several ways: 1. Those who reject the truth out of arrogance or selfish desires, actively working against its spread. 2. Those who hypocritically claim belief while their actions betray their true intentions, thereby corrupting the message from within. 3.  Those who cause discord and spread falsehood, undermining the unity and moral principles promoted by the message.  The verse concludes by reassuring that God is fully aware of those who choose disbelief and engage in corruption, suggesting an eventual accountability for their actions.  It also offers comfort to believers, reminding them that despite opposition, God is just and aware.
orig: ومنهم من يؤمن به ومنهم من لا يؤمن به وربك أعلم بالمفسدين

translation: And if they deny you, then say, "For me are my deeds, and for you are your deeds. You are disassociated from what I do, and I am disassociated from what you do."
interpretation: This verse emphasizes personal responsibility and accountability before God.  It addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) in a context where he faced rejection and denial of his message.  God advises him not to be overly concerned with their disbelief. Instead, he should focus on his own actions and leave their judgment to God.  The verse highlights the principle that each individual is responsible only for their own actions and will be held accountable for them. It reinforces the idea that faith is a personal choice and no one can force another to believe.  The phrase "For me are my deeds, and for you are your deeds" creates a clear separation of responsibility, emphasizing that the Prophet's duty is to convey the message, and people's acceptance or rejection of it is their own affair. The mutual disassociation expressed by "You are disassociated from what I do, and I am disassociated from what you do" further reinforces this separation, indicating that the Prophet cannot be held responsible for their choices, nor can they claim credit for his actions.  This verse provides comfort and guidance not only to the Prophet but also to all believers facing opposition or rejection for their faith. It reminds them to remain steadfast in their own beliefs and actions, leaving the ultimate judgment to God.
orig: وإن كذبوك فقل لي عملي ولكم عملكم أنتم بريئون مما أعمل وأنا بريء مما تعملون

translation: And among them are those who listen to you, but can you make the deaf hear, even if they do not understand?
interpretation: This verse speaks to the Prophet Muhammad's frustration with those who refused to accept his message.  It highlights the limitations of even a prophet's power.  He could deliver the message, but he could not force understanding or acceptance.  The 'deafness' mentioned is not necessarily a physical one, but rather a deafness of the heart, a willful refusal to listen and comprehend.  Even if they physically hear his words, they cannot grasp the deeper meaning because they choose not to understand. The verse emphasizes the importance of individual responsibility in accepting guidance. Faith is not something that can be forced, but a choice each person must make. It also serves as a comfort to the Prophet, reminding him that his duty is only to convey the message, not to ensure its acceptance.
orig: ومنهم من يستمعون إليك أفأنت تسمع الصم ولو كانوا لا يعقلون

translation: And among them are those who look at you. But can you guide the blind, even if they do not see?
interpretation: This verse speaks to the resistance and willful blindness some people display towards the Prophet Muhammad's (peace be upon him) message.  It highlights the limitations of even a Prophet's influence.  While the Prophet was sent as a guide, he could not force understanding or belief upon those who chose to remain closed off to the truth. Their "blindness" is not a physical one, but rather a blindness of the heart and mind, a refusal to see and accept the truth even when it's presented to them. The verse uses the rhetorical question "But can you guide the blind, even if they do not see?“ to emphasize the point that guidance is only effective for those willing to receive it.  Ultimately, the decision to believe and follow the guidance rests with the individual.  The verse also implies a sense of compassion and perhaps even a subtle sadness on the part of the Prophet for those who choose this path of willful ignorance.
orig: ومنهم من ينظر إليك أفأنت تهدي العمي ولو كانوا لا يبصرون

translation: Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people at all, but it is the people who are wronging themselves.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the justice of God and the concept of free will in Islam.  It asserts that God never initiates injustice towards humanity. Any suffering or hardship experienced by people is a consequence of their own actions or choices.  This doesn't negate the existence of trials and tribulations, but it reframes them as opportunities for growth, learning, or tests of faith, rather than divine punishment.  The verse encourages introspection and taking responsibility for one's actions, as ultimate accountability rests with the individual. It also suggests that by aligning their actions with divine guidance, humans can avoid self-inflicted harm and find a path to prosperity and well-being.
orig: إن الله لا يظلم الناس شيئا ولكن الناس أنفسهم يظلمون

translation: And on the Day He gathers them, [it will be] as if they had not remained [in the world] except for an hour of the day, recognizing each other.  Those will have lost who denied the meeting with Allah and were not guided.
interpretation: This verse paints a vivid picture of the Day of Judgment.  It emphasizes the fleeting nature of earthly life in comparison to the eternal afterlife. The phrase "as if they had not remained [in the world] except for an hour of the day" highlights how the vast expanse of worldly existence will feel incredibly short in retrospect on the Day of Judgment.  People will recognize each other, suggesting a continuation of individual consciousness and relationships.  The verse then declares the ultimate loss of those who disbelieved in meeting God and following His guidance. This 'meeting' implies accountability for one's deeds during their earthly life.  The lack of guidance refers to their rejection of divine instruction and their consequent inability to find the right path. Thus, the verse serves as a powerful reminder of the importance of believing in the afterlife and seeking divine guidance in this life to avoid eternal loss.
orig: ويوم يحشرهم كأن لم يلبثوا إلا ساعة من النهار يتعارفون بينهم قد خسر الذين كذبوا بلقاء الله وما كانوا مهتدين

translation: And whether We show you some of what We promise them, or We take you [in death], then to Us is their return. Then Allah is, over what they do, a Witness.
interpretation:
This verse emphasizes God's absolute knowledge and control over human destiny and actions. It addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), assuring him that regardless of whether he lives to witness the fulfillment of God's promises (likely referring to the consequences faced by those who opposed him and his message) or passes away before that, the ultimate return of all people is to God for judgment.  Their deeds are fully witnessed and recorded by God, ensuring accountability. 

Several key points can be derived:

* **Certainty of God's Plan:**  The phrase "whether We show you...or We take you" highlights that divine plans are not contingent upon any individual's lifespan, including the Prophet's. God's will shall be carried out regardless.
* **Ultimate Accountability:** The phrase "to Us is their return" underscores the fundamental Islamic belief in the Day of Judgment, where everyone will be held accountable for their actions in this life.
* **God as the All-Seeing Witness:**  The concluding phrase "Then Allah is, over what they do, a Witness" emphasizes God's omniscience.  Nothing is hidden from God, and this knowledge serves as the basis for the final judgment.
* **Consolation and reassurance for the Prophet:** The verse can also be interpreted as a source of comfort for the Prophet, assuring him that he need not be overly concerned with the immediate outcome of his mission.  His responsibility is to convey the message, and God will take care of the rest. The ultimate judgment rests with God.

This verse thus serves as a powerful reminder of God's ultimate authority, the importance of righteous actions, and the certainty of accountability in the hereafter.
orig: وإما نرينك بعض الذي نعدهم أو نتوفينك فإلينا مرجعهم ثم الله شهيد على ما يفعلون

translation: And for every nation is a messenger. So when their messenger comes, it will be judged between them with justice, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the principle of divine justice and accountability.  It asserts that God sends a messenger to every nation or community to guide them towards the truth.  The arrival of this messenger marks a point of reckoning, where justice will be established.  "Judged between them with justice" implies a fair and impartial assessment of their actions in light of the message they received.  The phrase "they will not be wronged" assures that God's judgment will be perfectly equitable, with no one unjustly punished or deprived of their due.  This concept of a messenger for every nation also highlights the universality of God's message, while acknowledging the diverse contexts in which it is delivered.  It reinforces the idea that all people will be held accountable based on the guidance they received.
orig: ولكل أمة رسول فإذا جاء رسولهم قضي بينهم بالقسط وهم لا يظلمون

translation: And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"
interpretation: This verse reflects the skepticism and challenge posed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his followers by those who disbelieved in the message of Islam.  The "promise" refers to the predictions of the Day of Judgement, the consequences of disbelief, and the triumph of truth.  The disbelievers mockingly demanded to know *when* these events would transpire, implying doubt in their veracity and using the question as a way to dismiss the Prophet's claims.  It highlights the resistance faced by early Muslims and the constant demands for immediate, tangible proof of the unseen realities described in the Quran.  The phrase "if you are truthful" carries a sarcastic tone, suggesting that the disbelievers considered the believers to be liars or deluded.  This verse is a recurring motif in the Quran, demonstrating the psychological tactics employed by those who opposed the Prophet's message and the importance of maintaining faith despite doubt and ridicule.
orig: ويقولون متى هذا الوعد إن كنتم صادقين

translation: Say, "I do not possess for myself [power of] harm or benefit, except what Allah has willed. For every nation is a term; when their term comes, they will not remain behind an hour, nor will they precede [it]."
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute sovereignty and power of God (Allah).  The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is instructed to declare his own lack of autonomous control over benefit or harm, highlighting that all power ultimately resides with God.  Everything that happens, good or bad, is according to God's will and plan. The verse also speaks to the concept of a predetermined lifespan or 'term' for every nation or community. This 'term' is fixed by God, and when it arrives, there is no delaying or hastening it. This reinforces the idea of divine decree and the inevitability of destiny as ordained by God. It teaches humility and acceptance of God's will, while also suggesting that individuals and communities are accountable for their actions within the timeframe allotted to them.
orig: قل لا أملك لنفسي ضرا ولا نفعا إلا ما شاء الله لكل أمة أجل إذا جاء أجلهم فلا يستأخرون ساعة ولا يستقدمون

translation: Say, "Tell me, if His punishment should come upon you by night or by day, what aspect of it would the criminals hasten?"
interpretation: This verse poses a rhetorical question, challenging those who deny the truth and invite divine punishment.  It highlights the inescapable nature of God's judgment. Whether it arrives unexpectedly at night or during the day, the criminals, those who have rejected faith and righteous action, would desire nothing more than to postpone or escape it.  The question implies that there's no escaping divine retribution when it is decreed, and the timing of it is entirely in God's hands. The emphasis is on the inevitability of accountability for one's actions and the futility of trying to avoid the consequences of wrongdoing. It serves as a warning and a call to repentance and righteousness before it is too late.
orig: قل أرأيتم إن أتاكم عذابه بياتا أو نهارا ماذا يستعجل منه المجرمون

translation: Then, when it has actually occurred, will you believe in it? Now? While you were hastening it?
interpretation: This verse reflects a rhetorical question posed with divine irony. It addresses those who doubted the warnings and prophecies mentioned in the Quran, specifically about a coming punishment or calamity.  They are depicted as previously dismissive and even eager for this event to happen, perhaps to challenge the prophecy's validity. However, the verse suggests that when the predicted event finally transpires, their belief becomes meaningless.  Their prior skepticism and impatience expose the hollowness of their newfound faith. It highlights the importance of genuine belief and sincere reflection rather than a reactive faith born out of fear or immediate experience. The verse emphasizes that true faith precedes the fulfillment of prophecies, not the other way around.
orig: أثم إذا ما وقع آمنتم به آلآن وقد كنتم به تستعجلون

translation: Then it will be said to those who wronged themselves, "Taste the punishment of eternity. Are you being recompensed for anything except what you used to earn?"
interpretation: This verse describes the fate of those who have committed injustices (zulum).  The Arabic term 'zulum' encompasses a broad range of wrongdoing, from oppression and transgression against others to harming oneself through sin and disobedience to God. The verse emphasizes the principle of just recompense in the afterlife.  The punishment of eternity ('adhab al-khuld') is presented not as arbitrary retribution, but as a direct consequence of their own actions ('ma kuntum taksibun').  The rhetorical question highlights the inescapable justice of this outcome. They are experiencing the results of their choices and deeds, reinforcing the concept of accountability for one's actions in Islam.  The verse serves as a powerful warning against wrongdoing and a reminder of the eternal consequences that await those who persist in injustice.
orig: ثم قيل للذين ظلموا ذوقوا عذاب الخلد هل تجزون إلا بما كنتم تكسبون

translation: And they ask you, [O Muhammad], whether it is true. Say, "Yes, by my Lord, indeed it is true, and you will not escape [the punishment of Allah ]."
interpretation: This verse addresses a situation where the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is being questioned about the truthfulness of his message, likely by those skeptical or hostile to his claims of divine revelation.  His response is a powerful affirmation of the truth, swearing by God ('by my Lord') to emphasize the certainty and unwavering nature of his conviction.  The second part of the verse carries a warning: 'and you will not escape [the punishment of Allah].' This suggests that denying the truth, despite the clear evidence presented, will have consequences.  It highlights the importance of accepting the truth and the potential repercussions of rejecting it.  The specific 'punishment' could refer to both worldly consequences and divine judgment in the hereafter.  This verse underscores the seriousness of the message and the accountability individuals face regarding their response to it. It also demonstrates the Prophet's confidence in his mission and the divine origin of his message.
orig: ويستنبئونك أحق هو قل إي وربي إنه لحق وما أنتم بمعجزين

translation: If every soul that has wronged itself possessed all that is on earth, it would surely offer it as ransom. They will conceal their remorse when they see the punishment, and it will be judged between them with justice, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: This verse paints a vivid picture of the Day of Judgement and the profound regret of those who have lived unrighteous lives.  It emphasizes the utter despair and helplessness of those who face the consequences of their actions.  The phrase "If every soul that has wronged itself possessed all that is on earth" highlights the magnitude of the punishment and the desperate desire to escape it.  Even if one possessed all the worldly riches imaginable, it would be insufficient to buy their way out.  The act of "concealing their remorse" speaks to the shame and humiliation they will feel, realizing the futility of their past deeds.  Finally, the verse underscores God's perfect justice. While the punishment will be severe, it will be meted out with absolute fairness; no one will be unjustly punished ("they will not be wronged").  This verse serves as a powerful reminder of the importance of living a righteous life and seeking God's forgiveness before it is too late.
orig: ولو أن لكل نفس ظلمت ما في الأرض لافتدت به وأسروا الندامة لما رأوا العذاب وقضي بينهم بالقسط وهم لا يظلمون

translation: Indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Indeed, the promise of Allah is truth, but most of them do not know.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's absolute ownership and sovereignty over all creation, encompassing everything in the heavens and the earth.  It affirms that God's promises, whether of reward or punishment, are absolutely true and will inevitably come to pass. However, the verse also laments the lack of awareness and understanding among most people regarding this fundamental truth.  Their ignorance prevents them from truly recognizing God's power and the certainty of His promises, leading them to stray from the righteous path. This verse serves as both a declaration of God's dominion and a subtle rebuke of those who fail to acknowledge it.
orig: ألا إن لله ما في السماوات والأرض ألا إن وعد الله حق ولكن أكثرهم لا يعلمون

translation: He gives life and causes death, and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: This verse succinctly encapsulates the absolute power and authority of God over life and death.  "He gives life" refers to God as the ultimate source of all existence, the creator and sustainer of every living thing.  "And causes death" highlights God's role in ending life, a reminder of the inevitable nature of mortality.  Finally, "and to Him you will be returned" emphasizes the concept of accountability and the afterlife.  It asserts that all beings will ultimately return to God for judgment, signifying the importance of living a righteous life in accordance with His will.  This verse thus serves as a powerful reminder of God's omnipotence, the temporary nature of earthly existence, and the ultimate purpose of life which is to serve and return to Him.
orig: هو يحيي ويميت وإليه ترجعون

translation: O mankind, there has come to you instruction from your Lord and healing for what is in the breasts and guidance and mercy for the believers.
interpretation: This verse addresses all of humanity, emphasizing the universality of the Qur'an's message.  "Instruction from your Lord" (موعظة من ربكم) refers to the guidance and wisdom found within the Qur'an, serving as a reminder and admonition to live a righteous life. "Healing for what is in the breasts" (شفاء لما في الصدور) speaks to the Qur'an's ability to alleviate spiritual ailments like doubt, hypocrisy, and anxiety. It offers solace and tranquility to the heart. "Guidance and mercy for the believers" (هدى ورحمة للمؤمنين) highlights that those who accept the message and believe will receive further guidance on how to live according to God's will and will also be recipients of God's mercy.
orig: يا أيها الناس قد جاءتكم موعظة من ربكم وشفاء لما في الصدور وهدى ورحمة للمؤمنين

translation: Say, "In the bounty of Allah and in His mercy - in that let them rejoice; it is better than what they accumulate."
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the true source of joy and lasting value.  Material possessions, wealth, and all that people amass are fleeting and ultimately less fulfilling than the bounty and mercy of God.  "Bounty" (فضل - fadl) refers to God's abundant gifts and blessings, both material and spiritual, bestowed upon all creation, exceeding what is deserved or earned.  "Mercy" (رحمة - rahmah) encompasses God's compassion, forgiveness, and love, which are essential for spiritual well-being and ultimate happiness. The verse encourages a shift in focus from worldly gains to divine grace. True rejoicing and contentment come from recognizing and appreciating God's blessings and mercy, which are infinitely more valuable and enduring than any material accumulation.
orig: قل بفضل الله وبرحمته فبذلك فليفرحوا هو خير مما يجمعون

translation: Say, "Have you considered the provision that Allah has sent down for you, and you have made of it some lawful and some unlawful?" Say, "Has Allah permitted you [to do so], or do you invent [lies] about Allah?"
interpretation: This verse challenges the practice of declaring certain foods or provisions lawful (halal) and others unlawful (haram) without a clear basis in divine revelation.  It questions the authority by which people make such distinctions.  The verse emphasizes that Allah is the ultimate authority on what is permissible and impermissible. When people create their own prohibitions and permissions regarding sustenance, they are essentially attributing their own rules to God, a serious accusation implied by the phrase "or do you invent [lies] about Allah?"  It's a reminder that dietary laws should be based on divine guidance, not personal preferences or cultural norms falsely attributed to God. The verse implicitly suggests that such practices might stem from arrogance or a desire to control others by imposing restrictions not sanctioned by God.
orig: قل أرأيتم ما أنزل الله لكم من رزق فجعلتم منه حراما وحلالا قل آلله أذن لكم أم على الله تفترون

translation: And what do those who invent falsehood about Allah think that the Day of Resurrection will be like? Indeed, Allah is full of bounty to the people, but most of them are not grateful.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the consequences of those who spread lies and fabricate falsehoods against God (Allah). It questions their understanding of the Day of Resurrection (Yawm al-Qiyāmah), implying they haven't grasped the seriousness of their actions.  It emphasizes God's abundant grace and blessings upon all humanity, yet highlights the unfortunate reality that most people fail to recognize and appreciate these blessings.  The verse can be interpreted as both a warning against slandering God and a reminder of the importance of gratitude.  The question posed about their perception of the Day of Judgement suggests a disconnect between their actions in this life and the ultimate accountability they will face. Their fabrication of lies against God, the ultimate source of truth and bounty, demonstrates a deep ingratitude and lack of awareness of His generosity. This lack of thankfulness further compounds their transgression.  Therefore, the verse serves as a powerful call to reflect on God's favors and to refrain from attributing falsehood to Him, especially considering the impending judgment.
orig: وما ظن الذين يفترون على الله الكذب يوم القيامة إن الله لذو فضل على الناس ولكن أكثرهم لا يشكرون

translation: And you are not [engaged] in any matter or recite any of the Qur'an or do any deed except that We are witnesses over you while you are involved in it. And not absent from your Lord is any [part] of an atom's weight within the earth or within the heavens or [anything] smaller than that or greater but that it is in a clear register.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's complete and comprehensive knowledge and awareness of everything that happens, both large and small, both internally and externally.  No action, thought, or even the smallest particle escapes God's notice.  "Not absent from your Lord is any [part] of an atom's weight..." highlights the meticulous nature of this divine knowledge.  It transcends the limitations of human perception and encompasses all of creation.  The mention of a "clear register" suggests a precise and detailed record of all things, reinforcing the concept of accountability and divine justice.  Therefore, the verse serves as a reminder of God's constant presence and watchfulness, encouraging mindfulness and responsibility in all human endeavors.  Reciting the Quran, engaging in any matter or doing any deed is witnessed by God.  This verse emphasizes the importance of sincerity and truthfulness in all actions, as they are all known and recorded by God.
orig: وما تكون في شأن وما تتلو منه من قرآن ولا تعملون من عمل إلا كنا عليكم شهودا إذ تفيضون فيه وما يعزب عن ربك من مثقال ذرة في الأرض ولا في السماء ولا أصغر من ذلك ولا أكبر إلا في كتاب مبين

translation: Behold! Indeed, the allies/friends/protectors of Allah -  no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: This verse (10:62) offers profound reassurance and comfort to those who are true allies of God ("Awliya' Allah").  The term "Awliya'" implies a deep, committed relationship of love, obedience, and trust.  It's not simply about believing in God, but actively striving to live according to His guidance and seeking His pleasure in all matters.  The verse promises that those who achieve this state of closeness with God will be free from fear of the future and grief over the past.  This doesn't mean they won't face challenges in life, but rather that they will possess an inner peace and unwavering faith that allows them to navigate difficulties with resilience and trust in God's plan.  Their hearts are anchored in divine love, and they find solace in the knowledge that God is with them, protecting and guiding them. This state is often associated with spiritual enlightenment and contentment, where worldly concerns lose their power to disturb inner peace.
orig: ألا إن أولياء الله لا خوف عليهم ولا هم يحزنون

translation: Those who have believed and were fearing Allah (or were righteous/God-conscious)
interpretation: This verse describes a group of people characterized by two key qualities: *iman* (faith/belief) and *taqwa* (fear of Allah/God-consciousness/righteousness).  'Iman' implies not just intellectual acceptance of God's existence and message, but also a sincere commitment and trust in Him. 'Taqwa' often translated as 'fear of God,' doesn't imply a terror of punishment, but rather a profound awareness of God's presence and a cautiousness against displeasing Him. It leads to acting righteously and avoiding sin.  Therefore, the verse speaks of those who possess true faith and strive to live a righteous life in accordance with that faith. It emphasizes the inseparable connection between belief and action in Islam, highlighting that true faith must manifest in righteous conduct.
orig: الذين آمنوا وكانوا يتقون

translation: For them are good tidings in the life of this world and in the Hereafter. No change is there in the words of Allah. That is indeed the supreme triumph.
interpretation: This verse speaks of a great reward, a 'supreme triumph' (al-fawz al-'azeem), promised to believers. This reward comes in the form of 'good tidings' (al-bushra) both in this worldly life and in the afterlife.  The 'good tidings' in this life could refer to the inner peace, contentment, and guidance that comes with faith, as well as the blessings Allah bestows upon those who follow His path. The 'good tidings' in the Hereafter naturally refer to the ultimate reward of Paradise.  The crucial part of the verse is the affirmation that 'No change is there in the words of Allah.'  This emphasizes the certainty and unwavering nature of God's promise. The rewards mentioned are guaranteed because God's words are absolute and unchanging.  This verse thus offers a powerful message of hope and assurance to believers, reminding them of the ultimate reward that awaits them and emphasizing the trustworthiness of God's promises.
orig: لهم البشرى في الحياة الدنيا وفي الآخرة لا تبديل لكلمات الله ذلك هو الفوز العظيم

translation: And do not be grieved by their words. Indeed, all honor belongs to Allah. He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse offers comfort and reassurance to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and, by extension, to all believers facing opposition or mockery.  It instructs them not to be saddened or disheartened by the dismissive or hostile words of those who reject their message. The reason for this steadfastness lies in the understanding that true power and honor reside solely with God (Allah).  He is the ultimate source of authority and strength, and therefore, human disapproval carries no real weight.  The verse concludes by emphasizing God's attributes as the All-Hearing and the All-Knowing. This highlights that God is fully aware of the believers' struggles, their sincerity, and the falsehood of their opponents. It further implies that He will ultimately judge all things justly and that truth will prevail.  Therefore, believers should place their trust in God's plan and not be swayed by worldly criticism or opposition.
orig: ولا يحزنك قولهم إن العزة لله جميعا هو السميع العليم

translation: Indeed, to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth. And those who invoke other deities besides Allah do not follow [anything] but assumptions, and they are not but falsifying.
interpretation: This verse asserts God's absolute sovereignty over all creation, both in the heavens and on earth. It then criticizes those who associate partners (shirk) with God, emphasizing that their worship of other deities is based solely on conjecture and unfounded claims.  They lack any real knowledge or evidence to support their beliefs. The word "ظن" (than) often translated as "assumption" or "conjecture" refers to an opinion without proof, highlighting the baselessness of polytheistic beliefs. The term "يخرصون" (yakhrusun) translated as "falsifying" or "conjecturing" further emphasizes that their claims are fabricated and untrue.  The verse underscores the futility and falsehood inherent in worshipping anything other than the one true God.
orig: ألا إن لله من في السماوات ومن في الأرض وما يتبع الذين يدعون من دون الله شركاء إن يتبعون إلا الظن وإن هم إلا يخرصون

translation: It is He who made for you the night that you may rest therein and the day giving sight. Indeed in that are signs for a people who listen.
interpretation: This verse highlights God's benevolent design in creating the cycle of night and day.  The night is described as a time for "rest" (sukun), encompassing not only physical sleep, but also a general calming and cessation of the day's activities.  This period of rest allows for physical and mental rejuvenation, preparing individuals for the activities of the coming day. The day, on the other hand, is described as "giving sight" (mubsiran), referencing the sunlight that facilitates vision and enables people to engage in their worldly pursuits. The verse emphasizes the importance of recognizing these alternating cycles as "signs" (ayat) of God's wisdom and power.  These are not merely natural phenomena, but rather demonstrations of divine purpose and provision. However, the verse also specifies that these signs are only truly understood by those who "listen" (yasma'un). This 'listening' implies not just hearing the words of the Qur'an, but also paying attention to the world around them and reflecting on the intricate workings of nature as evidence of a divine creator. It emphasizes the importance of mindful observation and contemplation in recognizing God's presence and plan.
orig: هو الذي جعل لكم الليل لتسكنوا فيه والنهار مبصرا إن في ذلك لآيات لقوم يسمعون

translation: They said, "God has taken a son." Exalted is He! He is the Rich [beyond need]. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Do you have any authority for this? Do you say about God that which you do not know?
interpretation: This verse addresses the pre-Islamic Arabian belief that angels were the daughters of God. It strongly refutes this idea by emphasizing God's transcendence and absolute richness. He is self-sufficient and needs no offspring.  The rhetorical question "Do you have any authority for this?" challenges the basis of this claim, highlighting its lack of evidence and rationality.  It further condemns such assertions as speaking about God without knowledge, emphasizing the gravity of making baseless claims about the Divine.
orig: قالوا اتخذ الله ولدا سبحانه هو الغني له ما في السماوات وما في الأرض إن عندكم من سلطان بهذا أتقولون على الله ما لا تعلمون

translation: Say, "Indeed, those who invent falsehood about Allah will not succeed."
interpretation: This verse asserts that those who fabricate lies and attribute them to God are destined for failure.  'Success' (falah) in the Quranic context encompasses both worldly prosperity and, more importantly, salvation in the hereafter.  Therefore, the verse warns against the grave sin of falsely ascribing things to God, including fabricating narratives, rituals, or doctrines not based on divine revelation.  This encompasses everything from outright lies about God's nature or commands to falsely claiming divine sanction for personal desires or actions.  The verse serves as a strong deterrent against religious innovation based on falsehood and emphasizes the importance of truthfulness and adherence to authentic divine guidance.
orig: قل إن الذين يفترون على الله الكذب لا يفلحون

translation: A temporary enjoyment in this world, then to Us is their return, and then We will make them taste the severe punishment because they used to disbelieve.
interpretation: This verse speaks about the fleeting nature of worldly pleasures and the ultimate consequence of disbelief.  "متاع" (mata') refers to temporary enjoyment or fleeting goods, highlighting that worldly possessions and delights are not lasting. The verse emphasizes that true, permanent life lies with God.  "ثم إلينا مرجعهم" (thumma ilayna marji'uhum) affirms that all will eventually return to God for judgment. This return is inevitable, regardless of one's beliefs or actions in this life.  Finally, "ثم نذيقهم العذاب الشديد بما كانوا يكفرون" (thumma nudhiquhum al-'adhab al-shadid bima kanu yakfurun) states that those who disbelieve will face severe punishment as a consequence of their rejection of God's truth.  The punishment is directly linked to their disbelief (kufr), implying a just recompense for their choices. The verse serves as a reminder of the importance of prioritizing the hereafter over the temporary allure of this world and adhering to faith in God.
orig: متاع في الدنيا ثم إلينا مرجعهم ثم نذيقهم العذاب الشديد بما كانوا يكفرون

translation: And recite to them the story of Noah, when he said to his people, "O my people, if my presence and my reminding you of the signs of Allah has become burdensome upon you, then I have relied upon Allah. So resolve your matter, along with your partners [i.e., idols], then let not your matter be hidden from you, then carry out your purpose against me and do not give me respite.
interpretation:
This verse captures a pivotal moment in Noah's prophetic mission.  He had been preaching to his people for an extended period, warning them about the punishment of God if they persisted in their disbelief and idolatry.  However, his message was met with resistance and rejection.  This verse highlights Noah's unwavering faith and reliance on God despite the adversity he faced. 

Here's a breakdown of the key elements:

* **"And recite to them the story of Noah..."** This is a command to the Prophet Muhammad (and by extension, to all Muslims) to recount the story of Noah as a reminder and a lesson.
* **"if my presence and my reminding you of the signs of Allah has become burdensome upon you..."** Noah acknowledges his people's aversion to his presence and his message.  They were tired of hearing his warnings and considered him a nuisance.
* **"then I have relied upon Allah."** This showcases Noah's complete trust and dependence on God. Despite the rejection and hostility, he found solace and strength in his faith.
* **"So resolve your matter, along with your partners [i.e., idols]..."** Noah challenges his people to unite with their false gods and decide on their course of action. This is a sarcastic challenge, highlighting the futility of relying on idols.
* **"then let not your matter be hidden from you..."** This implies that their plans should be clear and open, without any secrecy. They should not hesitate to carry out their intentions against him.
* **"then carry out your purpose against me and do not give me respite."** Noah, having put his trust in God, is prepared for whatever his people decide to do. He demonstrates courage and steadfastness in the face of potential harm. 

In essence, this verse portrays the struggle between truth and falsehood, faith and disbelief.  It emphasizes the importance of perseverance in delivering God's message, even in the face of overwhelming opposition. It also underscores the concept of tawhid (the oneness of God) by contrasting Noah's reliance on God with his people's reliance on false idols.
orig: واتل عليهم نبأ نوح إذ قال لقومه يا قوم إن كان كبر عليكم مقامي وتذكيري بآيات الله فعلى الله توكلت فأجمعوا أمركم وشركاءكم ثم لا يكن أمركم عليكم غمة ثم اقضوا إلي ولا تنظرون

translation: So if you turn away, [O Muhammad], I have not asked you for any payment. My reward is only from Allah, and I have been commanded to be of the Muslims.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the Prophet Muhammad's sincerity and selfless nature in delivering the message of Islam.  It addresses a potential rejection of his message by his audience. He clarifies that he isn't seeking any personal gain or worldly reward from them. His only reward comes from God. The verse also highlights his obedience to God's command to be among those who submit to Him (Muslims).  It reinforces that his motivation stems from divine instruction and not personal ambition or desire for material compensation.  This declaration strengthens the credibility of his message and underscores the pure intention behind his prophetic mission.
orig: فإن توليتم فما سألتكم من أجر إن أجري إلا على الله وأمرت أن أكون من المسلمين

translation: So they denied him, and We saved him and those with him in the Ark, and made them successors, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. So see how was the end of those who were warned.
interpretation: This verse recounts the story of Noah (Nuh).  God sent Noah to warn his people against their idolatry and wickedness.  They rejected his message and mocked him.  Consequently, God saved Noah and his followers from the great flood by having them board the Ark.  He made them inheritors of the earth after the flood, establishing them as the new generation.  Those who disbelieved Noah's warnings and God's signs were drowned as a punishment for their rejection of the truth. The verse concludes by highlighting the dire consequences faced by those who were warned by God's messengers but chose to ignore them.  It serves as a reminder of the importance of heeding divine warnings and the ultimate accountability for one's choices. It emphasizes the theme of divine justice and the eventual triumph of truth over falsehood.
orig: فكذبوه فنجيناه ومن معه في الفلك وجعلناهم خلائف وأغرقنا الذين كذبوا بآياتنا فانظر كيف كان عاقبة المنذرين

translation: Then We sent after him messengers to their people, and they came to them with clear proofs. But they were not to believe in that which they had rejected before. Thus do We seal over the hearts of the transgressors.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the cycle of disbelief and the hardening of hearts.  After a prophet (mentioned prior to this verse) is rejected, God sends subsequent messengers with clear evidence to their people.
