The final clause, "and they will have no helpers," reinforces the isolation and vulnerability of those who refuse guidance, highlighting the importance of accepting the truth while it is offered.
orig: إن تحرص على هداهم فإن الله لا يهدي من يضل وما لهم من ناصرين

translation: And they swear by Allah, with the strongest of their oaths, that Allah will not raise up those who die. Yes, [He will], a promise [binding] upon Him, true, but most of the people do not know.
interpretation: This verse describes the strong denial of the resurrection by some people during the time of the Prophet Muhammad. They swore vehemently, using the name of God, that resurrection was impossible. The verse then affirms the truth of the resurrection, emphasizing it as a promise from God that is absolutely true and binding.  The tragic irony is highlighted: they swear by God that God won't do something that God has promised to do. This illustrates their profound ignorance and lack of understanding of God's power and the reality of the afterlife.  The phrase "most of the people do not know" points to the widespread nature of this disbelief at the time, and perhaps serves as a timeless reminder that true knowledge of the divine is often obscured by limited human understanding and worldly preoccupations.
orig: وأقسموا بالله جهد أيمانهم لا يبعث الله من يموت بلى وعدا عليه حقا ولكن أكثر الناس لا يعلمون

translation: So He will make clear to them that about which they used to differ, and those who disbelieved will know that they were liars.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the ultimate judgment and clarification that God will provide on the Day of Resurrection.  The 'differences' mentioned here likely refer to the disputes and disagreements people had regarding God's message, His prophets, and the truth of the religion.  On that final day, all ambiguity will be removed, and the truth will be undeniably revealed.  Those who rejected faith and persisted in their disbelief will then realize the error of their ways and understand that their denial was based on falsehood.  The verse underscores the certainty of divine judgment and the eventual exposure of those who knowingly rejected the truth.
orig: ليبين لهم الذي يختلفون فيه وليعلم الذين كفروا أنهم كانوا كاذبين

translation: Indeed, Our word to a thing when We intend it is but that We say to it, "Be," and it is.
interpretation: This verse eloquently describes God's absolute power and creative ability.  It emphasizes the immediate and effortless nature of God's creation. When God wills something into existence, it happens instantaneously, simply by His command "Be."  There is no elaborate process, no struggle, and no intermediary steps.  The phrase "Our word" signifies God's divine will and decree, highlighting His complete control over all of existence.  This verse is often cited as evidence of God's omnipotence and the ease with which He brings forth the universe and everything in it from nothingness.
orig: إنما قولنا لشيء إذا أردناه أن نقول له كن فيكون

translation: And those who emigrated for the cause of God after being wronged - We will surely settle them in this world in a good place, and the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew.
interpretation: This verse offers comfort and a promise of reward to those who have been persecuted for their faith and forced to leave their homes.  "Emigrated for the cause of God" (هاجروا في الله) refers to the concept of *hijra*, leaving one's home or land for the sake of preserving or practicing one's religion. This doesn't necessarily imply physical relocation; it can also encompass a spiritual or intellectual migration away from oppressive influences. The verse specifies that this emigration follows being wronged (ظلموا), highlighting the injustice suffered by these individuals.  God promises them a "good place" (حسنة) in this world, which can refer to both physical safety and prosperity as well as spiritual contentment and peace.  However, the verse emphasizes that the true reward lies in the Hereafter (الآخرة), and it will be far greater (أكبر) than any worldly comfort.  The phrase "if only they knew" (لو كانوا يعلمون) underscores the immeasurable value of the reward awaiting them in the afterlife and serves as an encouragement to remain steadfast in their faith despite present hardships. It also implies that the full extent of this reward is beyond human comprehension.
orig: والذين هاجروا في الله من بعد ما ظلموا لنبوئنهم في الدنيا حسنة ولأجر الآخرة أكبر لو كانوا يعلمون

translation: Those who are patient and upon their Lord they rely.
interpretation: This verse highlights two crucial characteristics of believers: patience (sabr) and reliance on God (tawakkul).  Patience refers not only to enduring hardships with steadfastness but also to remaining consistent in performing good deeds and abstaining from sinful acts, even when faced with challenges or temptations.  Reliance on God, or tawakkul, signifies placing one's trust and confidence in God's plan and provision, believing that He is the best disposer of affairs.  The verse suggests that these two qualities are interconnected; true patience is rooted in the belief that God is in control and will ultimately bring about the best outcome.  It implies that by cultivating patience and placing our trust in God, we can find strength and peace in navigating life's difficulties and uncertainties.
orig: الذين صبروا وعلى ربهم يتوكلون

translation: And We sent not before you [O Muhammad] except men to whom We revealed [Our message]. So ask the people of the message if you do not know.
interpretation: This verse asserts the continuity of Muhammad's prophethood within a long line of prophets sent to humanity.  It emphasizes that divine revelation wasn't a new phenomenon with Muhammad but a consistent practice of God communicating with humankind through chosen messengers. These messengers were all men, ordinary humans, chosen by God. The phrase "people of the message/remembrance" (Ahl al-Dhikr) refers to those who possess previous scriptures, likely implying Jews and Christians in this context. The verse instructs those uncertain about the truth of Muhammad's message to consult those who have knowledge of the earlier scriptures, as these scriptures would contain prophecies and narratives foreshadowing Muhammad's arrival. This suggests that the previous scriptures support and validate Muhammad's claims, and by studying them, one can find evidence for his prophethood.  It therefore calls for inquiry and research rather than blind faith, acknowledging that those who are unfamiliar with the previous revelations might have legitimate questions. This also implicitly underscores the interconnectedness of divine messages across time and highlights the importance of seeking knowledge from reliable sources.
orig: وما أرسلنا من قبلك إلا رجالا نوحي إليهم فاسألوا أهل الذكر إن كنتم لا تعلمون

translation: With clear proofs and scriptures, and We have revealed to you the Reminder [the Qur'an] that you may make clear to the people what has been revealed to them, and perhaps they will reflect.
interpretation: This verse highlights the purpose and importance of the Qur'an.  "Clear proofs" (al-bayyinat) refers to the evident signs of God's existence and power in the creation, as well as the internal consistency and miraculous nature of the Qur'an itself.  "Scriptures" (al-zubur) refers to previous divine revelations, acknowledging a continuity of God's message throughout history. The Qur'an is then identified as "the Reminder" (al-dhikr), emphasizing its function to remind people of the truth, their purpose, and their responsibilities. The verse emphasizes the Prophet Muhammad's role as a clarifier of the revelation, explaining its meaning and application to the people. Finally, the verse states the ultimate hope that through this clarification and reminder, people will engage in thoughtful reflection (tafakkur) and ultimately choose the path of guidance.
orig: بالبينات والزبر وأنزلنا إليك الذكر لتبين للناس ما نزل إليهم ولعلهم يتفكرون

translation: Do those who plan evil deeds feel secure that Allah will not cause the earth to swallow them, or that the punishment will not come upon them from where they do not perceive?
interpretation: This verse serves as a warning against those who plot and scheme evil acts.  It emphasizes the power and knowledge of God, highlighting that He is fully aware of the concealed plans of evildoers.  The verse suggests that divine retribution can manifest in unexpected ways, either through dramatic earthly catastrophes like earthquakes (symbolized by the earth swallowing them), or through other forms of punishment that arrive suddenly and without warning, catching the perpetrators completely unaware. The question posed is rhetorical, implying that such security is misplaced and foolish. Ultimately, the verse emphasizes the importance of righteous conduct and the certainty of divine justice, reminding individuals that their actions have consequences, even if those consequences aren't immediately apparent.
orig: أفأمن الذين مكروا السيئات أن يخسف الله بهم الأرض أو يأتيهم العذاب من حيث لا يشعرون

translation: Or He takes them while they are heedless [of His plan], and they are unable to escape.
interpretation: This verse describes the absolute power and control of God over human destiny.  It highlights two possible scenarios concerning the punishment of wrongdoers. The first, implied from the preceding verses, is a gradual decline and punishment. This verse presents the second scenario: a sudden and swift seizure of the wrongdoers.  The phrase "في تقلبهم" can be understood as "in their heedlessness," "in their distractions," or "in their state of constant change/activity."  This implies they may be caught completely unaware, engaged in their daily affairs, oblivious to the impending divine intervention. The crucial point is their inability to escape or prevent this divine judgment ("فما هم بمعجزين"). This reinforces the idea of God's ultimate authority and the futility of resisting His will. It serves as a reminder of the importance of living righteously and being mindful of God's presence.
orig: أو يأخذهم في تقلبهم فما هم بمعجزين

translation: Or He takes them gradually by reducing their sustenance [through drought, famine, etc.], for indeed, your Lord is All-Gentle, Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the various ways God interacts with humanity, specifically referencing the consequences of straying from His path. While sometimes punishment might be swift and decisive, this verse highlights a more gradual approach.  God might progressively diminish blessings, such as livelihood or sustenance, through difficulties like drought, famine, economic hardship, or other means.  This acts as a warning, a gentle nudge to encourage reflection and a return to righteousness. The emphasis on God's attributes of "Ra'uf" (All-Gentle) and "Rahim" (Most Merciful) underscores that even in the midst of hardship brought about as a consequence of actions, God's mercy and gentleness remain. The gradual nature of the hardship allows space for repentance and reform. It's not meant to utterly destroy, but rather to guide back to the right path.  This verse encourages contemplation on the subtle ways God communicates with us and reminds us of His unwavering mercy, even in times of difficulty.
orig: أو يأخذهم على تخوف فإن ربكم لرءوف رحيم

translation: Do they not see what Allah has created, [things] whose shadows incline to the right and to the left, prostrating to Allah, while they are subservient?
interpretation: This verse invites reflection on the natural world as a testament to God's power and the universality of submission to Him.  Everything in creation, even the shadows cast by objects as they move with the sun, is depicted as prostrating to God.  This 'prostration' is not necessarily a literal bowing down, but rather symbolizes their inherent obedience to God's laws and their dependence on Him. The phrase 'while they are subservient (dahiroon)' further emphasizes this complete submission and humility before God.  The verse serves as a reminder of God's majesty and encourages humans, who are endowed with intellect and free will, to also recognize and submit to their Creator.
orig: أولم يروا إلى ما خلق الله من شيء يتفيأ ظلاله عن اليمين والشمائل سجدا لله وهم داخرون

translation: And to Allah prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures, and the angels [as well], and they are not arrogant.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the universal submission to God.  Everything in the heavens (stars, planets, galaxies, etc.) and everything on earth that moves (animals, insects, humans, etc.), including the angels, prostrates to God. This prostration isn't necessarily a physical act, but rather signifies a state of complete obedience, subservience, and recognition of God's absolute power and authority.  The addition of "and they are not arrogant" highlights the contrast between the created beings and their humble submission, and the potential for humans, who possess free will, to fall into arrogance and refuse this natural inclination towards God.
orig: ولله يسجد ما في السماوات وما في الأرض من دابة والملائكة وهم لا يستكبرون

translation: They fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded.
interpretation: This verse describes the righteous believers.  "They fear their Lord above them" refers to a deep reverence and awe of God, recognizing His ultimate authority and power. This fear is not one of terror, but rather a respectful awareness of God's greatness and a desire to avoid displeasing Him.  It motivates them to obedience, as indicated by the second part of the verse, "and they do what they are commanded."  This obedience encompasses all of God's commands, both those revealed in scripture and those understood through reason and conscience.  The verse highlights the essential connection between true faith and righteous action, emphasizing that genuine fear of God leads to fulfilling His will.
orig: يخافون ربهم من فوقهم ويفعلون ما يؤمرون

translation: And Allah has said, "Do not take for yourselves two deities. He is but one God, so fear only Me."
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the core Islamic principle of Tawhid (Oneness of God).  It unequivocally rejects polytheism, the worship of multiple gods.  The Arabic word "إلهين" (ilahayn) specifically refers to two deities, but the implication extends to any number greater than one.  The verse asserts that there is only one true God, and therefore, all worship, reverence, and fear (rahbah) should be directed solely towards Him.  This "fear" is not merely terror, but rather a deep respect, awe, and consciousness of God's power and authority, which motivates obedience and submission to His will.  The verse thus establishes the foundational concept of exclusive devotion to God as the basis of Islamic belief and practice.
orig: وقال الله لا تتخذوا إلهين اثنين إنما هو إله واحد فإياي فارهبون

translation: To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and to Him is [due] religion constantly. So is it other than Allah that you fear?
interpretation: This verse asserts God's absolute sovereignty and ownership of everything in the heavens and the earth.  The phrase "and to Him is [due] religion constantly" emphasizes the permanence and unwavering nature of devotion owed to God alone.  This highlights the concept of *tawḥīd* (oneness of God) as the core principle of Islam. By posing the rhetorical question "So is it other than Allah that you fear?", the verse challenges the notion of fearing or giving ultimate allegiance to any other power or authority. It underscores that true piety and reverence should be directed solely towards God, the ultimate source of all things and the only one deserving of such devotion. The verse implies that fearing anything else besides God is misplaced and illogical, given His complete dominion over all creation.
orig: وله ما في السماوات والأرض وله الدين واصبا أفغير الله تتقون

translation: And whatever blessing you have is from Allah. Then when adversity touches you, to Him you cry for help.
interpretation: This verse highlights the ultimate source of all good things in life and the natural human inclination to turn to God in times of hardship.  It emphasizes that every blessing, be it health, wealth, family, or any other form of prosperity, originates from God.  Despite this, humans often forget this divine source in times of ease and comfort.  However, when faced with adversity, difficulty, or suffering, their innate disposition is to turn to God and implore Him for aid and relief. This verse serves as a reminder of our dependence on God in all circumstances, both good and bad.  It encourages gratitude for His blessings and emphasizes the importance of turning to Him in prayer during challenging times. It subtly suggests a human tendency to sometimes forget God's role in our successes and remember Him only during our struggles.  Ultimately, the verse reinforces the concept of God's omnipotence and mercy, while highlighting the inherent human need for divine assistance.
orig: وما بكم من نعمة فمن الله ثم إذا مسكم الضر فإليه تجأرون

translation: Then, when the harm is removed from you, behold! a group among you associate others with their Lord.
interpretation: This verse describes the human tendency towards ingratitude and forgetfulness of God, especially after experiencing relief from hardship.  When faced with adversity, people often turn to God in supplication and prayer. However, once the difficulty passes, some individuals revert to their old ways, attributing their deliverance to other forces or entities, thus associating partners (shirk) with God. This can manifest in different forms, such as believing in luck, charms, or attributing power to other individuals or idols. The verse highlights the fickle nature of faith for some, reminding us of the importance of consistent devotion and gratitude to God regardless of circumstance.
orig: ثم إذا كشف الضر عنكم إذا فريق منكم بربهم يشركون

translation: So they may disbelieve in what We have given them, so enjoy yourselves. You will soon know.
interpretation: This verse speaks of the defiant attitude of those who reject the guidance and blessings bestowed upon them by God.  The phrase "So they may disbelieve in what We have given them" highlights their conscious choice to deny the truth, even with the evidence before them.  "So enjoy yourselves" carries a tone of irony and warning.  It isn't a genuine invitation to pleasure but rather a sarcastic acknowledgment of their temporary indulgence in worldly pursuits while ignoring the spiritual consequences.  The concluding phrase, "You will soon know," serves as a powerful reminder of the inevitable accountability and judgment that awaits them. It emphasizes that their current state of disbelief and fleeting enjoyment will ultimately lead to understanding, albeit through a painful realization of their error.  This verse often appears in contexts where God is describing the consequences of rejecting His messengers and disobeying His commands. It underscores the theme of divine justice and the ultimate triumph of truth.
orig: ليكفروا بما آتيناهم فتمتعوا فسوف تعلمون

translation: And they assign to what they do not know a share of what We have provided them. By Allah, you will surely be questioned about what you used to fabricate.
interpretation: This verse condemns the practice of ascribing partners or intermediaries to God, particularly in the context of receiving sustenance and blessings.  It highlights the ignorance involved in such attributions, as people assign a portion of what God has given them to entities they have no true knowledge of.  These entities could be idols, spirits, or even fabricated concepts.  The verse emphasizes the accountability for such actions, asserting that individuals will be questioned by God about these false attributions and fabrications. The oath "By Allah" reinforces the seriousness and certainty of this questioning. Essentially, the verse warns against diverting gratitude and recognition away from the true source of all provision, which is God, and towards invented or misunderstood powers.
orig: ويجعلون لما لا يعلمون نصيبا مما رزقناهم تالله لتسألن عما كنتم تفترون

translation: And they attribute to Allah daughters - Exalted is He - and for themselves what they desire.
interpretation: This verse condemns the pre-Islamic practice of some Arabs who considered daughters as less desirable than sons.  It highlights the injustice and ignorance of this belief system.  "Exalted is He" (Subhanahu) emphasizes God's transcendence above such flawed human perceptions.  The phrase "and for themselves what they desire" ironically points out their hypocrisy: they ascribe daughters to God, whom they view as undesirable, while keeping sons for themselves, whom they value more.  This verse asserts God's absolute purity and condemns gender discrimination.
orig: ويجعلون لله البنات سبحانه ولهم ما يشتهون

translation: And when one of them is informed of [the birth of] a female, his face becomes dark, and he suppresses grief.
interpretation: This verse describes a pre-Islamic Arabian cultural practice where the birth of a daughter was often met with disappointment and shame.  The darkening face and suppressed grief depict the father's negative reaction.  The verse doesn't condone this practice but rather highlights the societal injustice prevalent at the time. It serves as a critique of this jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance) attitude towards female children. The Qur'an, in numerous other verses, elevates the status of women and condemns such discriminatory practices. This verse therefore forms part of a larger discourse on gender equality and the inherent worth of every human life, regardless of gender.
orig: وإذا بشر أحدهم بالأنثى ظل وجهه مسودا وهو كظيم

translation: He hides from the people, because of the evil of what he has been given of news - should he keep it with him in humiliation, or bury it in the dust? Unquestionably, evil is what they judge.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the societal pressure surrounding the birth of daughters in pre-Islamic Arabia.  The 'evil news' (سوء ما بشر به) refers to the news of a female child's birth.  The father of the newborn girl is described as being torn between two terrible choices.  'Should he keep it with him in humiliation (أيمسكه على هون),' meaning should he bear the social shame and stigma associated with having a daughter, the 'it' referring to either the child or the news itself. The other option, 'or bury it in the dust (أم يدسه في التراب),' is a chilling reference to the horrific practice of female infanticide. The verse ends with a powerful condemnation of this societal mindset and these practices: 'Unquestionably, evil is what they judge (ألا ساء ما يحكمون).'  This highlights the injustice and moral bankruptcy of such judgments and actions, emphasizing the Quran's strong stance against them. It condemns the cultural norms that valued sons over daughters and allowed for such atrocities.
orig: يتوارى من القوم من سوء ما بشر به أيمسكه على هون أم يدسه في التراب ألا ساء ما يحكمون

translation: For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the likeness of evil, and for Allah is the highest similitude, and He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: This verse contrasts the flawed understanding of those who disbelieve in the Hereafter with the perfect knowledge and attributes of God.  The phrase "likeness of evil" (مثل السوء) suggests that their understanding of reality is distorted, incomplete, and ultimately harmful.  They base their actions and judgments on a limited, worldly perspective, leading to flawed choices and a lack of true purpose. Their actions and perspectives are likened to something negative, impure, or deficient, mirroring their flawed belief system.  Conversely, "for Allah is the highest similitude" (ولله المثل الأعلى) affirms that God's knowledge, wisdom, and power are the ultimate standard of truth and perfection.  Only God possesses the complete picture, and true understanding comes only from aligning oneself with His will. The attributes "Exalted in Might" (العزيز) and "Wise" (الحكيم) further emphasize God's absolute authority and perfect judgment, highlighting the contrast between the limited perspective of disbelievers and the boundless wisdom of the Creator.  The verse, therefore, serves as both a warning against the pitfalls of disbelief and an affirmation of God's supreme power and wisdom.
orig: للذين لا يؤمنون بالآخرة مثل السوء ولله المثل الأعلى وهو العزيز الحكيم

translation: If Allah were to take people to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave on it (the earth) a single moving creature, but He postpones them until an appointed term. And when their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour, nor can they advance it.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's mercy and patience with humanity.  While people consistently commit wrongs and injustices, God doesn't immediately punish them for every transgression.  Instead, He grants a reprieve, a period of time in which they can repent, reform, and experience the consequences of their actions within the natural order of life.  This 'appointed term' could refer to an individual's lifespan or a designated period for a community or even humanity as a whole.  The verse highlights the certainty and inescapability of this appointed time.  When the time comes for accountability, whether it be death or another form of divine reckoning, there's no postponement or advancement possible.  It stresses the importance of using the time given wisely, recognizing God's mercy, and preparing for the inevitable moment of accountability.
orig: ولو يؤاخذ الله الناس بظلمهم ما ترك عليها من دابة ولكن يؤخرهم إلى أجل مسمى فإذا جاء أجلهم لا يستأخرون ساعة ولا يستقدمون

translation: And they attribute to Allah what they dislike, and their tongues describe the lie that they will have the best [reward]. Assuredly, for them is the Fire, and indeed, they are [left] neglected.
interpretation: This verse describes the hypocrisy of some individuals who outwardly profess belief in God but inwardly harbor resentment towards His decrees. They attribute to God things they find unpleasant or undesirable, reflecting a lack of genuine acceptance of His will.  Furthermore, they deceive themselves and others by claiming they are destined for Paradise (al-Husna, the best reward), even though their actions contradict this claim. Their deceitful words are highlighted as "the lie" uttered by their tongues. The verse concludes with the stark reality of their situation: they are destined for Hellfire (an-Nar) because of their hypocrisy and self-deception, and they will be abandoned and neglected (mufratun), forsaken by God's mercy due to their persistent denial of truth.
orig: ويجعلون لله ما يكرهون وتصف ألسنتهم الكذب أن لهم الحسنى لا جرم أن لهم النار وأنهم مفرطون

translation: By Allah, We indeed sent [messengers] to nations before you, but Satan made their deeds attractive to them. So he is their protector today, and they will have a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the recurring historical pattern of divine messengers being sent to guide humanity, and the persistent influence of Satan in leading people astray.  It highlights how Satan can deceive people by making their wrongful actions appear appealing and righteous in their own eyes. This deception prevents them from recognizing the truth and following the guidance of the messengers.  The phrase "he is their protector today" signifies that in the Hereafter, those who succumbed to Satan's deception will be under his dominion, separated from God's mercy. The verse concludes by emphasizing the inevitable consequence of following Satan's path: a painful punishment in the afterlife.
orig: تالله لقد أرسلنا إلى أمم من قبلك فزين لهم الشيطان أعمالهم فهو وليهم اليوم ولهم عذاب أليم

translation: And We have not revealed to you the Book, [O Muhammad], except for you to make clear to them that about which they differ [i.e., religious matters], and as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.
interpretation:
This verse highlights the core purpose of the Qur'an's revelation to Prophet Muhammad.  It emphasizes three key functions:

1. **Clarification of Disputes:** The Qur'an serves as the ultimate authority to resolve disagreements and conflicting interpretations regarding religious matters.  It addresses the questions and debates prevalent among the people, providing clear guidance and settling disputes.

2. **Guidance (Huda):** The Qur'an provides comprehensive guidance for all aspects of life, showing the straight path and offering principles for moral, ethical, and spiritual living.  This guidance leads to a deeper understanding of God's will and purpose for humanity.

3. **Mercy (Rahma):** The Qur'an acts as a source of mercy, specifically for those who believe.  By adhering to its teachings, believers find solace, forgiveness, and hope.  The guidance it provides leads them to a path of righteousness and ultimately to God's mercy. 

It's important to note the specification of "a people who believe." While the Qur'an aims to clarify disputes for all, its guidance and mercy are particularly emphasized for those who accept its message and strive to live by its principles. This implies that the full benefit of the Qur'an's wisdom can only be realized through faith and active engagement with its teachings.
orig: وما أنزلنا عليك الكتاب إلا لتبين لهم الذي اختلفوا فيه وهدى ورحمة لقوم يؤمنون

translation: And Allah has sent down rain from the sky and given life thereby to the earth after its lifelessness. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who listen.
interpretation:
This verse highlights the life-giving power of rain sent by God (Allah).  The earth is described as being lifeless or dead (mawta) before the rain revitalizes it. This imagery emphasizes the transformative effect of water and its essential role in sustaining life.  The verse concludes by stating that this phenomenon is a clear "sign" (ayah) for those who are receptive and pay attention.  This 'sign' can be understood on multiple levels:

* **A sign of God's power and mercy:**  Rain is a tangible manifestation of God's ability to create and sustain life. It demonstrates His mercy and provision for all living things.
* **A sign inviting reflection and understanding:**  Observing the cycle of death and rebirth in nature, as symbolized by the dry earth coming alive with rain, should prompt contemplation about the greater cycles of life, death, and resurrection.
* **A sign pointing towards the importance of listening and heeding God's message:** The phrase "for a people who listen" (li-qawmin yasmaʿūn) emphasizes the importance of being attentive not only to the physical world but also to the spiritual lessons it conveys.  True understanding requires not just hearing, but actively listening and reflecting on the signs of God present in creation.  It suggests that those who truly 'listen' – both to the natural world and to God's revealed word – will recognize the divine wisdom at play.
orig: والله أنزل من السماء ماء فأحيا به الأرض بعد موتها إن في ذلك لآية لقوم يسمعون

translation: And indeed, for you in livestock is a lesson. We give you drink from what is in their bellies - between excretion and blood - pure milk, palatable to drinkers.
interpretation: This verse highlights the wonder of God's creation and provision for humanity through the example of livestock.  It draws attention to the remarkable process by which milk, a pure and wholesome nourishment, is produced within the animal's body, specifically originating from a location between digested matter (excretion/dung) and blood. This seemingly improbable source emphasizes the divine power and wisdom in transforming something seemingly impure into a pure and beneficial substance.  The verse invites contemplation on the intricate workings of nature and the blessings that God bestows upon us through seemingly ordinary creatures like livestock.  It encourages gratitude and recognition of the divine hand in providing sustenance for humanity. The palatable nature of milk is also emphasized, signifying the ease and enjoyment with which we consume this divinely provided nourishment.
orig: وإن لكم في الأنعام لعبرة نسقيكم مما في بطونه من بين فرث ودم لبنا خالصا سائغا للشاربين

translation: And from the fruits of the date palms and grapes, you obtain intoxicating drink and wholesome provision. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who reason.
interpretation:
This verse highlights the multifaceted nature of God's creation, using the examples of date palms and grapes.  These fruits provide both "sakran" (often understood as intoxicating drink, though interpretations vary as discussed below) and "rizqan hasanan" (wholesome provision, good sustenance).  This duality points to the potential for both benefit and harm, good and bad use, residing within the same creation.  The verse concludes by emphasizing that the presence of these contrasting elements within the same fruit serves as a "sign" or "ayah" for those who use their intellect and reflect.  This encourages contemplation on the following aspects:

* **Human Responsibility:**  God provides the raw materials, but humans have the choice of how to utilize them.  They can choose to process grapes and dates into wholesome food or into intoxicating substances.
* **The Balance in Creation:**  God has created a world of diverse elements, some beneficial and some potentially harmful.  This balance allows for free will and the opportunity for humans to choose wisely.
* **The Importance of Reason:**  The verse specifically addresses "those who reason."  This suggests that understanding the deeper meaning of God's creation requires intellectual effort and reflection, not just blind faith.
* **Varying Interpretations of "Sakran":** The word "sakran" primarily means intoxication, typically referring to alcoholic beverages.  However, some interpretations also include non-alcoholic intoxicating substances or even simply the sweet, rich juice that can be derived from these fruits before fermentation occurs.  This broader understanding suggests that even natural sweetness, if consumed excessively, can be intoxicating or lead to imbalance. Regardless of the specific interpretation of "sakran," the verse emphasizes the importance of moderation and responsible use of God's gifts.
orig: ومن ثمرات النخيل والأعناب تتخذون منه سكرا ورزقا حسنا إن في ذلك لآية لقوم يعقلون

translation: And your Lord inspired the bee, saying: "Take you habitations in the mountains and in the trees and in what they construct."
interpretation:
This verse speaks to the divine guidance bestowed upon even the smallest of creatures, the bee.  The command "take you habitations" highlights the agency granted to the bee, suggesting an innate understanding and capability to follow this instruction. The mention of "mountains, trees, and what they construct" refers to the diverse locations where bees build their hives, encompassing natural structures like mountain crevices and tree hollows, as well as man-made structures or hives.  This verse can be interpreted in several ways:

1. **Divine Wisdom in Nature:** It demonstrates the inherent wisdom and order present in the natural world, where even insects are guided by a higher power to fulfill their role in the ecosystem.  It points towards the intricate interconnectedness of all living things and their dependence on divine guidance.

2. **The Importance of Bees:** The specific mention of bees highlights their significance in the natural world, likely referencing their crucial role in pollination and honey production, which are vital for sustaining life.

3. **A Metaphor for Human Endeavor:** Some interpretations suggest the verse serves as a metaphor for human endeavor and the importance of establishing stable homes and communities.  Just as bees build hives, humans are encouraged to build societies based on order, cooperation, and productivity.

4. **Reflecting on Creation:**  The verse encourages reflection on the wonders of creation and the divine power that governs it. By observing the behavior of even a small creature like the bee, one can gain insights into the wisdom and grandeur of God's creation.

Ultimately, this verse serves as a reminder of the divine presence in every aspect of creation and encourages humans to appreciate and learn from the natural world around them.
orig: وأوحى ربك إلى النحل أن اتخذي من الجبال بيوتا ومن الشجر ومما يعرشون

translation: Then eat from all the fruits and follow the ways of your Lord laid down [for you]. There emerges from their bellies a drink, varying in colors, in which there is healing for people. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who give thought.
interpretation: This verse, often associated with bees and honey, speaks to the wonder of God's creation and the signs within it for those who reflect.  "Eat from all the fruits" can be interpreted literally, encouraging the consumption of diverse and wholesome foods provided by God.  It can also be understood metaphorically, as an encouragement to explore diverse experiences and paths in life. "Follow the ways of your Lord laid down [for you]" emphasizes adherence to the natural laws and divine guidance provided by God. This connects to the subsequent description of bees producing honey.  They instinctively follow the paths set for them, diligently working and producing a substance with healing properties. The "drink, varying in colors" clearly refers to honey, known for its diverse hues and medicinal qualities.  The verse highlights not just the physical healing provided by honey but also alludes to a deeper, spiritual healing available to those who contemplate God's creation and recognize the signs embedded within it.  The emphasis on "a people who give thought" underscores the importance of reflection and contemplation. The verse encourages us to move beyond simply observing the natural world and to actively engage with it intellectually and spiritually, recognizing the divine wisdom manifested in even the smallest creatures and their products.  It serves as a reminder that God's signs are everywhere for those who seek them, prompting us to appreciate the interconnectedness of creation and the profound lessons it holds.
orig: ثم كلي من كل الثمرات فاسلكي سبل ربك ذللا يخرج من بطونها شراب مختلف ألوانه فيه شفاء للناس إن في ذلك لآية لقوم يتفكرون

translation: And Allah created you, then He takes your souls (in death); and among you is he who is brought back to the most abject time of life so that he knows nothing after having known (much). Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Powerful.
interpretation: This verse speaks about the human lifecycle from creation to death, highlighting God's absolute power over life and death. It also points to the phenomenon of senility, where some individuals, after a lifetime of knowledge and experience, revert to a state of mental decline where they lose their accumulated knowledge.  This serves as a reminder of the transient nature of worldly life and the vulnerability of human intellect.  God, being All-Knowing and All-Powerful, is the one who ordains this process. The phrase "most abject time of life" (أرذل العمر) refers to extreme old age where one might experience physical and mental decline, highlighting the humbling nature of the human experience and the ultimate return to a state of dependence. The contrast between possessing knowledge and losing it emphasizes the importance of utilizing knowledge wisely during one's prime and recognizing God's ultimate authority over all things.
orig: والله خلقكم ثم يتوفاكم ومنكم من يرد إلى أرذل العمر لكي لا يعلم بعد علم شيئا إن الله عليم قدير

translation: And Allah has favored some of you over others in provision. But those who have been favored are not going to share their provision with those whom their right hands possess, so they become equal in it. Then, do they deny the favor of Allah?
interpretation: This verse addresses the issue of economic disparity and the moral responsibility that comes with wealth.  Allah acknowledges that some people are granted more sustenance (rizq) than others. However, the verse criticizes those who hoard their wealth and don't share it with those under their care, specifically referencing 'those whom their right hands possess,' which historically referred to slaves but can be interpreted more broadly as those who are dependent or less fortunate.  The verse questions the behavior of the wealthy who fail to recognize that their wealth is a blessing from Allah and that they are expected to use it justly and compassionately. By not sharing their wealth and acting as if everyone is equal in their access to it (which they are clearly not), the wealthy deny Allah's favor, implying ingratitude and a disregard for the social responsibility that comes with being blessed with abundance.  It challenges the notion that wealth is solely earned through individual effort and emphasizes the role of divine grace. Therefore, the verse encourages generosity, social justice, and recognizing that wealth disparity should be addressed through compassionate sharing, not selfish hoarding.
orig: والله فضل بعضكم على بعض في الرزق فما الذين فضلوا برادي رزقهم على ما ملكت أيمانهم فهم فيه سواء أفبنعمة الله يجحدون

translation: And Allah has made for you mates from yourselves, and has made for you from your mates, sons and grandsons, and has provided for you from the good things. Then in falsehood do they believe, and in the blessing of Allah they disbelieve?
interpretation: This verse highlights the blessings of Allah (God) in providing spouses, children, and grandchildren, as well as sustenance. It then contrasts these blessings with the ingratitude of those who reject faith (believing in falsehood) and deny the source of these blessings.  It emphasizes the irony and illogical nature of disbelief in the face of such evident divine provision. The 'good things' (الطيبات - at-tayyibat) can refer to both physical sustenance like food and drink, and also the emotional and spiritual fulfillment that comes from family and relationships. The verse serves as a reminder to appreciate the gifts bestowed by God and to acknowledge Him as the ultimate source of all good.
orig: والله جعل لكم من أنفسكم أزواجا وجعل لكم من أزواجكم بنين وحفدة ورزقكم من الطيبات أفبالباطل يؤمنون وبنعمت الله هم يكفرون

translation: And they worship besides Allah things that do not possess for them any provision from the heavens and the earth, and [they] are not capable [of doing so].
interpretation: This verse critiques the practice of idolatry, emphasizing the powerlessness of false gods.  It highlights the logical fallacy of worshipping that which cannot even sustain itself, let alone provide sustenance or any benefit to its worshippers.  "Provision" (rizq) here refers not only to physical necessities like food and water but also to any form of blessing or aid. The verse asserts that only Allah is the true source of all sustenance and power, both in the heavens and on earth. The idols, being inanimate objects or created beings themselves, are utterly incapable of providing anything. This incapacity demonstrates their fundamental inadequacy as objects of worship and reinforces the exclusive divinity of Allah.
orig: ويعبدون من دون الله ما لا يملك لهم رزقا من السماوات والأرض شيئا ولا يستطيعون

translation: So do not make comparisons for Allah. Indeed, Allah knows and you do not know.
interpretation: This verse cautions against attempting to understand or explain God's actions, attributes, or nature through human analogies or comparisons.  Humans, with their limited knowledge and perspective, cannot truly grasp the divine essence.  Making comparisons or drawing parallels between God and created things is inherently flawed and can lead to misunderstandings and misrepresentations of God's true nature. The verse emphasizes the vast difference in knowledge between God and humanity. God's knowledge is all-encompassing, while human knowledge is finite and imperfect.  Therefore, any attempt to define or limit God based on human understanding is futile and potentially disrespectful. It encourages a sense of humility and awe before the divine, acknowledging the inherent limitations of human comprehension when it comes to the divine reality.  It's a call to accept God's wisdom and authority without attempting to impose human logic or frameworks onto it.
orig: فلا تضربوا لله الأمثال إن الله يعلم وأنتم لا تعلمون

translation: God sets forth the example of a slave owned by another, who has no power over anything, and [another person] whom We have provided with good provision from Us, and he spends thereof secretly and openly. Are they equal? Praise be to God! But most of them do not know.
interpretation: This verse highlights the vast difference between those who are truly free and those enslaved, not just physically, but also metaphorically by their limited resources and circumstances.  The 'slave owned by another' represents someone who lacks agency and control over their life and resources. They are dependent and unable to act independently.  In contrast, the individual 'whom We have provided with good provision' represents someone blessed with resources and the freedom to utilize them.  Their ability to spend 'secretly and openly' demonstrates their agency and control over their wealth. Spending secretly signifies charitable acts done discreetly, while spending openly indicates their ability to provide for themselves and others publicly. The rhetorical question 'Are they equal?' emphasizes the stark disparity between these two situations. It's a clear indication that God values generosity and the freedom to act righteously. The verse concludes by lamenting the lack of understanding among most people regarding this important distinction. Many fail to recognize the true value of freedom and the responsibility that comes with having resources, focusing instead on superficial comparisons. This verse can be interpreted as a call to appreciate the blessings of God, to utilize them wisely and generously, and to recognize the profound difference between true freedom and dependence.
orig: ضرب الله مثلا عبدا مملوكا لا يقدر على شيء ومن رزقناه منا رزقا حسنا فهو ينفق منه سرا وجهرا هل يستوون الحمد لله بل أكثرهم لا يعلمون

translation: God sets forth the example of two men: one of them is mute, unable to do anything, and he is a burden on his guardian; wherever he directs him, he brings no good. Is he equal to one who commands justice and is on a straight path?
interpretation: This verse uses a parable to illustrate the stark contrast between those who are unproductive and misguided, and those who actively strive for righteousness. The mute man, incapable of action and dependent, symbolizes those who lack understanding and contribute nothing positive. His guardian's efforts, despite directing him, yield no benefit, representing the futility of guiding someone unwilling or unable to comprehend. This man is then compared to someone who commands justice and follows a straight path, representing those who possess knowledge, act righteously, and contribute to the well-being of society. The rhetorical question at the end emphasizes the clear disparity between the two, highlighting the value and superiority of those who actively pursue justice and guidance.  It emphasizes the importance of striving for knowledge, understanding, and righteous action, contrasting it with the futility of ignorance and inaction. This can be applied to individuals, communities, and even nations, urging them to actively pursue justice and follow a path of righteousness.
orig: وضرب الله مثلا رجلين أحدهما أبكم لا يقدر على شيء وهو كل على مولاه أينما يوجهه لا يأت بخير هل يستوي هو ومن يأمر بالعدل وهو على صراط مستقيم

translation: And to Allah belongs the unseen [aspects] of the heavens and the earth. And the matter of the Hour is not but as a twinkling of the eye or even nearer. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's absolute knowledge and power.  "The unseen [aspects] of the heavens and the earth" refers to everything beyond human comprehension, past, present, and future. This includes not only physical phenomena but also the destinies of individuals and the timing of events.  The "Hour" (al-Sā'ah) signifies the Day of Judgment, a pivotal moment in Islamic eschatology. The verse highlights the suddenness and imminence of the Hour, comparing it to the blink of an eye or even something faster. This isn't necessarily meant to specify a literal timeframe, but rather to emphasize that it could happen at any moment and that humanity should always be prepared.  The concluding phrase, "Indeed, Allah is over all things competent," reinforces God's omnipotence and ability to bring about the Hour, along with any other event, whenever He wills. It underscores the idea that God is not bound by time or any other limitations and possesses complete control over creation.
orig: ولله غيب السماوات والأرض وما أمر الساعة إلا كلمح البصر أو هو أقرب إن الله على كل شيء قدير

translation: And Allah brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers when you knew nothing; and He gave you hearing and sight and intellect that you might be grateful.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the profound blessings of Allah upon humanity from the very beginning of life.  It highlights our complete dependence on Him at birth, coming into the world knowing absolutely nothing.  Then, it points to the gifts He bestows upon us – hearing, sight, and intellect (often interpreted as the capacity for understanding and reason). These are not mere biological functions, but divine endowments that enable us to experience and interact with the world, to learn, to grow, and ultimately, to understand and appreciate the Creator. The verse culminates with the purpose of these gifts: that we might be grateful (تشكرون - tashkuroon).  This gratitude is not simply a feeling, but should manifest in acknowledging Allah's favors through obedience, worship, and using these gifts in ways that please Him and benefit ourselves and others. It underscores the inherent link between our blessings and our responsibility to use them wisely and thankfully.
orig: والله أخرجكم من بطون أمهاتكم لا تعلمون شيئا وجعل لكم السمع والأبصار والأفئدة لعلكم تشكرون

translation: Do they not see the birds, subjected [to Allah's command] in the atmosphere of the sky? None holds them [aloft] except Allah. Indeed, in that are surely signs for a people who believe.
interpretation: This verse invites reflection on the natural world, specifically the flight of birds, as a testament to God's power and control.  The Arabic word "musakhkharat" emphasizes the birds' subjugation to God's will, highlighting that their ability to fly is not their own doing, but a gift from God.  They are held aloft not by their own strength, but by God's command.  This observation serves as a 'sign' (ayah) for those who are open to believing in God. These signs are not just observable phenomena, but prompts for deeper thought and understanding about the divine reality underlying the apparent world.  Observing the natural world with an attentive eye, and recognizing the divine hand at play, strengthens faith and deepens appreciation for God's power and wisdom. The verse also implicitly contrasts the intricate system that keeps birds airborne with the perceived freedom and self-sufficiency of humans, suggesting a deeper dependence on God than we might typically acknowledge.
orig: ألم يروا إلى الطير مسخرات في جو السماء ما يمسكهن إلا الله إن في ذلك لآيات لقوم يؤمنون

translation: And Allah has made for you from your houses a place of dwelling, and has made for you from the hides of the cattle houses which you find light (to carry) on the day of your movement and on the day of your staying (in a place), and from their wool and fur and hair (He has made) furnishings and articles of convenience for a while.
interpretation: This verse highlights God's provision and care for humanity.  It speaks of the multiple blessings derived from animals, specifically focusing on their utility in providing shelter and comfort.  "Houses" initially refers to established dwellings, signifying security and rest.  Then, the verse moves to the portable tents made from animal hides, useful for nomadic life, emphasizing practicality and ease of transport during travel ("day of your movement") and temporary settlement ("day of your staying").  Furthermore, it points to the use of wool, fur, and hair for furnishings and other necessities ("articles of convenience"), underscoring how God has provided resources for both basic needs and comfort.  The phrase "for a while" (or "to a time") suggests the temporary nature of worldly possessions and serves as a reminder that ultimate reliance should be on God, the true provider.
orig: والله جعل لكم من بيوتكم سكنا وجعل لكم من جلود الأنعام بيوتا تستخفونها يوم ظعنكم ويوم إقامتكم ومن أصوافها وأوبارها وأشعارها أثاثا ومتاعا إلى حين

translation: And Allah has made for you from what He created shades, and has made for you from the mountains shelters, and has made for you garments which protect you from the heat, and garments which protect you from your [enemies'] violence. Thus does He complete His favor upon you that you might submit.
interpretation: This verse highlights God's provision and protection for humanity. It emphasizes the various ways God cares for us, using examples from the natural world and human creations.  'Shades' can refer to the shade of trees, clouds, or even buildings, providing relief from the sun's heat. 'Shelters' from mountains suggest protection from the elements and potential dangers.  The mention of garments protecting from heat and violence points to both physical comfort and safety in conflict, likely referencing armor. The verse culminates by connecting these blessings to God's ultimate purpose: that we might surrender to Him ('submit' or 'become Muslim'). This implies that recognizing and appreciating God's blessings should lead us to gratitude and devotion.  It suggests that these provisions are not merely for our physical well-being but are also intended to guide us towards spiritual fulfillment through submission to the divine will.
orig: والله جعل لكم مما خلق ظلالا وجعل لكم من الجبال أكنانا وجعل لكم سرابيل تقيكم الحر وسرابيل تقيكم بأسكم كذلك يتم نعمته عليكم لعلكم تسلمون

translation: So if they turn away, [O Muhammad], your duty is only clear notification.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the Prophet Muhammad's primary role as a messenger.  His responsibility was to deliver the divine message clearly and unequivocally.  If people chose to reject it, he was not held accountable for their disbelief. The focus is on the clarity of the message (al-balāgh al-mubīn) and the discharge of the prophetic duty.  It signifies that guidance ultimately rests with God, and the Prophet's task was limited to conveying the truth.  This verse offers comfort and reassurance to those engaging in da'wah (inviting to Islam), emphasizing the importance of conveying the message effectively and leaving the outcome to God.
orig: فإن تولوا فإنما عليك البلاغ المبين

translation: They recognize the favor of God, then they deny it, and most of them are disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the human tendency of ingratitude and denial, particularly concerning God's blessings.  It highlights a paradoxical behavior: people acknowledge God's favors in their lives, benefiting from His provisions and experiencing His mercy, yet they subsequently deny His existence or His role in bestowing those blessings. This denial can manifest in various forms, from outright rejection of faith to a more subtle disregard for God's commands and a lack of thankfulness. The verse concludes by emphasizing the prevalence of this behavior, stating that 'most' fall into this category of disbelievers or ungrateful individuals.  This 'disbelief' doesn't necessarily imply a formal rejection of religious dogma, but can also encompass a practical denial reflected in one's actions and attitudes, a failure to live in accordance with the recognized truth of God's beneficence. It underscores the moral and spiritual consequences of such ingratitude and serves as a warning against its pervasiveness.
orig: يعرفون نعمت الله ثم ينكرونها وأكثرهم الكافرون

translation: And [beware] the Day when We will raise up from every nation a witness, then permission [to repent] will not be granted to those who disbelieved, nor will they be asked to appease [ Allah ].
interpretation:
This verse speaks of the Day of Judgment.  A "witness" (shahid) from each nation will be raised. This witness could be interpreted in a few ways: 

1. **A prophet sent to that nation:**  Each nation has received guidance through a prophet, and they will testify to the message they delivered and the responses they received.  This emphasizes the fairness of God, as no nation can claim ignorance of divine guidance.

2. **A person from among them:**  This could also signify a representative individual from each nation who embodies their collective actions and beliefs. They would testify to the prevalent practices and attitudes of their people.

3. **Their own actions and deeds:**  Alternatively,  "witness" could refer to the individuals' own deeds, which will bear witness against or for them.  Everything they did in their earthly life will be brought forth as evidence.

The latter part of the verse highlights the finality of judgment for those who disbelieved. They will not be given an opportunity to repent (la yu'dhanu) or seek forgiveness/make amends (la hum yusta'tabun).  This signifies that the time for repentance is in this world, not after the Day of Judgment. It emphasizes the importance of choosing faith and acting righteously within one's lifetime.
orig: ويوم نبعث من كل أمة شهيدا ثم لا يؤذن للذين كفروا ولا هم يستعتبون

translation: And when those who wronged see the punishment, it will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved.
interpretation: This verse describes the absolute and irreversible nature of the punishment awaiting those who committed injustice (ẓalamū) in their earthly lives.  The word "al-'adhab" (the punishment) refers to the consequences of their actions in the afterlife.  The verse emphasizes the severity and finality of this punishment.  It states that there will be no mitigation ("la yukhaffaf") of the punishment, meaning no reduction in its intensity or duration.  Furthermore, they will not be granted any respite or postponement ("wa la hum yunẓarūn").  This highlights the certainty and inescapability of the consequences for their wrongful deeds.  The verse serves as a stern warning against injustice and a reminder of the ultimate accountability that awaits in the hereafter.
orig: وإذا رأى الذين ظلموا العذاب فلا يخفف عنهم ولا هم ينظرون

translation: And when those who associated others with Allah see their "partners", they will say, "Our Lord, these are our partners [to You] whom we used to invoke besides You." But they [i.e., the false deities] will fling back to them the statement, "Indeed, you are liars."
interpretation: This verse depicts a dramatic scene on the Day of Judgement.  Those who committed *shirk* (polytheism or associating partners with God) during their earthly lives will confront the idols and deities they worshipped. In a desperate attempt to shift blame and avoid accountability, they will point to these false gods as the ones they invoked.  However, these idols, powerless and exposed as mere creations, will disown those who worshipped them, declaring them liars. This highlights the futility of worshipping anything other than the One True God.  The verse underscores the absolute sovereignty and uniqueness of God and the deception inherent in polytheistic beliefs. It serves as a stark warning against the emptiness of worshipping false idols, emphasizing that on the Day of Judgement, only God will hold ultimate authority, and no one can escape accountability for their actions.
orig: وإذا رأى الذين أشركوا شركاءهم قالوا ربنا هؤلاء شركاؤنا الذين كنا ندعو من دونك فألقوا إليهم القول إنكم لكاذبون

translation: And on that Day, they will offer submission to Allah, and lost from them will be what they used to invent.
interpretation: This verse depicts the Day of Judgment.  It describes the ultimate realization and surrender of those who denied the truth during their earthly lives.  "They will offer submission to Allah" signifies their forced acknowledgement of God's sovereignty and their helplessness before Him.  It is not a willing submission born of faith, but rather a compelled submission in the face of undeniable truth.  The phrase "lost from them will be what they used to invent" refers to the falsehoods, fabrications, and deceptions they constructed regarding Allah, His Messenger, and His message. Their lies, excuses, and justifications will be exposed as worthless and powerless on that Day.  All their attempts to mislead themselves and others will vanish, leaving them with nothing but the stark reality of their disobedience.  This verse serves as a potent reminder of the accountability that awaits everyone on the Day of Judgment, and the futility of falsehood in the face of ultimate truth.
orig: وألقوا إلى الله يومئذ السلم وضل عنهم ما كانوا يفترون

translation: Those who disbelieve and avert [people] from the path of Allah - We will increase them in punishment over [their] punishment for what corruption they were causing.
interpretation: This verse speaks about the consequences faced by those who actively reject faith (kufr) and obstruct others from following the path of God (sabil Allah).  It emphasizes a compounding punishment. The initial punishment is for their disbelief, while the additional punishment is specifically due to their efforts in spreading corruption (fasad). This corruption can take various forms, such as leading people astray, promoting injustice, or sowing discord. The verse highlights the severity of hindering others' spiritual journeys and causing harm within society. It underscores the principle of accountability for one's actions, particularly actions that negatively impact others and obstruct the divine message. It's important to note that the nature and extent of the 'punishment' mentioned in the Quran are understood in different ways by various theological interpretations, some focusing on worldly consequences and others on consequences in the afterlife.
orig: الذين كفروا وصدوا عن سبيل الله زدناهم عذابا فوق العذاب بما كانوا يفسدون

translation: And [mention] the Day when We will raise up in every nation a witness against them from among themselves. And We will bring you [O Muhammad] as a witness against these [people]. And We revealed to you the Book, explaining all things, and as guidance and mercy and good tidings to the Muslims.
interpretation: This verse speaks about the Day of Judgment and the establishment of divine justice.  God will raise a witness from within each community to testify about their actions and beliefs. This internal witness could be a prophet sent to that nation, a righteous person among them, or even their own conscience.  Specifically, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is identified as the witness against his own community, the people of Mecca and, by extension, all of humanity. The Qur'an, revealed to him, serves as the ultimate proof and testimony.  It is described as a comprehensive guide, explaining everything necessary for humanity's guidance, offering mercy to those who follow it, and bringing good news of salvation and paradise to those who embrace Islam.  The verse underscores the importance of accountability, the universality of God's message, and the role of the Qur'an as a complete and final revelation.
orig: ويوم نبعث في كل أمة شهيدا عليهم من أنفسهم وجئنا بك شهيدا على هؤلاء ونزلنا عليك الكتاب تبيانا لكل شيء وهدى ورحمة وبشرى للمسلمين

translation: Indeed, Allah commands justice, and good conduct, and giving to relatives, and He forbids immorality, and bad conduct, and oppression. He admonishes you that perhaps you will be reminded.
interpretation: This verse encapsulates core Islamic ethical principles.  Allah commands actions that promote societal harmony and individual well-being, beginning with 'justice' (al-'adl) which refers to fairness and equity in all dealings.  This is followed by 'good conduct' (al-ihsan),  a broader term encompassing kindness, compassion, generosity and excellence in character. Then, the verse emphasizes the importance of 'giving to relatives' (ita'i dhi al-qurba), highlighting familial responsibility and social solidarity.  The verse then shifts to prohibitions.  Allah forbids 'immorality' (al-fahsha'), which refers to lewd or indecent acts and behaviors.  He also forbids 'bad conduct' (al-munkar),  which encompasses all actions that are reprehensible and contrary to established moral norms, often including those that harm others.  Finally, He forbids 'oppression' (al-baghi), referring to transgression and violation of others' rights, including through violence, exploitation, or injustice.  The concluding phrase, 'He admonishes you that perhaps you will be reminded,' underscores the didactic purpose of this verse.  It serves as a gentle reminder to reflect on these principles and strive to live by them.  The verse implies that adhering to these commands and prohibitions leads to individual and collective well-being, both in this life and the hereafter.
orig: إن الله يأمر بالعدل والإحسان وإيتاء ذي القربى وينهى عن الفحشاء والمنكر والبغي يعظكم لعلكم تذكرون

translation: And fulfill the covenant of Allah when you have taken it, [and] do not break oaths after their confirmation while you have made Allah , over you, a witness. Indeed, Allah knows what you do.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the sanctity of commitments and agreements, particularly those made in the name of God.  It highlights the importance of upholding promises and oaths once they have been made.  The phrase "and you have made Allah, over you, a witness" underscores the weight of such commitments, as God is invoked as the ultimate guarantor and observer.  It serves as a reminder that God is aware of all our actions, including whether we honor our pledges or break them, implying accountability for our choices in this regard.  Therefore, the verse calls for integrity and trustworthiness in all dealings, emphasizing that fulfilling promises is a fundamental aspect of a righteous life according to Islamic principles.
orig: وأوفوا بعهد الله إذا عاهدتم ولا تنقضوا الأيمان بعد توكيدها وقد جعلتم الله عليكم كفيلا إن الله يعلم ما تفعلون

translation: And do not be like she who untwisted her yarn, after it was strong, into scattered threads, making your oaths a means of deception among yourselves, lest a nation be more numerous than another nation. Allah only tries you thereby, and He will surely make clear to you on the Day of Resurrection that about which you used to differ.
interpretation: This verse discourages the breaking of oaths and using them deceptively for personal or tribal gain.  It uses the analogy of a woman who painstakingly spins strong yarn only to unravel it, representing the wasted effort and damage caused by breaking agreements.  The verse warns against exploiting oaths to create an advantage for one group over another.  It clarifies that these tests of integrity are from God, who will ultimately judge and reveal the truth concerning the disputes on the Day of Resurrection.  The emphasis is on upholding promises and maintaining trust, essential for a just and harmonious society. The specific reference to a nation being more numerous than another may allude to using oaths to manipulate political alliances or gain numerical advantage in conflicts, thereby highlighting the potential for social disruption caused by such deceitful practices.
orig: ولا تكونوا كالتي نقضت غزلها من بعد قوة أنكاثا تتخذون أيمانكم دخلا بينكم أن تكون أمة هي أربى من أمة إنما يبلوكم الله به وليبينن لكم يوم القيامة ما كنتم فيه تختلفون

translation: And if Allah had willed, He would have made you one nation, but He leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, and you will surely be questioned about what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's absolute will and the concept of free will within a divinely ordained framework.  While God has the power to make everyone follow one path, He has chosen to allow humans the freedom to choose their beliefs and actions. This freedom, however, is not absolute; God guides those He wills, and leaves astray those He wills.  This 'leaving astray' (idlal) can be understood in several ways, including withholding guidance, allowing one to be misled by their own desires, or as a consequence of earlier choices.  The verse concludes with a reminder of accountability – that all actions will be judged on the Day of Judgement. Therefore, while humans have free will, they are responsible for the choices they make within the scope of that free will. The verse implicitly encourages reflection and striving towards righteousness, knowing that guidance comes from God, and ultimately, we are accountable for our actions.
orig: ولو شاء الله لجعلكم أمة واحدة ولكن يضل من يشاء ويهدي من يشاء ولتسألن عما كنتم تعملون

translation: And do not make [your] oaths a means of deception among yourselves, lest a foot slip after it was [firmly] planted, and you taste evil [i.e., adversity] because you prevented [others] from the way of Allah, and for you is a great punishment.
interpretation: This verse warns against using oaths deceptively or frivolously.  It emphasizes the importance of upholding promises and commitments made in God's name.  Breaking oaths, especially those made to facilitate deceit or manipulate others, is condemned.  Such actions can lead to instability and misfortune ("a foot slip after it was firmly planted") for those involved.  Furthermore, the verse highlights the gravity of hindering others from following God's path, suggesting that this act carries significant consequences, including a "great punishment."  Preventing others from accessing the way of Allah can manifest in various forms, including actively obstructing their religious practice or spreading misinformation that leads them astray. The verse serves as a reminder of the importance of honesty, integrity, and upholding one's commitments, particularly in religious matters.
orig: ولا تتخذوا أيمانكم دخلا بينكم فتزل قدم بعد ثبوتها وتذوقوا السوء بما صددتم عن سبيل الله ولكم عذاب عظيم

translation: And do not exchange the covenant of Allah for a paltry price. Indeed, what is with Allah is better for you, if you only knew.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the immense value of upholding one's covenant or agreement with God.  It warns against prioritizing immediate, worldly gains (described as a "paltry price") over the ultimate, lasting rewards that come from faithfulness to God.  The "covenant of Allah" can refer to a variety of commitments, including adherence to His commands, fulfilling religious obligations, and maintaining moral integrity.  The verse suggests that worldly gains, however attractive they may seem, are insignificant compared to the spiritual and eternal blessings that await those who remain true to their covenant with God.  The phrase "if you only knew" highlights the importance of knowledge and understanding in recognizing the true value of divine rewards and choosing the path of righteousness over short-term worldly benefits.  It implies that if people truly grasped the magnitude of God's blessings, they would never compromise their faith or principles for fleeting material gains.
orig: ولا تشتروا بعهد الله ثمنا قليلا إنما عند الله هو خير لكم إن كنتم تعلمون

translation: What is with you will vanish, but what is with Allah will endure. And We will certainly reward those who are patient with the best of what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the transient nature of worldly possessions and the permanence of what lies with God.  "What is with you" refers to material wealth, health, relationships, and any worldly blessings we enjoy. These are temporary and will inevitably fade away.  In contrast, "what is with Allah" refers to spiritual rewards, divine grace, and the eternal life in the hereafter. These are everlasting.  The verse also highlights the importance of patience (sabr). Those who endure hardships and remain steadfast in their faith, trusting in God's plan, will be rewarded abundantly.  Their reward will not be merely equivalent to their deeds, but "the best of what they used to do," suggesting a magnification of reward and God's immense generosity. This serves as a powerful reminder to prioritize the eternal over the temporary and to persevere in righteousness, knowing that true and lasting reward lies with God.
orig: ما عندكم ينفد وما عند الله باق ولنجزين الذين صبروا أجرهم بأحسن ما كانوا يعملون

translation: Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer - We will surely cause them to live a good life, and We will surely give them their reward [in the Hereafter] according to the best of what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the fundamental principle of equality and justice in Islam.  It clearly states that reward and a good life are based on righteous actions (amal salih) and faith (iman), irrespective of gender.  "ذكر أو أنثى" (male or female) explicitly highlights this gender neutrality.  The promise of "a good life" (hayatan tayyibah) can refer to both blessings in this world and the ultimate reward in the Hereafter. This good life is linked to both faith and righteous deeds, implying that true well-being comes from living a life of purpose and moral integrity. The phrase "according to the best of what they used to do" (bi ahsan ma kanu ya'malun) suggests that God judges individuals based on their sincere efforts and intentions, even if they fall short of perfection.  It highlights the mercy and grace of God, who rewards people based on their best actions.  In essence, this verse is a powerful affirmation of God's justice, the importance of faith and good deeds, and the equal standing of men and women in the eyes of God.
orig: من عمل صالحا من ذكر أو أنثى وهو مؤمن فلنحيينه حياة طيبة ولنجزينهم أجرهم بأحسن ما كانوا يعملون

translation: So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from Satan, the outcast.
interpretation: This verse instructs Muslims to seek protection from Allah against the whispers and temptations of Satan before engaging with the Qur'an.  "Satan, the outcast (al-Shaytan al-Rajim)" refers to Satan's expulsion from divine grace.  Seeking refuge in Allah (isti'adha) is achieved by saying "A'udhu Billahi min ash-Shaytan ir-Rajim" which means "I seek refuge in Allah from Satan, the outcast." This act acknowledges Allah's power and protection, establishing a spiritual barrier against satanic influence which might hinder understanding, corrupt the meaning, or distract from the message of the Qur'an.  It emphasizes the importance of approaching the sacred text with humility and sincerity, seeking divine guidance and protection from any internal or external forces that could distort its true meaning or prevent its beneficial impact.
orig: فإذا قرأت القرآن فاستعذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم

translation: He has no authority over those who believe and put their trust in their Lord.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the limitations of Satan's power.  He holds no sway over those who possess genuine faith and rely firmly on God. Their belief acts as a shield, and their trust in God's protection renders them immune to Satan's influence.  It highlights the importance of faith and reliance on God as the ultimate source of strength and protection against evil.
orig: إنه ليس له سلطان على الذين آمنوا وعلى ربهم يتوكلون

translation: His authority is only over those who take him as a protector and those who associate others with him [in worship].
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the limited scope of Satan's influence.  He has no power over those who reject him and sincerely worship God alone. His dominion extends only to those who willingly choose to follow him – those who "take him as a protector" by obeying his temptations and whispers – and those who are "mushrikun" or those who commit shirk, associating partners with God. This association can manifest in various ways, including idol worship or prioritizing worldly desires and attachments over God.  By choosing disobedience and shirk, these individuals effectively submit themselves to Satan's sway, giving him power over their actions and decisions.  The verse thus underscores the importance of tawhid (the oneness of God) and highlights the freedom and protection that comes from sincere devotion to God alone.
orig: إنما سلطانه على الذين يتولونه والذين هم به مشركون

translation: And when We substitute a verse in place of a verse - and Allah is most knowing of what He sends down - they say, "You are but a fabricator." But most of them do not know.
interpretation: This verse addresses the issue of abrogation (naskh) in the Qur'an, where certain verses were superseded by later revelations.  It highlights the divine authority of God to change or replace verses as He sees fit.  The reaction of some disbelievers to this process is also depicted. They accuse the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) of inventing the Qur'an, calling him a "fabricator" (muftari).  Their accusation stems from a lack of understanding of God's wisdom and the progressive nature of revelation.  They fail to grasp that a divine message can be tailored to address changing circumstances and the evolving understanding of the audience.  The phrase "most of them do not know" emphasizes the widespread ignorance concerning the divine process of revelation and God's ultimate knowledge of what is best for humanity.
orig: وإذا بدلنا آية مكان آية والله أعلم بما ينزل قالوا إنما أنت مفتر بل أكثرهم لا يعلمون

translation: Say, "It has been sent down by the Holy Spirit from your Lord in truth, to strengthen those who believe and as a guidance and good tidings to the Muslims."
interpretation:
This verse refers to the revelation of the Qur'an.  "The Holy Spirit" (Rūḥ al-Qudus) is generally understood by Muslims to refer to the Angel Gabriel, who is believed to have transmitted the Qur'an to Prophet Muhammad. The phrase "from your Lord" emphasizes the divine origin of the revelation, establishing its authority and truthfulness. The purpose of this revelation is threefold: 

1. **Strengthening the believers (li-yuthabbit al-ladhīna āmanū):**  The Qur'an provides spiritual and moral support to those who have already embraced faith, reinforcing their conviction and helping them persevere in the face of challenges.

2. **Guidance (hudan):** The Qur'an serves as a comprehensive guide for life, offering principles and teachings that address all aspects of human existence, from individual conduct to social interactions and governance.

3. **Good tidings/Glad tidings (wa bushran lil-muslimīn):** The Qur'an brings the good news of God's mercy, forgiveness, and the ultimate reward of Paradise for those who submit to His will.  It also offers hope and reassurance in times of difficulty.
