The verse marks the beginning of the narrative of Mary's unique experience and sets the scene for the divine intervention that would lead to the birth of Jesus. It emphasizes Mary's piety and her chosen seclusion as a prelude to the extraordinary events that were to follow.
orig: واذكر في الكتاب مريم إذ انتبذت من أهلها مكانا شرقيا

translation: So she took a barrier/screen from them, and We sent to her Our angel (Rooh/Spirit), and he appeared before her in the form of a well-proportioned man.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Maryam (19:17), describes the Annunciation to Mary, the mother of Jesus.  "She took a barrier/screen from them" refers to Mary secluding herself for prayer and devotion. The exact nature of the "barrier" is debated, but it generally signifies her seeking privacy.  The Arabic word "Rooh" (translated here as angel/Spirit) can also mean "spirit" or "breath."  In this context, Islamic tradition interprets it as the Angel Gabriel. The verse emphasizes the miraculous nature of the conception of Jesus, as Gabriel appeared to Mary in a human form and announced the birth of a son, despite her being a virgin. The phrase "well-proportioned man" highlights the normalcy of Gabriel's appearance, lessening the potential fear Mary might experience.  This verse affirms the divine origin of Jesus and highlights Mary's piety and chosen status.
orig: فاتخذت من دونهم حجابا فأرسلنا إليها روحنا فتمثل لها بشرا سويا

translation: She said, "Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful (Ar-Rahman) from you, if you should be righteous/God-fearing."
interpretation: This verse depicts a woman seeking protection from a man's advances. The woman's invocation of God, specifically using the name "Ar-Rahman" (The Most Merciful), adds a layer of significance.  It suggests that true righteousness, or taqwa (تقوى) as expressed in the Arabic, would prevent the man from harassing her.  Her statement implies that if the man truly fears God (is truly righteous), he would respect her boundaries and not pursue her in this unwanted manner. She uses the man's claimed piety against him, highlighting the hypocrisy of his actions if his intentions are impure.  The verse subtly emphasizes the importance of genuine piety being reflected in one's behavior and respect for others, particularly in situations of vulnerability.
orig: قالت إني أعوذ بالرحمن منك إن كنت تقيا

translation: He said, "I am only a messenger of your Lord to give you [news of] a pure boy."
interpretation:
This verse recounts the angel Gabriel's announcement to the Prophet Zechariah that he would have a son, John (Yahya).  Several key elements are highlighted:

* **"He said"**: This refers to the angel Gabriel.
* **"I am only a messenger of your Lord"**: This emphasizes Gabriel's role as a divine intermediary, carrying out God's will. He is not acting independently.  It also underscores the miraculous nature of the birth, coming as it does from a divine command.
* **"to give you [news of]"**:  The angel's primary purpose is to deliver this glad tiding. This act of giving emphasizes the gift-like nature of the child.
* **"a pure boy"**: The term "pure" (zakiyya) can be interpreted in several ways. It can refer to physical purity, ritual purity, or moral purity. In John's case, it likely encompasses all three.  He was to be a dedicated servant of God, free from sin, and destined for a life of righteousness. This purity also foreshadows John's role as a forerunner to Jesus, preparing the way for his ministry.

This verse thus conveys the miraculous nature of John's birth, emphasizes his divinely ordained purity, and hints at his future importance as a prophet.
orig: قال إنما أنا رسول ربك لأهب لك غلاما زكيا

translation: She said, "How can I have a boy while no man has touched me and I have not been unchaste?"
interpretation: This verse recounts Mary's (Maryam's) reaction to the angel Gabriel's announcement that she will conceive a child, Jesus (Isa).  Her question expresses astonishment and disbelief.  She affirms her virginity and emphasizes her chastity, highlighting the miraculous nature of the conception.  The verse sets the stage for the explanation of the divine intervention that will lead to the birth of Jesus, emphasizing that it is by God's will and power, not through any human agency or transgression on Mary's part.  It underscores the purity and righteousness of Mary, chosen by God for this extraordinary event.
orig: قالت أنى يكون لي غلام ولم يمسسني بشر ولم أك بغيا

translation: Thus said your Lord: "It is easy for Me. And We will make him a sign to the people and a mercy from Us. And it was a matter [already] decreed."
interpretation: This verse typically refers to the miraculous birth of Jesus (Isa) to Mary (Maryam), although some interpretations apply it more broadly to God's power to create and bring about anything He wills.  'Thus said your Lord' emphasizes the divine authority behind the statement. 'It is easy for Me' highlights God's absolute power and ability to perform what might seem impossible to humans, such as virgin birth.  'And We will make him a sign to the people' refers to Jesus being a sign or proof of God's power and a messenger to humanity. 'And a mercy from Us' signifies that Jesus's birth and prophethood were a blessing and mercy for mankind.  Finally, 'And it was a matter [already] decreed' affirms that this event was part of God's preordained plan, emphasizing its inevitability and purpose within the larger divine scheme.
orig: قال كذلك قال ربك هو علي هين ولنجعله آية للناس ورحمة منا وكان أمرا مقضيا

translation: So she conceived him, and she withdrew with him to a remote place.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Maryam (19:22), describes Mary's experience after conceiving Jesus miraculously.  "So she conceived him" refers to the divine conception of Jesus without a father.  "She withdrew with him to a remote place" suggests Mary's seeking seclusion and privacy due to the extraordinary nature of her pregnancy.  This withdrawal could be understood as both a physical retreat to a distant location and a metaphorical withdrawal into herself to cope with the social implications and personal weight of her situation.  The remoteness emphasizes her vulnerability and the unusual circumstances surrounding Jesus's birth, as well as her desire to protect herself and her unborn child from potential scrutiny and judgment.
orig: فحملته فانتبذت به مكانا قصيا

translation: Then the pangs of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree. She said, "Oh, I wish I had died before this and was in oblivion, forgotten."
interpretation: This verse describes the intense pain and despair experienced by Mary (Maryam) during the birth of Jesus (Isa).  She is alone and overwhelmed by the physical and emotional challenges of childbirth. The phrase "trunk of a palm tree" highlights her isolation and vulnerability.  Her words "Oh, I wish I had died before this and was in oblivion, forgotten" express a deep sense of anguish and a desire to escape the present suffering.  It is a profoundly human moment, depicting the raw emotion of a woman facing an immense challenge. It emphasizes the extraordinary circumstances surrounding Jesus' birth and underscores Mary's humanness despite her divinely appointed role.  This verse is often interpreted as showing the very real struggles even divinely chosen individuals face, making Mary relatable and her perseverance inspiring.
orig: فأجاءها المخاض إلى جذع النخلة قالت يا ليتني مت قبل هذا وكنت نسيا منسيا

translation: Then he called to her from below her, "Do not grieve; your Lord has provided for you a stream beneath you."
interpretation:
This verse recounts a moment in the story of Mary (Maryam), mother of Jesus, during her labor.  Overwhelmed by the pains of childbirth and the social implications of giving birth out of wedlock, she is distressed.  God then reassures her through a divine call originating from below her, likely from the direction of a small stream or spring.  The reassurance is twofold:

1. **"Do not grieve" (ألا تحزني):** This is a direct command of comfort and solace, aiming to alleviate Mary's anxiety and fear. It signifies divine support and protection in her vulnerable state.

2. **"Your Lord has provided for you a stream beneath you" (قد جعل ربك تحتك سريا):**  This highlights God's provision and care for Mary in a very practical way.  The miraculously appearing stream serves multiple purposes:
    * **Physical sustenance:** It provides water for drinking, essential during and after labor.
    * **Hygiene:**  It offers a means of cleansing herself and the newborn child.
    * **Symbolic reassurance:** The stream represents God's constant provision and care, reminding Mary that she is not alone and that her needs will be met.  It symbolizes the ease and support God grants her in this difficult situation. 

This verse emphasizes God's mercy and responsiveness to those in distress.  It underscores the importance of trust in God's plan, even in seemingly impossible circumstances.  It also highlights the miraculous aspects surrounding the birth of Jesus, further emphasizing his unique status.
orig: فناداها من تحتها ألا تحزني قد جعل ربك تحتك سريا

translation: And shake towards you the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you fresh ripe dates.
interpretation: This verse describes a miraculous event experienced by Mary, mother of Jesus, during her childbirth.  Alone and in labor, she is instructed to shake the trunk of a date palm.  This seemingly simple act yields a remarkable result: fresh, ripe dates fall to her, providing her with much-needed sustenance and comfort.  The verse is often interpreted symbolically as well. The date palm, a symbol of resilience and provision in arid environments, represents God's mercy and support in times of need.  The dropping of the ripe dates signifies divine provision being readily available, even in unexpected ways.  The act of shaking the tree can be seen as an act of faith and reliance on God, prompting divine assistance.  Furthermore, the fresh, ripe dates can be understood as a symbol of the blessings and ease bestowed upon Mary during a challenging time.  Overall, this verse highlights God's care for Mary, demonstrating His ability to provide sustenance and comfort miraculously, even in the most difficult circumstances.  It serves as a reminder of God's constant support and the importance of placing trust in Him during times of trial.
orig: وهزي إليك بجذع النخلة تساقط عليك رطبا جنيا

translation: So eat and drink and be comforted. And if you see from among humanity anyone, say, 'Indeed, I have vowed a fast to the Most Gracious (Allah) so I will not speak to [any] human being today.'
interpretation: This verse pertains to the story of Maryam (Mary), mother of Isa (Jesus), when she was divinely instructed to seclude herself and abstain from speaking.  After giving birth to Isa, she was instructed to eat, drink, and find comfort.  If she were to encounter anyone, she was to indicate that she had taken a vow of silence, a fast of speech, dedicated to God (Ar-Rahman, the Most Gracious).  This fast was not a traditional fast from food and drink but a fast of communication, likely meant to protect her and her newborn son from questioning and potential harm given the miraculous nature of his birth.  It emphasizes Maryam's obedience to God's command and her reliance on Him for protection and provision.  The verse highlights the importance of devotion, trust, and reliance on God in challenging circumstances, using silence as a form of worship and a protective measure.
orig: فكلي واشربي وقري عينا فإما ترين من البشر أحدا فقولي إني نذرت للرحمن صوما فلن أكلم اليوم إنسيا

translation: So she brought him to her people, carrying him. They said, "O Mary, you have certainly done a strange thing."
interpretation: This verse describes the moment when Mary returns to her community with the newborn Jesus.  The Arabic word "فريا" (fariyya) translates to something monstrous, extraordinary, or unprecedented.  It highlights the shock and disapproval of Mary's community upon seeing her with a child out of wedlock. Their reaction stems from their cultural norms and understanding, where such a birth was considered scandalous.  The verse sets the stage for the miraculous events that follow, where Mary, through divine intervention, will demonstrate the exceptional nature of Jesus's birth.
orig: فأتت به قومها تحمله قالوا يا مريم لقد جئت شيئا فريا

translation: O sister of Aaron, your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother a woman unchaste.
interpretation: This verse is addressed to Mary, mother of Jesus, and refers to her lineage and upbringing.  The reference to "sister of Aaron" is not a literal familial connection, as they lived centuries apart.  Rather, Islamic scholars interpret this as referring to her piety and righteous lineage within the Israelite prophetic tradition, similar to Aaron, the brother of Moses.  The verse emphasizes Mary's virtuous parentage and upbringing, refuting accusations against her chastity and emphasizing the miraculous nature of Jesus's birth.  It underscores her purity and innocence, highlighting her as a chosen woman for a divine purpose.
orig: يا أخت هارون ما كان أبوك امرأ سوء وما كانت أمك بغيا

translation: So she pointed to him. They said, "How can we speak to one who is in the cradle a child?"
interpretation: This verse describes the reaction of the people when Mary, mother of Jesus, pointed to the infant Jesus to answer their questions about the miraculously provided food.  They were astonished and questioned how they could possibly converse with a baby still in the cradle.  The implication is that they expected a divine explanation or sign to come from a more conventional, adult source. This highlights the extraordinary nature of the event, where the infant Jesus, by the will of God, spoke miraculously from the cradle to defend his mother and proclaim his prophethood.
orig: فأشارت إليه قالوا كيف نكلم من كان في المهد صبيا

translation: He said, "Indeed, I am a servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet."
interpretation:
This verse represents a declaration of humble servitude and divine appointment.  It's often attributed to prophets, highlighting several key aspects:

* **"Servant of Allah (عبد الله)":** This emphasizes the prophet's fundamental relationship with God.  It signifies complete submission and obedience to God's will, establishing that the prophet's authority derives solely from God.  It also counters any potential misconception of the prophet's divinity or inherent power.

* **"He has given me the Scripture (آتاني الكتاب)":** This indicates divine revelation as the source of the prophet's message and authority.  The "Scripture" refers to the specific revelation granted to that prophet, whether it be scrolls, tablets, or inspiration.  It underscores that the message is not of the prophet's own creation but comes directly from God.

* **"Made me a prophet (جعلني نبيا)":** This confirms the prophet's divinely ordained role as a messenger and intermediary between God and humanity.  It signifies their selection and empowerment by God to convey His message, guidance, and warnings to the people.  It highlights the prophet's responsibility and the significance of their mission.

Overall, this verse concisely expresses the core elements of prophethood in Islam: humble servitude to God, reception of divine revelation, and appointment as a messenger to humanity.  It emphasizes the source and nature of prophetic authority, grounding it firmly in God's will and revelation.
orig: قال إني عبد الله آتاني الكتاب وجعلني نبيا

translation: And He has made me blessed wherever I am and has enjoined upon me prayer and zakah as long as I live
interpretation: This verse, often attributed to the words of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham), reflects several key Islamic themes.  "Blessed wherever I am" can be interpreted in multiple ways. It suggests that Ibrahim was granted spiritual and potentially material prosperity, regardless of his location. It also highlights the universal nature of God's blessings, available to those who follow His guidance. The phrase could also refer to Ibrahim's role as a source of blessing for others, spreading monotheism and righteous conduct wherever he went.  The injunction to perform prayer (salat) and charity (zakah) "as long as I live" emphasizes the lifelong commitment expected of believers to these fundamental pillars of Islam.  Prayer represents a direct connection with God, while zakah signifies social responsibility and care for the less fortunate.  This verse thus portrays Ibrahim as a model of devotion and obedience, consistently fulfilling his religious duties throughout his life, and highlights the importance of prayer and charity in the Islamic faith.
orig: وجعلني مباركا أين ما كنت وأوصاني بالصلاة والزكاة ما دمت حيا

translation: And dutiful to my mother, and He has not made me a wretched tyrant.
interpretation: This verse, often attributed to the words of Jesus in the Quran (Surah Maryam 19:32), speaks to his piety and humility.  "Dutiful to my mother" (بِرًّا بِوَالِدَتِي - birran bi-walidati) highlights Jesus's respect and obedience towards Mary, emphasizing the importance of honoring one's parents in Islam. This resonates with a broader Quranic theme of filial piety.  The phrase "He has not made me a wretched tyrant" (وَلَمْ يَجْعَلْنِي جَبَّارًا شَقِيًّا - wa lam yaj'alni jabbaran shaqiyya) is a declaration of Jesus's gentle nature and submission to God's will.  "Jabbaran" (جَبَّارًا) refers to someone who is arrogant, oppressive, and forces their will upon others. "Shaqiyya" (شَقِيًّا) describes someone who is wretched, miserable, and ultimately distanced from God's mercy.  Jesus, through these words, denies any claim to tyrannical power or inherent wickedness, reinforcing his role as a humble prophet and servant of God.
orig: وبرا بوالدتي ولم يجعلني جبارا شقيا

translation: And peace be upon me the day I was born, and the day I die, and the day I am resurrected alive.
interpretation: This verse, often attributed to Jesus in Islamic tradition (though not found verbatim in the Bible), expresses a profound yearning for divine peace throughout the entirety of existence. It encapsulates the key stages of life according to Islamic belief: birth, death, and resurrection.  'Peace' here signifies not merely the absence of conflict, but rather the encompassing grace and blessing of God.  Jesus's plea for peace at these pivotal moments underscores the significance of divine protection and mercy during life's transitions.  Birth represents entry into the world and its trials, death marks the passage from this life to the next, and resurrection signifies the ultimate judgment and the beginning of eternal life.  By invoking peace on each of these occasions, the verse emphasizes a complete reliance on God and a desire for His constant presence and favor throughout the journey of existence.
orig: والسلام علي يوم ولدت ويوم أموت ويوم أبعث حيا

translation: That is Jesus, son of Mary -  the word of truth about which they are in doubt.
interpretation: This verse asserts the truth of Jesus's identity as the son of Mary and emphasizes the divine origin of his birth. The phrase "word of truth" (قول الحق) can be interpreted in several ways.  It could refer to Jesus himself being a manifestation of God's truth, or it could refer to the truth of his message and prophethood.  The final clause, "about which they are in doubt," highlights the disbelief and skepticism surrounding Jesus's miraculous birth and his status as a prophet, particularly among those who rejected his message. This verse serves as a confirmation of Jesus's divine origin and a rebuke to those who questioned it.
orig: ذلك عيسى ابن مريم قول الحق الذي فيه يمترون

translation: It is not befitting for Allah to take a son. Exalted is He! When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.
interpretation: This verse emphatically denies the Christian concept of Jesus as the son of God, a notion that clashes with the Islamic understanding of God's absolute oneness and transcendence.  The Arabic word "سبحانه" (subhanahu), translated as "Exalted is He" or "Glory be to Him," reinforces this idea of God being far above any human limitations or familial relationships.  The verse then highlights God's absolute power and creative authority.  His will is immediately effective; simply by commanding "Be," anything comes into existence. This demonstrates that God is the ultimate source of all creation and doesn't require any intermediary or partner in this process.  It underscores the effortless ease with which God brings about His will, further emphasizing His omnipotence.
orig: ما كان لله أن يتخذ من ولد سبحانه إذا قضى أمرا فإنما يقول له كن فيكون

translation: And indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the shared Lordship of Allah over all of creation, including the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and all other people. It asserts the fundamental Islamic principle of Tawhid (Oneness of God).  The verse commands the worship of Allah alone, highlighting that this exclusive devotion is the 'Sirat al-Mustaqim' (straight path). This 'straight path' signifies the path of righteousness, truth, and guidance that leads to salvation and eternal peace.  By acknowledging Allah as the one and only Lord and by worshipping Him sincerely, individuals align themselves with this divinely ordained path, avoiding deviation and misguidance.
orig: وإن الله ربي وربكم فاعبدوه هذا صراط مستقيم

translation: So the factions differed among themselves. So woe to those who disbelieved from the witnessing of a tremendous Day.
interpretation: This verse speaks of the disunity and discord among those who rejected the message of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).  The Arabic word 'ahzab' (أحزاب) refers to groups or parties, and their internal disagreements are highlighted. This disunity is contrasted with the unity of the believers. The verse then pronounces a severe warning ('woe,' indicated by the word 'wayl' - ويل) specifically to the disbelievers concerning the witnessing ('mashhad' - مشهد) of a momentous and awe-inspiring Day ('yawm azeem' - يوم عظيم), which is generally understood to be the Day of Judgment. This 'witnessing' implies not only seeing the events of that Day unfold but also experiencing the consequences of their disbelief. The verse emphasizes the gravity of rejecting the truth and foreshadows the dire consequences that await those who persist in their disbelief on the Day of Judgment.
orig: فاختلف الأحزاب من بينهم فويل للذين كفروا من مشهد يوم عظيم

translation: I hear and see them when they come to Us, but the wrongdoers today are in manifest error.
interpretation: This verse speaks of God's complete knowledge and awareness of those who approach Him, specifically mentioning both hearing and seeing. This emphasizes that nothing is hidden from God, including the intentions and actions of people. The verse then contrasts this divine awareness with the state of the wrongdoers (\"al-zalimun\"), who are described as being in "manifest error" (\"dalal mubin\"). This phrase indicates that their wrongdoing and their deviation from the right path are clear and obvious, not only to God but potentially even to themselves and others.  They may attempt to approach God, perhaps seeking forgiveness or reward, but their continued persistence in wrongdoing makes their error apparent. The verse doesn't specify the exact context of \"coming to Us,\" which could refer to approaching God in prayer, in the afterlife during judgment, or even in this life through their actions and choices.  The emphasis is on the contrast between God's all-encompassing knowledge and the self-deception of those who persist in wrongdoing, despite the clarity of their error.
orig: أسمع بهم وأبصر يوم يأتوننا لكن الظالمون اليوم في ضلال مبين

translation: And warn them of the Day of Regret, when the matter will have been decided while they were in heedlessness and they did not believe.
interpretation: This verse speaks of a future Day of Regret (Yawm al-Hasrah), a time of intense remorse and anguish.  It emphasizes the finality of judgment ('when the matter will have been decided') and highlights the state of those being judged: heedlessness (ghafla) and disbelief (kufr).  'Heedlessness' here refers to a state of unawareness or distraction from the reality of God and the consequences of one's actions.  It implies that they were preoccupied with worldly matters and neglected their spiritual obligations.  Their disbelief further compounds their predicament, as it prevented them from accepting the truth and preparing for the inevitable judgment.  The verse serves as a powerful warning to turn away from heedlessness and embrace faith before it's too late, before the 'matter is decided' and regret becomes overwhelming.
orig: وأنذرهم يوم الحسرة إذ قضي الأمر وهم في غفلة وهم لا يؤمنون

translation: Indeed, it is We who will inherit the earth and whoever is on it, and to Us they will be returned.
interpretation: This verse asserts God's absolute sovereignty and ultimate authority over all creation.  "Inherit" here signifies not just taking possession after someone's death, but rather encompassing complete and ultimate control.  Everything on earth, including all living beings, is temporary and ultimately belongs to God.  The phrase "and to Us they will be returned" emphasizes the inevitable return of all beings to God for judgment and accountability after their time on earth. This highlights the cyclical nature of existence as understood within Islamic theology, with God as the beginning and the end. The verse serves as a reminder of God's power and the transient nature of worldly life, encouraging reflection on one's actions and responsibilities before returning to their Creator.
orig: إنا نحن نرث الأرض ومن عليها وإلينا يرجعون

translation: And mention in the Book [the story of] Abraham. Indeed, he was a truthful prophet.
interpretation: This verse instructs us to remember and reflect upon the story of Abraham (Ibrahim), highlighting two key attributes: his truthfulness (siddiq) and his prophethood (nabi).  'Siddiq' goes beyond simply telling the truth; it implies a deep, unwavering commitment to truthfulness in all aspects of life, a complete sincerity and integrity.  This characteristic made him a trustworthy messenger of God.  His status as a 'nabi' signifies that he was chosen by God to receive divine revelation and communicate it to his people.  The verse emphasizes the importance of learning from Abraham's example of unwavering faith, obedience, and commitment to truth, serving as a role model for believers.
orig: واذكر في الكتاب إبراهيم إنه كان صديقا نبيا

translation: When he said to his father, "O my father, why do you worship that which does not hear and does not see and will not benefit you at all?"
interpretation:
This verse depicts a pivotal moment in the Quranic narrative of Prophet Abraham (Ibrahim) and his father, Azar.  Abraham, having recognized the futility of idol worship, confronts his father with a powerful and logical argument.  The verse highlights Abraham's burgeoning monotheism against the backdrop of his father's polytheism.

Abraham's question emphasizes the illogical nature of worshipping idols, inanimate objects lacking the basic senses of hearing and sight, and utterly incapable of providing any real benefit or assistance. The phrase "will not benefit you at all" underscores the complete powerlessness of these idols.  It is a direct challenge to the prevailing belief system, emphasizing the absurdity of attributing divine qualities to such powerless entities.

This verse is not simply about idol worship, but about the search for truth and the courage to question established traditions.  It represents a crucial step in Abraham's spiritual journey and his eventual embrace of monotheism.  It also highlights the importance of using reason and intellect in matters of faith, showcasing Abraham's use of logic to challenge the prevailing beliefs of his time.  The respectful yet firm tone of "O my father" also demonstrates the importance of maintaining respect even while challenging deeply held beliefs of loved ones.  This verse serves as an inspiration for critical thinking and engaging in respectful dialogue about faith and belief.
orig: إذ قال لأبيه يا أبت لم تعبد ما لا يسمع ولا يبصر ولا يغني عنك شيئا

translation: O my father, indeed, [some] knowledge has come to me that has not come to you, so follow me; I will guide you to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Maryam (19:43), depicts the plea of the prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) to his father, Azar, who was an idol worshipper.  Ibrahim, having received divine knowledge and recognizing the falsehood of idolatry, implores his father to abandon his misguided beliefs and follow the path of monotheism.  The 'knowledge' mentioned refers to the understanding of God's oneness and the futility of worshipping idols. Ibrahim's words convey not only his newfound understanding but also his deep concern for his father's spiritual well-being.  The 'straight path' (siratan sawiyan) symbolizes the path of righteousness and truth, leading to God's favor and salvation.  This verse highlights the importance of seeking knowledge, standing up for truth even against family, and the compassionate effort to guide others towards the right path. It also demonstrates the respectful yet firm manner in which one can address elders even when disagreeing with them on fundamental beliefs.
orig: يا أبت إني قد جاءني من العلم ما لم يأتك فاتبعني أهدك صراطا سويا

translation: O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed, Satan has been disobedient to the Most Gracious (Ar-Rahman).
interpretation: This verse, often attributed to Prophet Abraham addressing his father Azar, encapsulates a powerful message about the nature of faith and obedience.  'Abt', meaning father, can refer to a biological father, but also a figure of authority or a respected elder.  Abraham's plea highlights the severity of worshipping anything other than the Most Gracious (Ar-Rahman), a name of God emphasizing His boundless mercy and encompassing compassion.  Satan, by his very nature, embodies disobedience to God's will.  Therefore, worshipping Satan is not only a rejection of God but also an embrace of rebellion against divine guidance.  The verse underscores the importance of discerning truth from falsehood and choosing the path of righteousness over the allure of disobedience, even when faced with pressure from those we respect.  It's a reminder of the constant struggle between good and evil and the individual's responsibility to choose allegiance to the Most Gracious.
orig: يا أبت لا تعبد الشيطان إن الشيطان كان للرحمن عصيا

translation: O my father, I fear that there will touch you a punishment from the Most Gracious so you would be to Satan a companion.
interpretation: This verse expresses deep concern and filial piety. A son (typically understood to be Prophet Noah's son) is pleading with his father, who has refused to believe in God's message. The son fears that his father's disbelief will lead to divine punishment.  "A punishment from the Most Gracious (Ar-Rahman)" refers to the impending flood.  The phrase "you would be to Satan a companion" signifies that by rejecting God's guidance, the father is essentially aligning himself with Satan, who represents disobedience and rebellion against God. It highlights the spiritual consequence of disbelief – becoming a follower of Satan, separated from God's mercy and protection. The verse underscores the tragic consequences of rejecting faith, even when warned by loved ones, and the profound sorrow it causes those who witness it.
orig: يا أبت إني أخاف أن يمسك عذاب من الرحمن فتكون للشيطان وليا

translation: He said, "Are you turning away from my gods, O Abraham? If you do not desist, I will surely stone you. So leave me for a long while."
interpretation: This verse depicts a confrontation between Abraham (Ibrahim) and a powerful figure, likely Nimrod, the king of Babylon.  Nimrod, enraged by Abraham's rejection of idolatry and his unwavering monotheism, threatens him with stoning, a common form of capital punishment at the time.  The phrase "my gods" highlights Nimrod's polytheistic beliefs and the prevailing societal norms that Abraham challenged.  Nimrod's demand that Abraham "desist" signifies his intolerance towards dissenting beliefs and his attempt to suppress Abraham's message. The threat of stoning demonstrates the severe consequences faced by those who dared to challenge the established religious order. The final part, "So leave me for a long while," can be interpreted in a couple of ways.  It could be an expulsion order, banishing Abraham from his land, or a dismissive command meant to silence him and prevent further religious debate.  This verse encapsulates the struggle between faith and tyranny, highlighting Abraham's courage in the face of persecution for his beliefs.
orig: قال أراغب أنت عن آلهتي يا إبراهيم لئن لم تنته لأرجمنك واهجرني مليا

translation: He said, "Peace be upon you. I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord. Indeed, He has been to me ever Gracious."
interpretation: This verse describes a powerful moment of forgiveness and divine grace.  It depicts someone, often identified as an angel or a prophet, encountering another person. The speaker offers not just a greeting of peace ("Salam alayka") but also a profound promise of intercession: "I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord." This demonstrates the speaker's closeness to God and their willingness to advocate on behalf of another. The concluding phrase, "Indeed, He has been to me ever Gracious" ("innahu kaana bi hafiyya"), reveals the speaker's deep gratitude and awareness of God's constant mercy and kindness towards them. This motivates their desire to extend that same mercy to others.  The verse highlights themes of divine forgiveness, intercession, and the importance of showing grace and compassion to others, inspired by God's own example. It also suggests the possibility of redemption and forgiveness even after wrongdoing, providing a message of hope and encouragement.
orig: قال سلام عليك سأستغفر لك ربي إنه كان بي حفيا

translation: And I will forsake you and what you invoke besides Allah, and I will invoke my Lord. Perhaps I will not be wretched by invoking my Lord.
interpretation: This verse expresses a decisive break with polytheism and a firm commitment to monotheism. The speaker declares their abandonment of all false deities and their exclusive devotion to Allah.  The phrase "what you invoke besides Allah" refers to idols, spirits, or any other entity worshipped alongside God.  The speaker also expresses hope that by solely invoking and relying upon Allah, they will be spared from misery and find guidance and salvation.  The uncertainty conveyed by "perhaps" (عسى) doesn't imply doubt in God's power, but rather reflects the speaker's humility and recognition that ultimate success is dependent on God's will and acceptance of their supplication. This verse can be interpreted as both a personal declaration of faith and a powerful message against idolatry, emphasizing the importance of sincere devotion to the one true God.
orig: وأعتزلكم وما تدعون من دون الله وأدعو ربي عسى ألا أكون بدعاء ربي شقيا

translation: Then, when he had withdrawn from them and from what they worshipped other than Allah, We granted him Isaac and Jacob, and each of them We made a prophet.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 19:49) speaks to the reward and blessings bestowed upon Abraham (Ibrahim) after his decisive break from idolatry and his exclusive devotion to Allah.  Abraham's withdrawal ('i'tizal') signifies not just a physical distancing from his polytheistic community, but also a complete rejection of their beliefs and practices. This separation was crucial to his spiritual purification and establishment of a monotheistic lineage.  As a reward for his steadfast faith and obedience, Allah blessed him with two sons, Isaac (Ishaq) and Jacob (Ya'qub), both of whom became significant prophets, continuing the legacy of monotheism and carrying forward the divine message. The verse highlights the importance of sincere devotion to God and the blessings that follow such commitment. It also emphasizes the hereditary nature of prophethood within Abraham's family, establishing a continuous chain of divine guidance through his descendants.
orig: فلما اعتزلهم وما يعبدون من دون الله وهبنا له إسحاق ويعقوب وكلا جعلنا نبيا

translation: And We bestowed upon them from Our mercy, and We made for them a high tongue [of praise].
interpretation: This verse speaks of God's bestowal of special favors upon certain individuals or a group.  "Mercy" (Rahma) in this context likely refers to both material and spiritual blessings, including prophecy, leadership, or intellectual prowess.  The "high tongue [of praise]" (Lisaan Sidq Aliya) is generally understood in two ways.  First, it could refer to a truthful and eloquent manner of speech, granting them the ability to effectively communicate truth and inspire others.  This could also relate to a position of honor and renown, where their words carried weight and influence. Second, it could refer to a widespread and lasting reputation for truthfulness and integrity, ensuring their message and legacy are respected and remembered. Ultimately, this verse emphasizes God's grace and the elevation of those chosen to receive His special blessings, allowing them to achieve great things and leave a positive impact on the world.
orig: ووهبنا لهم من رحمتنا وجعلنا لهم لسان صدق عليا

translation: And mention in the Book [the story of] Moses. Indeed, he was chosen, and he was a messenger and a prophet.
interpretation: This verse instructs us to recall and reflect upon the story of Moses as recounted in the Quran. The emphasis on Moses's status highlights his significance in Islamic tradition.  "Chosen" (mukhlasan) signifies his sincere devotion and purity, suggesting a close relationship with God.  Furthermore, identifying him as both a "messenger" (rasulan) and a "prophet" (nabiyan) underscores his dual role: he delivered God's message (Sharia) to his people and also received divine revelations, including prophecies about the future.  The verse encourages believers to learn from Moses's life, his steadfast faith in the face of adversity, and his unwavering commitment to God's commands. This serves as a reminder of the importance of piety, obedience, and trust in God's plan.
orig: واذكر في الكتاب موسى إنه كان مخلصا وكان رسولا نبيا

translation: And We called to him from the right side of the Mount, and We drew him near, [to Us], in communion.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Prophet Moses' encounter with God at Mount Sinai (referred to here as at-Tur).  "The right side of the Mount" can be interpreted both literally and metaphorically.  Literally, it may refer to a specific location on the mountain. Metaphorically, the right side is often associated with honor and closeness, suggesting the privileged nature of Moses' communication with God.  "We drew him near" signifies the intimate nature of this divine encounter, where Moses was brought into a state of close communion (najya) with God.  This communion likely refers to the revelation of the divine law and commandments to Moses.  The term "najya" implies a confidential and intimate conversation, highlighting the special relationship between God and Moses and the sacred nature of the revelation being imparted.
orig: وناديناه من جانب الطور الأيمن وقربناه نجيا

translation: And We granted him from Our mercy his brother Aaron, a prophet.
interpretation: This verse speaks of God's mercy and favor upon Moses by granting him his brother Aaron as a prophet.  It highlights the supportive role Aaron played in Moses's prophetic mission.  Aaron's prophethood was a gift not just to Moses, but also to the Children of Israel, as Aaron's eloquence and steadfastness complemented Moses's strengths and helped convey God's message effectively.  The phrase "from Our mercy" emphasizes that Aaron's prophethood was a divine bestowal and a blessing intended to ease Moses's burden and strengthen the prophetic message's impact.
orig: ووهبنا له من رحمتنا أخاه هارون نبيا

translation: And mention in the Book, Ishmael. Indeed, he was true to his promise and he was a messenger and a prophet.
interpretation: This verse instructs us to remember and learn from the story of Ishmael (Isma'il), son of Abraham (Ibrahim).  The verse highlights two key characteristics of Ishmael: his unwavering commitment to his promises (صادق الوعد) and his status as a divinely appointed messenger and prophet (رسولا نبيا).  'True to his promise' can refer to various aspects of Ishmael's life, including his patience and submission during the near-sacrifice, his dedication to God's commands, and his trustworthiness in his dealings with others. His designation as both a 'messenger' (رسول) and a 'prophet' (نبي) signifies that God communicated with him and entrusted him with delivering divine messages and guidance to his people. The verse underscores the importance of Ishmael's example as a model of piety, faithfulness, and devotion to God, encouraging believers to emulate his virtues.
orig: واذكر في الكتاب إسماعيل إنه كان صادق الوعد وكان رسولا نبيا

translation: And he used to enjoin his family with prayer and charity, and he was acceptable in the sight of his Lord.
interpretation: This verse speaks of a righteous individual, often understood to be Prophet Abraham (Ibrahim), although the specific person isn't named here.  It highlights two key pillars of Islam: prayer (salat) and charity (zakat). The phrase "enjoin his family" indicates not only his personal practice but also his active role in guiding and encouraging his household to uphold these religious obligations. This emphasizes the importance of family in Islamic teachings and the responsibility of individuals to cultivate faith within their homes.  The concluding phrase, "acceptable in the sight of his Lord," signifies God's approval of his actions and character.  This suggests that consistent observance of prayer and charity, coupled with righteous conduct, leads to divine acceptance and pleasure. It's a reminder that true piety extends beyond personal practice to encompass the well-being and spiritual guidance of one's family.
orig: وكان يأمر أهله بالصلاة والزكاة وكان عند ربه مرضيا

translation: And mention in the Book, Idris. Indeed, he was a truthful prophet.
interpretation: This verse refers to the prophet Idris, commanding the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to mention him in the Quran.  It affirms Idris's status as a prophet and highlights his defining characteristic of being "siddiq", often translated as "truthful" or "righteous".  This suggests a strong commitment to truthfulness in both his words and deeds, signifying a deep piety and unwavering adherence to God's message. The verse encourages reflection on Idris's exemplary life as a source of inspiration and guidance for believers.  Some scholars connect Idris with the biblical figure Enoch, but the Quran provides limited details about his life and narrative.  The emphasis is on remembering him as a truthful prophet, reinforcing the importance of truth and righteousness in Islamic teachings.
orig: واذكر في الكتاب إدريس إنه كان صديقا نبيا

translation: And We raised him to a high position.
interpretation:
This verse, depending on the context, can refer to several figures mentioned in the Qur'an.  Most commonly, it refers to the Prophet Idris (Enoch).  Other interpretations link it to Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) or even Jesus (peace be upon him), though less frequently.  The "high position" mentioned can be interpreted in several ways:

* **Physical elevation:**  This could refer to a literal ascension to heaven, as traditionally understood in the case of Prophet Idris.
* **Spiritual elevation:** This refers to an elevated status in the eyes of God, achieved through righteousness, piety, and devotion.  This applies to all prophets and messengers.
* **Exalted status among people:** This interpretation refers to the high esteem and respect granted to a prophet by their community or followers. 

Without the surrounding verses (Surah and Ayah number), it's impossible to definitively say who "him" refers to and the precise nature of the "high position."  The specific context is crucial for accurate interpretation. Therefore, providing the full context, including the surah and ayah number, would allow for a more precise and nuanced understanding.
orig: ورفعناه مكانا عليا

translation: Those are the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favor - from among the prophets, of the descendants of Adam, and of those We carried [in the ship] with Noah, and of the descendants of Abraham and Israel, and of those whom We guided and chose. When the verses of the Most Merciful were recited to them, they would fall down in prostration and weeping.
interpretation: This verse describes the characteristics of those who have earned Allah's favor.  It highlights their lineage and spiritual status. They come from the lineages of prominent prophets like Adam, Noah, Abraham, and Jacob (Israel), indicating a connection to a divinely guided heritage. Beyond lineage, it emphasizes their personal qualities: they are those whom God guided and specifically chose.  The key characteristic that distinguishes them is their deep humility and emotional response to divine revelation. When they hear the verses of the Qur'an, they are moved to prostrate themselves in submission and weep out of awe, gratitude, and a profound understanding of God's majesty and mercy. This prostration and weeping is not merely a ritualistic act, but a genuine expression of their inner state, reflecting a heart filled with love and reverence for God. This verse underscores the importance of both lineage and personal piety in attaining God's favor. It serves as an example for believers to cultivate similar humility and responsiveness to the divine word.
orig: أولئك الذين أنعم الله عليهم من النبيين من ذرية آدم وممن حملنا مع نوح ومن ذرية إبراهيم وإسرائيل وممن هدينا واجتبينا إذا تتلى عليهم آيات الرحمن خروا سجدا وبكيا

translation: Then there succeeded them a generation who neglected prayer and pursued their desires; so they are going to meet perdition.
interpretation: This verse speaks of a generation that came after a righteous one, and how they fell into corruption.  'Neglecting prayer (أضاعوا الصلاة)' doesn't necessarily mean abandoning it entirely, but could also refer to performing it inadequately, without sincerity or proper attention.  'Pursuing their desires (واتبعوا الشهوات)' refers to prioritizing worldly pleasures and impulses over their religious obligations and moral principles.  The consequence of this neglect and indulgence is 'meeting perdition (فسوف يلقون غيا),' which signifies encountering a disastrous outcome, likely referring to punishment in the afterlife. The verse serves as a warning against straying from the path of righteousness and highlights the importance of prayer and self-control in maintaining a strong spiritual connection.
orig: فخلف من بعدهم خلف أضاعوا الصلاة واتبعوا الشهوات فسوف يلقون غيا

translation: Except for those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds; such will enter Paradise and they will not be wronged at all.
interpretation: This verse highlights the core principles of Islamic belief and the path to salvation. It emphasizes that even if someone has committed sins in the past, they are not eternally condemned.  Sincere repentance (tawba), which involves genuine remorse and a firm resolve to change one's ways, coupled with true faith (iman) in God and His message, and followed by performing righteous actions (amal salih), paves the way for forgiveness and entry into Paradise (Jannah).  The promise of not being wronged at all ('wala yuzlamuna shay'an') underscores God's perfect justice and mercy. It signifies that those who follow this path will receive their full reward and will not be deprived of anything they are due in the afterlife. It also implies freedom from any form of injustice or oppression in Paradise.
orig: إلا من تاب وآمن وعمل صالحا فأولئك يدخلون الجنة ولا يظلمون شيئا

translation: Gardens of Eden, which the Most Gracious promised His servants in the unseen. Indeed, His promise is ever coming to pass.
interpretation: This verse speaks of Paradise (Jannah), specifically referred to as 'Gardens of Eden' (جنات عدن), highlighting its blissful and pristine nature.  The promise of these gardens is made by 'the Most Gracious' (الرحمن), one of the most beautiful names of God emphasizing His boundless mercy and compassion. This promise is made to 'His servants' (عباده), indicating that Paradise is a reward for those who believe in Him and strive to follow His guidance. The phrase 'in the unseen' (بالغيب) signifies that Paradise is a reality beyond our current perception and comprehension, a realm we cannot fully grasp in this worldly life. It emphasizes the importance of faith and trust in God's promises.  Finally, the affirmation 'Indeed, His promise is ever coming to pass' (إنه كان وعده مأتيا)  reinforces the certainty and inevitability of the fulfillment of God's promise. It assures believers that Paradise is not a mere fantasy but a guaranteed reality for those who earn it. This verse offers comfort and hope, encouraging believers to persevere in their faith and good deeds, knowing that their ultimate reward is secure in God's hands.
orig: جنات عدن التي وعد الرحمن عباده بالغيب إنه كان وعده مأتيا

translation: They will not hear therein any ill speech or any falsehood, but only [greetings of] peace, and they will have their provision therein, morning and evening.
interpretation:
This verse describes the blissful nature of Paradise (Jannah) promised to the righteous in the afterlife.  Several key aspects are highlighted:

* **Absence of negativity:**  "They will not hear therein any ill speech or any falsehood" signifies a complete absence of hurtful words, lies, gossip, or any form of harmful communication. This suggests a realm of perfect harmony and tranquility where only positive and truthful words are uttered. The phrase "except greetings of peace" (إلا سلاما) emphasizes this, indicating that the only sounds heard are those expressing peace, well-being, and security.

* **Abundant and timely sustenance:** "And they will have their provision therein, morning and evening" illustrates the constant and readily available sustenance provided to the inhabitants of Paradise. This provision is not just limited to physical nourishment but encompasses all forms of blessings and enjoyment, delivered consistently without any effort or worry. The mention of "morning and evening" signifies continuous and unfailing provision.

* **State of complete contentment:** Taken together, these aspects depict a state of complete peace, satisfaction, and security in Paradise.  The absence of negative speech highlights the psychological and emotional serenity experienced by its inhabitants, while the continuous provision of sustenance demonstrates their material well-being. This verse, therefore, paints a picture of a perfect existence free from the trials and tribulations of earthly life.
orig: لا يسمعون فيها لغوا إلا سلاما ولهم رزقهم فيها بكرة وعشيا

translation: That is the Paradise which We will give as inheritance to those of Our servants who were righteous.
interpretation: This verse speaks of Paradise (Jannah) as an inheritance bestowed upon those servants of God who possessed taqwa.  Taqwa is often translated as righteousness, piety, or God-consciousness, but it encompasses more than just outward actions. It implies a deep inner state of awareness and reverence for God, which manifests in both avoiding what God has forbidden and actively pursuing what He has commanded. The verse emphasizes that Paradise is not simply earned or achieved through deeds alone but is granted as a gift, an inheritance, from God to those who cultivate this state of taqwa.  The use of the word "inheritance" (نورث) suggests a sense of belonging, permanence, and an enduring relationship with God in the hereafter.  It also highlights the immense generosity and mercy of God, who bestows this ultimate reward upon His righteous servants.
orig: تلك الجنة التي نورث من عبادنا من كان تقيا

translation: And We do not descend except by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs what is before us and what is behind us and what is between that, and your Lord is never forgetful.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute authority and control of God (Allah).  It asserts that the revelation (represented here by the word 'descend', often understood as referring to the Angel Gabriel bringing the message to the Prophet Muhammad) is not arbitrary or accidental, but occurs solely by God's will and command.  The phrase 'To Him belongs what is before us and what is behind us and what is between that' signifies God's encompassing knowledge and power over all time – past, present, and future.  Everything that has happened, is happening, and will happen is within His awareness and control. This reinforces the idea that the revelation is part of God's grand plan and is perfectly timed and orchestrated.  The concluding phrase, 'and your Lord is never forgetful,' reassures that God is mindful of all things and will not neglect or overlook any aspect of His creation or His plan.  In the context of revelation, this assures that the message is complete and preserved, and that God is aware of the needs and circumstances of humanity.
orig: وما نتنزل إلا بأمر ربك له ما بين أيدينا وما خلفنا وما بين ذلك وما كان ربك نسيا

translation: Lord of the heavens and the earth and that which is between them, so worship Him and be patient in His worship. Do you know of any who is similar to Him?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute sovereignty of God. He is the Lord, the Master, and the Creator of everything in existence – the heavens, the earth, and all that lies within.  This encompassing dominion demands our exclusive worship and devotion.  The verse also highlights the importance of steadfastness and perseverance in worshipping God. This 'patience' (sabr) isn't merely endurance but implies a steadfast commitment to faith and obedience, especially in the face of difficulties or distractions.  The rhetorical question at the end, "Do you know of any who is similar to Him?", powerfully affirms God's uniqueness and incomparability. It reinforces the central message of Tawhid (Oneness of God) – there is no deity worthy of worship except Him. It invites reflection on the futility of ascribing divine attributes to anything or anyone else,  emphasizing the unmatched power, knowledge, and majesty of God.
orig: رب السماوات والأرض وما بينهما فاعبده واصطبر لعبادته هل تعلم له سميا

translation: And man says, "When I am dead, will I then be brought forth alive?"
interpretation: This verse captures the inherent human skepticism and questioning surrounding the concept of resurrection or life after death.  The Arabic word "أإذا" emphasizes the 'when' and suggests a sense of doubt or disbelief.  Man, in his earthly existence, finds it difficult to grasp the possibility of life after physical death.  This verse highlights the challenge of faith and the human struggle to reconcile the finite nature of earthly life with the promise of an eternal afterlife.  It's a rhetorical question expressing the common human doubt rather than a genuine inquiry, reflecting the difficulty of comprehending something beyond our tangible experience.
orig: ويقول الإنسان أإذا ما مت لسوف أخرج حيا

translation: Does man not remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the utter powerlessness and non-existence of humanity before God's act of creation.  It serves as a reminder of our humble origins and complete dependence on God.  The rhetorical question highlights the irony of human forgetfulness regarding this fundamental truth.  It encourages reflection on our existence and fosters a sense of gratitude and awe towards the divine Creator. The phrase "when he was nothing" (لم يك شيئا) underscores the absolute nothingness from which humanity emerged, emphasizing the magnitude of God's creative power and the profound ontological shift that creation represents.  This can be interpreted both literally as non-existence before physical birth and metaphorically as a state of ignorance and spiritual void before receiving divine guidance.
orig: أولا يذكر الإنسان أنا خلقناه من قبل ولم يك شيئا

translation: So by your Lord, We will surely gather them and the devils; then We will surely bring them forth around Hell, kneeling.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the certainty and totality of God's judgment.  The oath "by your Lord" underscores the seriousness of the declaration. The verse describes the gathering of both humans (implied by the earlier context in the surah) and devils, highlighting their shared accountability before God.  The phrase "bring them forth around Hell, kneeling" paints a vivid picture of their humiliation and helplessness on the Day of Judgment.  It signifies their ultimate defeat and submission to divine justice. This imagery underscores the consequences of rejecting God's guidance and following the path of evil, a path shared by both rebellious humans and devils.
orig: فوربك لنحشرنهم والشياطين ثم لنحضرنهم حول جهنم جثيا

translation: Then We will surely seize from every sect those of them who were most intense in their defiance of the Most Gracious (Allah).
interpretation: This verse speaks of a future judgment. After death and resurrection, God will identify and single out from every group or sect those individuals who were the most obstinate and rebellious against Him, specifically in their rejection of His mercy and grace (represented by the name "Ar-Rahman", the Most Gracious).  "Seize" implies a firm grasp and accountability for their actions.  The verse highlights the importance of accepting God's mercy and warns against hardened defiance against His divine attributes, emphasizing that such defiance will ultimately lead to severe consequences.
orig: ثم لننزعن من كل شيعة أيهم أشد على الرحمن عتيا

translation: Then surely We are more knowing of those who are more deserving of burning therein.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's absolute knowledge and just judgment.  It follows a passage usually understood to be describing the punishment of Hell.  The phrase "more deserving of burning therein" (أولى بها صليا) implies a degree of culpability. God, being all-knowing, is the ultimate judge of who deserves this punishment based on their actions and choices in life.  The verse asserts that divine justice will be perfectly applied, and no one will be unjustly punished. The use of "We" (نحن) reinforces God's majesty and authority in this judgment.  Some interpretations connect this to the previous verses, highlighting that those who deny the truth and follow falsehood are the ones most deserving of this punishment.  It serves as a warning and reminder of the consequences of rejecting God's guidance.
orig: ثم لنحن أعلم بالذين هم أولى بها صليا

translation: And there is not one of you except he will enter it. That is upon your Lord a decreed matter.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Maryam (19:71), speaks of the inevitability of everyone facing judgment before God.  The "it" referred to in the verse is often interpreted as Hellfire, implying that everyone will initially enter it.  However, this doesn't mean eternal damnation for all.  Many Islamic scholars understand this passage to mean a brief, symbolic passing through Hellfire, where the just will quickly pass over it like a bridge, while the wrongdoers will remain.  This aligns with other verses emphasizing God's justice and mercy.  Essentially, the verse emphasizes that no one escapes divine accountability. Everyone, regardless of belief or deed, will stand before God and be judged.  The ultimate fate, however, depends on individual actions and God's mercy.
orig: وإن منكم إلا واردها كان على ربك حتما مقضيا

translation: Then We will save those who were righteous and leave the wrongdoers therein, humbled.
interpretation: This verse describes the ultimate fate of the righteous and the wrongdoers on the Day of Judgement.  "Those who were righteous" (الذين اتقوا - *alladhina ittaqaw*) refers to those who feared God and lived their lives according to His guidance, embodying piety and awareness of divine accountability.  Their reward is salvation (ننجي - *nunajjee*) from the horrors of the Day of Judgement.  Conversely, the wrongdoers (الظالمين - *al-zalimeen*), those who transgressed against God's laws and oppressed others, are left behind (نذر - *nathar*) in the state of judgement (فيها - *feeha*),  in a state of humiliation and helplessness (جثيا - *jathiyya*). This word paints a vivid image of their abject condition, possibly kneeling or prostrated, signifying their utter defeat and powerlessness before divine justice.  The verse emphasizes the stark contrast between the destiny of the righteous and the wrongdoers, highlighting the importance of righteousness and the severe consequences of wrongdoing in the Islamic worldview.
orig: ثم ننجي الذين اتقوا ونذر الظالمين فيها جثيا

translation: And when Our clear verses are recited to them, those who disbelieve say to those who believe, "Which of the two groups is better in position and finer in assembly?"
interpretation: This verse describes a common scenario during the time of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). When the clear and evident verses of the Qur'an were recited, highlighting the truth and guidance of Islam, those who disbelieved would not engage with the message's content or consider its profound implications. Instead, they resorted to a superficial and worldly comparison, asking the believers which group appeared to be more prosperous and had a more impressive social gathering.  This reflects their focus on immediate, material advantages and social status as measures of success and truth, rather than divine guidance and the promise of the hereafter.  They judged based on outward appearances, ignoring the spiritual reality and the long-term consequences of their disbelief.  The verse highlights the shallowness of their criteria for judgment and their inability to grasp the true meaning of a 'good position,' which, in the Islamic context, refers to nearness to God and the eternal bliss of Paradise, not worldly status or wealth.  The 'finer assembly' (nadiya) also refers to a gathering of elegance and comfort, indicating that the disbelievers prided themselves on their worldly enjoyment, oblivious to the true assembly of believers in the presence of God in the hereafter.
orig: وإذا تتلى عليهم آياتنا بينات قال الذين كفروا للذين آمنوا أي الفريقين خير مقاما وأحسن نديا

translation: And how many a generation have We destroyed before them who were better in furnishings and in appearance?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the transient nature of worldly possessions and power.  It highlights that previous civilizations, even those who possessed superior wealth, resources ("furnishings"), and outward grandeur ("appearance"), were ultimately destroyed by God. This serves as a warning against arrogance and complacency, reminding us that material possessions and outward appearances are not indicators of divine favor or protection. True strength and lasting value lie in piety and obedience to God, not in worldly achievements. The verse also points to the cyclical nature of history and the recurring theme of rise and fall of civilizations, a pattern often linked to moral decay and forgetting the divine.
orig: وكم أهلكنا قبلهم من قرن هم أحسن أثاثا ورئيا

translation: Say, [O Muhammad], "To whoever is in error - let the Most Merciful extend for him an extension - until, when they see that which they are promised - either punishment or the Hour - they will surely know who is in the worst position and weaker in forces [or supporters]."
interpretation: This verse speaks to the divine wisdom in allowing a period of respite for those who disbelieve or are in error. God, the Most Merciful (Ar-Rahman), grants them a 'mada' - an extension or postponement - before the consequences of their actions become manifest. This 'mada' isn't a license to continue in wrongdoing but rather an opportunity for reflection and potential return to the right path. The verse emphasizes that this period is finite. Eventually, they will face the reality of what they were warned about - either the punishment in this life or the ultimate reckoning on the Day of Judgment (the Hour).  At that point, the reality of their situation will become undeniably clear. They will understand the true nature of their 'place' (literally and metaphorically) – a place of hardship and vulnerability. They will also realize the weakness of their 'forces' – be it their worldly allies, their perceived power, or their misguided beliefs.  This weakness is contrasted with the ultimate power and authority of God.  The verse subtly warns against complacency and highlights the eventual triumph of truth over falsehood. It also serves as a reminder of God's mercy in delaying punishment, giving individuals the time and opportunity to reconsider their choices before it's too late.
orig: قل من كان في الضلالة فليمدد له الرحمن مدا حتى إذا رأوا ما يوعدون إما العذاب وإما الساعة فسيعلمون من هو شر مكانا وأضعف جندا

translation: And Allah increases in guidance those who are guided. And the enduring good deeds are better to your Lord for reward and better for recourse.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the continuous and increasing nature of guidance from Allah. Those who actively seek and follow the path of righteousness will receive even more guidance from Him. It highlights the importance of "al-baqiyat as-salihat" which are often translated as "enduring good deeds." These are actions that have a lasting impact, both in this world and the hereafter, such as acts of charity, knowledge-seeking, and righteous conduct.  The verse clarifies that these enduring good deeds are superior in reward from Allah and provide a better ultimate return or destination (literally "recourse" or "place to return to").  This suggests that while all good deeds are rewarded, those with lasting impact hold a special place and contribute significantly to a believer's ultimate well-being in the afterlife.
orig: ويزيد الله الذين اهتدوا هدى والباقيات الصالحات خير عند ربك ثوابا وخير مردا

translation: Have you seen the one who disbelieves in Our signs and says, "I will surely be given wealth and children"?
interpretation:
This verse describes an individual who rejects God's signs (ayat), which can refer to both the verses of the Quran and the observable phenomena in the universe that point towards a Creator.  This individual's disbelief is coupled with a materialistic and worldly focus, expressed in their confident assertion that they will acquire abundant wealth and offspring.  This statement can be interpreted in several ways:

1. **Arrogance and self-reliance:** The individual believes their prosperity is solely due to their own efforts and merits, disregarding God's role in providing sustenance. They prioritize material possessions and family lineage over spiritual growth and connection with God.

2. **A challenge to God's authority:** Their claim may be seen as a direct challenge to God's power and judgment.  They believe they are immune to any divine consequences for their disbelief and will prosper regardless.

3. **A false sense of security:**  The individual finds comfort and security in material wealth and children, mistakenly believing these things will protect them from hardship and ultimate accountability in the afterlife.  This highlights the fleeting nature of worldly possessions and the importance of seeking true security in faith and good deeds.

The verse doesn't explicitly state the outcome of this person's actions, but it sets the stage for a deeper discussion on the consequences of prioritizing worldly gains over spiritual truth and the importance of recognizing God's ultimate authority.
orig: أفرأيت الذي كفر بآياتنا وقال لأوتين مالا وولدا

translation: Does he have knowledge of the unseen, or has he taken a covenant with the Most Gracious (God)?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical question challenging the claims of false prophets or those who claim to have divine knowledge.  It questions the source of their supposed knowledge of the future or unseen realities.  The first part, "Does he have knowledge of the unseen (al-ghayb)?" directly challenges the possibility of anyone other than God possessing knowledge of the unseen. The second part, "or has he taken a covenant with the Most Gracious (ar-Rahman)?" suggests that a true prophet's authority comes from a divine covenant or agreement with God, not from personal insight into the unseen.  Since such a covenant is exclusive to true messengers of God, the verse implies that those who claim knowledge of the unseen without divine appointment are imposters. The verse serves as a warning against blindly following individuals who make such claims, urging listeners to seek truth and guidance from God alone.
orig: أطلع الغيب أم اتخذ عند الرحمن عهدا

translation: No indeed! We will record what he says and extend for him a prolonged punishment.
interpretation: This verse reflects a strong divine rebuke and warning.  "Kalla" is an emphatic negation, dismissing the previous statement or attitude, which likely involved denial or defiance of God. The verse asserts that God meticulously records every word uttered, emphasizing His omniscience and accountability. The phrase "extend for him a prolonged punishment" signifies a severe and continuous consequence for such transgression. This doesn't necessarily refer to immediate worldly punishment, but rather highlights the certainty and gravity of ultimate divine judgment.  It underscores that words carry weight and have consequences in the divine reckoning.
orig: كلا سنكتب ما يقول ونمد له من العذاب مدا

translation: And We will inherit what he says and he will come to Us alone.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the ultimate accountability of each individual before God.  "What he says" refers not just to literal speech, but encompasses all a person's deeds, beliefs, and intentions throughout their life. Everything they've accumulated, materially and otherwise, is left behind.  The phrase "he will come to Us alone" emphasizes the solitary nature of facing divine judgment.  Stripped of worldly possessions, social status, and even family, each person stands alone before God to answer for their actions and choices.  It highlights the personal and direct relationship between the Creator and each individual soul.
orig: ونرثه ما يقول ويأتينا فردا

translation: And they have taken besides Allah [false] deities that they would be for them [a source of] honor.
interpretation: This verse highlights the human tendency to seek power and validation from sources other than God.  People throughout history have created idols, both physical and abstract,  attributing to them the power to bring honor, status, or protection.  These "false deities" can range from actual statues or images to concepts like wealth, fame, power, or even ideologies. The verse suggests that this pursuit is ultimately misplaced. True honor and strength, according to the Quranic worldview, come only from God.  By seeking it elsewhere, people are not only diverting their devotion from the true source but are also likely to be disappointed, as these substitutes can never truly fulfill the deep human longing for meaning and security.
orig: واتخذوا من دون الله آلهة ليكونوا لهم عزا

translation: No! They will soon disbelieve in their worship, and they will be against it.
interpretation: This verse speaks of the hypocrisy and eventual rejection of faith by some.  "Their worship" (عبادتهم - 'ibadatihim) can refer to several things depending on the context of the surrounding verses. It could mean idols or false deities they initially venerated, suggesting a future abandonment even of those. Alternatively, it might refer to the true message or prophets they initially seemed to accept, indicating a later turning away from the truth.  The phrase "and they will be against it" (ويكونون عليهم ضدا - wa yakūnu 'alayhim ḍiddā) emphasizes the active opposition and hostility they will develop towards that which they once professed to believe. This verse highlights the potential for insincerity in faith and the possibility of regression from belief to disbelief.  It serves as a warning against superficial adherence to religious principles and emphasizes the importance of genuine conviction and steadfastness.
orig: كلا سيكفرون بعبادتهم ويكونون عليهم ضدا

translation: Have you not seen that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with incitement?
interpretation:
This verse describes God's interaction with disbelievers through the agency of devils (shayāṭīn).  The Arabic word "tu'izzuhum" (تؤزهم) from the root "'az" (أز) implies a persistent and intense incitement, a constant urging towards wrongdoing.  This doesn't mean disbelievers are stripped of free will, rather, it highlights the influence of negative forces upon their decisions.  The verse can be interpreted in several ways:

1. **Whispers and Temptations:**  The devils whisper temptations and doubts into the hearts of disbelievers, encouraging them to reject faith and engage in sinful actions.

2. **Internal Struggles:**  The "devils" could also refer to the inner demons or base desires that lead individuals astray.  This interpretation aligns with the psychological understanding of internal conflicts and negative thoughts that can drive people away from righteousness.

3. **External Influences:** The devils may represent negative external influences such as corrupt leaders, harmful ideologies, or peer pressure that contribute to disbelief and immoral behavior.

4. **A Test and Trial:** The sending of the devils can be seen as a test from God.  It reveals the choices people make when confronted with negative influences and temptations, showcasing their true inclinations.

The opening question, "Have you not seen...?" is a rhetorical device drawing attention to an observable reality.  It invites reflection on the consequences of disbelief and the forces that contribute to it. It also implies that the truth is evident for those who seek it, but those inclined towards disbelief will be further driven towards it by these influences.  Ultimately, the verse serves as a reminder of the constant struggle between good and evil, and the importance of seeking refuge in God from negative influences, both internal and external.
orig: ألم تر أنا أرسلنا الشياطين على الكافرين تؤزهم أزا

translation: So do not hasten against them; We are only counting for them a [limited] number [of days].
interpretation: This verse emphasizes patience and divine timing. It often appears in contexts where prophets or believers feel a sense of urgency for divine punishment to befall their adversaries. The verse reassures them that God is fully aware and in control. He is keeping count of their actions and will deliver justice at the appointed time.  'Counting' can refer to counting their deeds, the days until their reckoning, or both.  The message is not to lose heart or rush the divine process.  Trust in God's plan and His perfect timing.
orig: فلا تعجل عليهم إنما نعد لهم عدا

translation: On the Day when We gather the righteous to the Most Merciful like a delegation.
interpretation: This verse depicts the honorable status of the righteous (\"al-muttaqeen\") on the Day of Judgment.  They will be gathered and presented to God, the Most Merciful (\"al-Rahman\"), not as scattered individuals or a judged multitude, but as a respected delegation (\"wafdan\").  This term 'wafdan' carries connotations of honor, special treatment, and being received with courtesy and esteem. It suggests a formal presentation of honored guests to a high authority.  The verse emphasizes the reward of piety and righteousness, highlighting the intimate and honored relationship the righteous will have with God in the afterlife.  It offers a powerful image of comfort and hope for believers, assuring them of divine grace and a privileged position in the presence of the Most Merciful.
orig: يوم نحشر المتقين إلى الرحمن وفدا

translation: And We will drive the criminals to Hell, thirsty.
interpretation: This verse depicts the fate of those deemed 'criminals' in the Quranic context.  The Arabic word 'ونسوق' implies a driving or herding, suggesting a forced and humiliating march towards their punishment. 'المجرمين' refers to those who have committed crimes against God's laws and disregarded His guidance. 'جهنم' is Hell, the ultimate destination of punishment.  The word 'وردا' describes their state as 'thirsty,' which can be interpreted on multiple levels.  Physically, it suggests the intense heat and suffering of Hell.  Spiritually, it can represent an unquenchable thirst for good, for God's mercy, or for the life they squandered. This thirst symbolizes the ultimate deprivation and despair of those who rejected faith and righteous action in their earthly lives.
orig: ونسوق المجرمين إلى جهنم وردا

translation: They do not possess the power of intercession, except for he who has taken a covenant with the Most Gracious (Allah).
interpretation: This verse discusses the concept of intercession on the Day of Judgment.  It emphasizes that no one can intercede for another with God except those whom God has specifically granted this privilege.  The "covenant with the Most Gracious" likely refers to individuals who have lived lives of exceptional piety and obedience to God's commands, earning His favor and the right to intercede.  This reinforces the Islamic principle that salvation is ultimately dependent on God's mercy and that true intercession can only come through His permission. Some interpretations specify Prophets, angels, and righteous believers as those who might have this covenant. It highlights the absolute authority of God and the limitations on the power of created beings, even those considered elevated in status.
orig: لا يملكون الشفاعة إلا من اتخذ عند الرحمن عهدا

translation: And they say, "The Most Gracious has taken [for Himself] a son."
interpretation: This verse refers to the pre-Islamic Arabian belief, and also accusations from other Abrahamic faiths at the time, that God had offspring.  The Quran strongly rejects this idea, emphasizing the absolute oneness and transcendence of God (Allah), the Most Gracious (Ar-Rahman).  Having a child implies physicality, limitations, and need for a partner, all of which are incompatible with God's divine nature.  The verse highlights the gravity of this misconception, as it ascribes human limitations to the limitless Creator.  It sets the stage for the Quran's consistent emphasis on tawhid (the oneness of God) as a core principle of Islam.
orig: وقالوا اتخذ الرحمن ولدا

translation: You have certainly come with something outrageous!
